Country of Publication: India Kuladīpikā (Uttaraṣaṭka), the Illuminator of the Six Vidyās || Kuladīpikā ||
The Northern Hexad from the Kuladīpikā.
The Lamp of the Family, Illuminating the Six Vidyās.
It has a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Above that, however, is the subtle crest (śikhā), which is the supreme digit (kalā) whose nature is consciousness.
One should contemplate oneself as united with it, having become one with it.
Proceeding by way of the path of the *hamsa* according to the sequence of the piercing of the *liṅgas*,
[one reaches that which] resembles ten million suns and is as cool as ten million moons.
The nectar situated within the emission, characterized by supreme bliss,
raining down a stream rich with intense red splendor.
Having drunk the divine nectar of the *kula*, one should enter the *kula* once again;
one should likewise go to the *akula* by means of the union with the *mātrā*, and not otherwise.
And that, O Supreme Goddess, is designated as the vital breath (prāṇa) in this tantra;
it is also called the upward thrust (udghāta) when it touches the end of the breath.
By practicing thus with daily certainty,
one is liberated from the flood of sufferings of old age and death, and from the bondage of existence.
The fourfold creation which proceeds within that womb dissolves back into it again, beginning with the Fire of Time (Kālāgni) and ending with Śiva.
That indeed is the supreme Yonimudrā; its binding has been proclaimed.
What on earth cannot be accomplished merely by the binding of this mudrā?
O Goddess of gods, he who recites the mantra in one way but performs the ritual in another way does not attain success; this is the truth, the truth, again and again.
Those mantras which are severed, obstructed, paralyzed, or intensely pinned down;
those that are burnt, deprived of their autonomy, defiled, or disregarded.

Those overcome by intoxication, those in deep sleep, those who have fainted, those who are distressed, as well as the dull-witted, children, the elderly, the experienced, and those censured for their youth;
Those who stand on the side of the enemy, who are seedless and devoid of reality,
who are bereft of their portions and cut into a hundred pieces;
When joined with this ritual procedure and employed by the preceptor, they all bestow accomplishment and liberation without delay.
Whatever form of syllable, whether auspicious or inauspicious, the mantra-practitioner utters,
each of those is accomplished without effort through the binding of the *yonimudrā*.
Having initiated [the disciple] according to the rule and having consecrated him a thousandfold, he then becomes qualified in this tantra, O Goddess; it cannot be otherwise.

Having indeed heated [the disciple] for a long time through the arrangement of mudrās and maṇḍalas, as well as recitation, fire-offerings, vows, and so forth, and having recognized his unwavering devotion;
Having understood his renunciation, strength, and suffering, one should then reveal that [truth] to him;
or else, O Goddess, at this time, the command of the Goddess arises.
In this regard, one should say: "If one explains this knowledge otherwise, one shall go to hell;
however, there is no savior for him who bestows it without having first examined [the recipient]."
Therefore, if one wishes to live for a long time, one should give only after careful examination,
O beautiful lady, even if one has committed thousands of innumerable sins.
By means of this mantra and the binding of the womb (*yonibandha*), and not otherwise,
his merits and sins [vanish], just as darkness [disappears] at the rising of the sun.
Having gratified Kāla in many ways with life-force, women, wealth, and so forth,
those desiring merit should therefore practice this constantly.
Success is born from practice; through practice one attains liberation.
Through practice one gains realization; yoga proceeds from practice. The mastery of mantras and the mastery of the vital winds arise solely from practice.
Through practice, one may deceive time, and likewise become a conqueror of death.
Thus ends the first chapter.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the great Trailokyadaṃmara mantra, which expresses Tripura and is endowed with the oral tradition (saṃpradāya).
On a level stretch of ground, free from depressions and elevations,
strewn with scattered flowers, and perfumed with incense and fragrances.
Adorned with a tilaka on his forehead, his eyes colored with collyrium,
his breath fragrant from betel, and his consciousness delighted by wine;
His limbs were smeared with saffron, adorned with red lac-dye;
he was clothed in red garments and graced with red garlands.
With his body smeared with camphor powder and free from deceitful speech,
he should uplift the Great Goddess, who bestows both seen and unseen fruits.
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus, rich with filaments and possessing a beautiful pericarp; at the tip of each petal there should be a knot, and at the end of that [knot] three prongs.
Having carefully drawn this wheel, the best of practitioners should subsequently arrange the Mātṛkā, the Pīṭhas, Bhairava, and the Yoginīs.
One should draw Kāmarūpa in the east, Kolagiri in the south;
Cauhāra should be drawn in the west, and Auṇaka in the north.
Mala is in the south-eastern direction, Kulāntaka in the south-west;
Jālandhara is in the north-west, and Devakoṭṭaka in the north-east.
One should place the Lords of the Seats (pīṭheśas) there— the Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga— and arrange them starting from Brāhmaṇī up to Caṇḍikā.
[The Bhairavas are] Asita, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmattabhairava.
Kapolabhīṣaṇa and Saṃhāra are likewise remembered as the eighth;
then there are Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍī, and Caṇḍikā as the eighth;
one should assign each of these names of the Mothers with long vowels.

The short vowels are called Bhairava; indeed, the Yamalas should be dried by fire. O auspicious lady, the letters beginning with *ka* are the knots, while those ending in *śa* are peaceful and auspicious.
All the various groups of phonemes are situated at the tips of the prongs; one should place the letters from *ka* to *kṣa* on the knot,
and the remainder should be placed upon its prongs.
One should assign the syllables beginning with *dakṣiṇā*, which bestow the fruit of all accomplishments,
starting from the eastern peak up to the northern peak, arranging them toward the south.
Then the wise practitioner should place them starting from that point along the path of withdrawal (*viramārgeṇa*);
those called *Śiva* are in the center of the pericarp, while those called *Haṃsa* are spread across the two feet.
The letter *ha*, together with the *sakāra* and *īkāra*, is the living being; it is called the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Both are designated as the "living being" (*jīva*) throughout the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
Having thus performed the twofold placement, one should worship according to the *Kulapaddhati*;
within this interval, the practitioner of the deity should meditate upon the Vāgbhava syllable.
Then, one should extract the mantra that bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation,
having taken the seed-syllable of Indrāṇī and adorned it with the *saṃhāra* (retraction) [mudrā].
O Goddess, that Vāgbhava [syllable] which has not been stepped upon is indeed worshipped;
it is the manifestation of the form of the letter *e*, whose nature is the triangle and the moon.
Compassion toward one's disciples, especially toward those devoid of devotion—
this, O Beloved, is the supreme seed, the source of the great seed of creation.
Having taken up the knot of desire (kāmagranthi) as the right horn of the peak,
and having joined it with Māheśvarī, make it equal through the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
O Goddess, he is the agitator of all sentient beings, the life-force that is higher than the highest,
worshipped by the three worlds, and the agent of creation and destruction.
This is the Kāmarāja, which bestows the accomplishment of the desires of the goddesses;
having unified the division between the higher and the lower, those who are composed [attain it].
The practitioner, with a one-pointed mind, should recite the mantra during the practice for attaining the subterranean realms and other such goals.
The deity is situated upon the seat of the vital breath (prāṇa), and then Cāmuṇḍā pierces it;
the seed-syllable that deludes the three worlds is then restrained within Caṇḍikā.
One should indeed perceive [the deity] seated upon the throne of Sadāśiva through the upward utterance;
one should constantly perform the preliminary service (pūrvasevā) with the *yonibandha* posture, remaining motionless.
Resorting to the door of the bilva tree, with a one-pointed mind and senses conquered;
by the first [syllable] it is dissolved, and by the middle one it is fixed.
But by the last [syllable], it is not cut off; therefore, knowledge is not accomplished.
The first, the beginningless first, and the middle, the middling-middle.
Tripurā, who bestows swift accomplishment, is at the end of the end and infinite;
she is established at the beginning of the middle, and at the end of the middle and the end.
O fair-faced one, by this procedure, practitioners should recite for the purpose of agitating the city, according to the sequence of short and long vowels; by that, [the city] is destroyed.
Having thus pronounced the qualifiers, one may accomplish even the three worlds.
|| The Second Chapter ||
The Goddess said:
"O Destroyer of Tripura, even now there remains a doubt regarding the means for attaining the reality of the Divine Will; tell me how one may attain that which consists of pure consciousness."
The venerable Bhairava said:
I shall describe, in brief, the characteristic of the principle of desire (*kāmatattva*).
Listen briefly to the supreme, divine, and most excellent method of attraction.
One should accomplish desire by means of desire—desire abiding in desire, situated in the midst of desire, and enclosed within the hollow of the belly of desire;
one should cast desire into desire.
Having performed the desired act with desire, one should certainly cause that which abides in desire to tremble;
in this wheel, one should meditate upon Kāmarāja, who is worshipped by the three worlds.
The world is to be known as situated within desire; the body is in the midst of desire;
the womb is the interior of desire; and that which has a clear end is designated as the *bindu*.
With this very desire, one should accomplish the reality of desire;
for one should indeed fashion that very desire within the womb of the sādhya.
Having performed the churning of the *bindu*,
the supreme nectar situated in the *visarga* is certainly dissolved by means of the path of power (*śaktimārga*) as it resides in the womb (*yoni*).
O fair-faced one, what is the use of speaking much here?
Having drawn the previously mentioned yantra, or the great wheel of Tripurā;
One should write [the mantra] on birch bark leaves using *kuṇḍa* and *svayambhū* flowers produced from a cow's horn, combined with *gorocanā*.
There is a great lotus with sixteen petals, and outside of that one with twelve petals;
the Vāgbhava syllable is in the pericarp, while the Kāmarāja is above it.
Above that, one should write the seed-syllable of Śakti situated within the Great Yoni (mahāyoni);
it consists of the triple-staff (tridaṇḍa) joined with the bindu and differentiated by the twelfth vowel.
She is known as Mahāyoni, the mother of the three worlds.
One should place the collection of vowels in the first [position] and the Kāmarāja [seed-syllable] in the second,
having divided them according to the distinction of the twelve vowels.
One should cause differentiation by means of the power of the vowels within the sixteen-petaled great lotus;
outside of that, one should place all the *mātṛkās* endowed with *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*.
O Supreme Goddess, one should cause [the goddess] to be mounted upon the *haṃsa* seed-syllable;
this supreme, divine yantra is difficult to find even throughout the three worlds.
One should envelop everything within the interior of the mandara with a hollow space;
then the best of practitioners should meditate upon the seed-syllable of Śakti within this wheel.
These divine ones have been proclaimed by me as Tripurabhairavī;
accompanied by the names of virgins, they reside at the entrance of the cave.
Having placed [the substance] below the *yoni-kuṇḍa*, one should perform the fire-oblation with handfuls of black mustard seeds;
after seven nights, O Great Goddess, those intoxicated by passion become agitated.
Consumed by the fire of separation, their bodies overwhelmed by fainting,
women stand as if made of jasmine flowers and fall before the practitioner.
O practitioner, O great being, O embodiment of Hāṭakeśvara!
Having entered together with the practitioners, exercise your authority over us.
Having entered, he too sports there until the dissolution of all beings.
The Third Chapter.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme yoga of Tripurā,
which resides in the center of the heart-lotus and is known by the name Haṃsa.
O Supreme Goddess, one should likewise conceive of the corpse called Sāda as seated upon the throne of the sky (vyomapīṭha), accompanied by Cāmuṇḍā and Caṇḍikā.
Upon that, one should place the form consisting of the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*;
with the entire mantra, one should fashion the faces and the limbs.
One should meditate upon the form of Maheśānī with an unwavering inner self—
[a form] possessing a splendor equal to the rising sun and crowded with many rays.
The Goddess has the luster of the Bandhūka flower, her body is as red as vermilion,
she is draped in crimson garments, and is adorned with every ornament.
She wears a mass of matted locks, is serene, has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament,
is endowed with all auspicious marks, and is seated in the paryanka posture.
Her breasts were elevated by the weight of her enjoyments, shaped like a full circle;
she was resplendent with a line of body hair situated amidst waves of skin-folds.
To the supreme goddess who intoxicates the three worlds, whose face is slightly smiling, and who generates supreme joy for those whose minds are delighted by the bliss of wine.
The Great Goddess of divine form, three-eyed and four-armed,
endowed with all ornaments, seated upon a lotus in the sky.
O lady of excellent hips, she holds in her left hand a divine book consisting of all knowledge, which bestows boons.
She is of divine form, strung together with severed heads resembling the solar disc and bearing garlands of blazing flames, and she emits drops of blood.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, the Mother of the World, who is fierce, composed of wisdom, stainless, and holding with her throat the pure [spear] that reaches down to the soles of her feet.
The lotus situated on the upward path is filled with a thousand petals;
it rains down a flood of nectar, possessing the luster of liquid lac.
With that very supreme nectar, one should bathe the Goddess;
thus for the wise practitioner who is engaged in this practice.
"O Great-souled One, O Goddess praised by heroes, the entire triple world is shaken; it cannot be otherwise.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.

The Śrī Devī said: "O Lord, how is the meditation on the mantra described, and how does its emergence occur? In what does dissolution take place, and what is taught as the state of rest and the stages of life?"

In the word *raghūṇām*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *tadrāja* suffix *aṇ*, which is applied in the sense of "descended from" (*apatya*), because it occurs in the plural and is not feminine, according to the rule *tenaiva astriyām*. The term *anvayam* means lineage, family, or continuous succession. This very [lineage] is what is heard of in the subsequent verse, for it is only that which can logically be the object of examination. Nor can it be argued that the word *tam* in that [verse] refers to something else, since no other masculine noun has been introduced as the subject; thus, [the author] says: "The life-story of the best of the Raghus... (p. 11).

"Listen to the slaying of the Ten-headed one ordained by the Sage"—this is for the sake of [your] fickleness; that is to say, for the purpose of performing a fickle deed for you. The fourth case (caturthī) is used here according to the rule *kriyārthopapadasya karmaṇi sthāninī* (Pāṇini 2.3.14). "Deceived" (*pratāritaḥ*) means either instigated by the context, or encouraged. Alternatively, Galāyudha says: "Excessive deception is *pratāraṇa*, which is a great gift. This refers to one who, having gained entry into the mind of the one who has formed this intention, is a prompter of the speaker's activity—though he may be dull-witted—by instigating him toward those qualities that obstruct his fortitude. To the question "What do they do? he says: "Having reached the ear... Now, desiring to examine the composition being performed, he requests him [to listen]. He requests him to listen until the end of the examination, since mere listening alone is not sufficient. It has been stated under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) that "he desires" (*ahanti*). By that, a request is obtained. Since the statement of the governing rule itself does not possess the power to impel action, the meaning is: "Request an examination preceded by listening. The manifestation of the distinction between good and bad, or merits and defects, is the subject at hand. The word "for" (*hi*) indicates a well-known illustration. The locative case in *agnyādiṣu* is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). "Pure" (*viśuddha*) means blazing due to the absence of contact with other alloys. "Darkness" (*śyāmikā*) is its opposite. The particle *api* denotes conjunction (*samuccaye*), while *vā* denotes option (*vikalpe*). Both purity and darkness are subjects for the examination of gold. This refers to the specific individual objects. The meaning is that it is perceived through an alternative state. This is the figure of speech *Pratīvastūpamā*. Indeed, that is *Pratīvastūpamā*.

(p. 12) [The text continues: ...the Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he apprehend any dharma as existing. He does not perceive form, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive forms, nor does he apprehend them; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive contact, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death, nor does he apprehend them. Subhūti, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not become conceited on account of that practice, one should know that he is irreversible from full enlightenment. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all those dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Since they are empty of intrinsic nature, they cannot be apprehended. That which is unapprehendable cannot be conceived, and that which cannot be conceived is not subject to birth or cessation. That which is neither born nor ceases is not subject to defilement or purification. That which is neither defiled nor purified is beyond conceptual proliferation. That which is beyond conceptual proliferation is the realm of the Tathāgata. Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skill in means regarding the perfection of wisdom. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva be known as irreversible? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when hearing this teaching of the perfection of wisdom, does not feel fear, nor does he feel terror or extreme dread, one should know him as irreversible. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when hearing the names of the Buddhas and Lords who reside in other world-systems, feels great joy and gives rise to a thought of longing to see them, one should know him as irreversible. Moreover, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when hearing the teachings of the Buddhas and Lords, retains them in memory and does not forget them, one should know him as irreversible. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva not forgetting the teachings of the Buddhas and Lords? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, it is because that bodhisattva mahāsattva has cultivated the perfection of wisdom and has been sustained by the power of the Buddhas and Lords. Therefore, Śāriputra, one should know that such a bodhisattva mahāsattva is irreversible.
