Where a common property (*sāmānya*) exists in two sentences, serving as the cause for the distinction between merit and defect, that common attribute is employed in both sentences through different words; for this very reason, it is not a *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration). In that case, because even the commonality exists in the relation of the original image and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*), nor is it an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by another matter), since the two sentences there exist as the subject of the general and the particular. Now, he introduces the subject to be described: "Vaivasvata" [etc.]. "This mantra of the one of limited luster (*mitatejas*), the pervasive one of the three abodes (*tridhāman*), is most powerful. By this sequence, O Bhairavī, when the mantras are uttered, the deities of the *kula* become angry with the practitioners and seize their bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Luster (*tejas*), when pierced by the reversal of names, becomes pure and arisen."
Those great-souled ones who recite the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, Śakti, Haṃsa, and Kuleśvara quickly attain spiritual perfection.
The deities bestow their grace upon those who take refuge in the sacrifice of the wheel of the lineage;
listen, O Bhairavī, as I speak of the convention of the initial syllables of the words.
O Kuleśvarī, it was by Śrīkaṇṭha, the primordial being, that [this] was taught for the sake of accomplishing the fruit resulting from the application of all mantras within the Vāgbhava family.
O beautiful one, the entire great Sārasvata wheel, which is the seed-syllable of desire, has been appropriated by the primordial Lord of Wrath.
O beautiful one, that wheel of wombs (yonicakra), which bestows the fruits of all desires,
was [established] by the primordial Lakulīśa through the seed-syllable of Śakti.
The science of the feet has been fully taught; it is the science of all things, transmitted through the lineage. Now, [you must explain] the characteristic of the pervasion of the wheel of the Kula.
One should always contemplate within the hollow center of the heart-lotus, in the triangle, the entire essence of Rudra, Bhairava, and the Vīras, which is the Kula of the Yoginīs.
The letters beginning with 'a' and ending with the visarga, visualized as having rightward strokes,
resembling ten million moons, are well-worshipped by means of the Vāgbhava mantra.
O Dear One, resting upon the lines of letters from *ka* to *ta*,
they shine like many suns, worshipped with the syllables of Kāmarāja.
O Dear One, [the deities] beginning with the letter *tha* and ending with the letter *sa* reside upon the lines of the syllables;
they shine like many suns and are honored by the syllables of Kāmarāja.
The letters beginning with *tha* and ending with *sa* rest upon the eastern line;
resembling a mass of lightning, they are excellent and are considered to be associated with the seed-syllable of Śakti.
In the center, the goddess Kulākulā is established as the science of the feet;
she is Caṇḍī, possessing the luster of a rainbow, who manifests the mantra of the swan.

Through the instructions of the Guru, your form consists of the wheel of the Kula, which is to be known by means of millions of scriptures that do not seek anything else; and it is the rosary of your senses.
And the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), O Goddess, belongs to you, O delight of the Kula;
thus, O beloved, it should always be meditated upon within the center of the heart-lotus.
O Mahādevī, O beloved, out of affection for you, I have explained the Kulacakra— the supreme means for the accomplishment of the Vidyā for yogins and yoginīs.
O Goddess, O Mistress of Kula, whatever one should constantly meditate upon within the support of the Command (ājñādhāra),
the entire world— both stationary and moving— quickly comes to sit before that person.
He who, with a disciplined mind, constantly meditates upon the *kulacakra* within the womb,
for him the *yoginīs* become afflicted with passion.
The family circle (kulacakra) should be understood as the very body of Śiva;
one should abandon other scriptures and mantras like the dust at one's feet.
But this, O fawn-eyed one, is an extreme secret that has been told to you;
it should be transmitted from ear to ear, but must not be written down in a book.
O beloved, this should always be given to one who observes the hero-vow, who is joyful,
devoted to the foremost of teachers, exalted, and established in his vows.
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
At the conclusion of one hundred thousand recitations performed by Kuṇḍanī, one should then perform the fire-oblation;
thus, the preliminary service (pūrva-sevā) for him is indeed accomplished—of this there is no doubt.
One who is joined with this method succeeds even if they are of meager fortune;
they are liberated from all diseases and may accomplish even that which is impossible to achieve.
Listen, O Beloved! After this, hear about the practitioner who should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, being focused on that [deity] and having conquered his senses.
Agitated by the mere sight [of him], all the women, afflicted by passion,
fall before the practitioner, devoid of shame and fear.
(15) Two hundred thousand people reside in this region;
they come to this sacred site just as those from very noble lineages approach a holy ford.
They give him their entire possessions, standing right before him;
when three hundred thousand recitations have been performed, the masters of the mandala appear together with the mandalas themselves.
They all come under one's control; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
By six hundred thousand [recitations], kings along with their servants, armies, and vehicles [are brought under control].
By reciting it twelve hundred thousand times, all the lords of the hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas come under one's control and constantly carry out one's commands.
O fair-faced one, when fifteen lakhs have been recited by the practitioner,
all the accomplished Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, Apsarases, and others [come under his control].
They all come under one's control; there is no need for deliberation on this point. The power of hearing from afar and omniscience arise.
When satisfied and purified, he bestows the nourishment of power; yet, if not so, he may cause death in an instant.
Likewise, by reciting [the mantra] one million eight hundred thousand times, the practitioner [attains success] with his very body.
Rising up and leaving the earth, he is born with a divine body;
he wanders through the worlds at his will and beholds the wondrous earth.
Then, by twenty lakhs [of recitations], one becomes a lord of the Vidyādharas;
O Goddess, the practitioner shall become capable of assuming any form at will and possessed of great strength.
O Goddess, by thirty million recitations, one becomes a lord of the Siddhas and Yogīs and merges into the supreme state as a Yakṣa.
By forty-four hundred thousand recitations, one attains the state of Brahmā and the eternal Viṣṇu; by sixty thousand, the state of Rudra; and by eighty thousand, the state of Īśvara.
The radiant energy of Bhairava, pertaining to the Triple City (Tripura), is Śiva, the ultimate cause.
O Goddess, he attains that inexhaustible, peaceful, immeasurable, and incomparable state, and all that he desires; of this there is no doubt.
The Fifth Chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, how is it that there are nine hundred thousand [sites], and what is their nature?
O Father, you who are armed with the trident, you ought to sever this doubt of mine."
Śrī Bhairava said:
O Goddess, the most essential of essentials, which is devoid of external enumeration, resides within the body; O Goddess, this *navalakṣa* is extremely difficult to attain.
O Goddess, from the support of the penis (meḍhrādhāra) there are four [centers], and then the Gahvara, the Throat-cavity (galagahvara),
the Lambikā, the Brow-aperture (bhrūbila), and the Brahma-randhra— this is the group of nine.
O beautiful goddess, one should contemplate the form of a lamp-flame at the genitals, shining within the *ādhāra*; and the youthful orb of the sun situated at the navel.
Above that is the flame-light in the form of a crest; above that, it has the appearance of the sun.
At the throat, it has the form of a lamp-flame; at the *lambikā*, it resembles the moon.
At the midpoint between the eyebrows, resembling a jewel and possessing universal splendor at the end of the nine [syllables],
the yogi situated in this place should practice nine hundred thousand [recitations].
Touching, gazing, conversing, seeing the drop,
and self-penetration— these are the five characteristics of the mantras.
Śrī Bhairava said:
O lady of excellent hips, I shall proclaim the treasury of knowledge which bestows all accomplishments;
one should worship the wheel of the Goddess with the Vāgbhava mantra.
In the midst of that, one should meditate upon the Goddess who possesses a divine body formed by an assembly of phonemes, consisting of *nāda* and *bindu*, according to the entire mantra;
having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the faces and limbs, O Dear One, one should worship her upon the corpse.
In the corners are the three deities: Rati, Prīti, and Manobhavā;
likewise, Rati is on the left and Prīti is on the right, in front of Madana.
Thereafter, one should recite the root-vidyā, endowed with its defining characteristics.
One should join the letter *kṣa* with the vowel *ā*,
the letter *la* with the vowel *ī*, and the letter *ha* with the vowel *ū*.
The letter *ṛ* is known as disease, and likewise, the conjunction with *ḷ* is another;
by means of *ai*, the letter *śa* is attained, and by means of *au*, the letter *va*.
One should worship with the syllable *Aṃ*, conjoined with the first letter of the name;
this is that root-vidyā known by the name Tripurabhairavī.
O Goddess, it becomes manifest and bestows the threefold accomplishment;
likewise, the other [form], Bhuvikā, grants them to the foremost of practitioners.
This has been told to you, O Goddess, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The supreme Goddess of Wisdom should not be given to one who is unworthy.
|| This is the sixth chapter. ||

Thus ends the Uttara-ṣaṭka (the latter hexad) within the *Ṣaḍvidyāprakāśā*, in the section on Nityaklinnā, in the Northern Portion brought down from the Seat of Knowledge (*Vidyāpīṭha*), in the *Śrīrudrayāmala* consisting of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses.
Its explanation.
Touching is said to be in the heart; light is in the region of the throat;
true speech is in the place of the palate; and vision is in the center of the bindu.
O Goddess, self-manifest immersion has been shown in the aperture of Brahmā;
I praise the supreme power of Śambhu, whose form is condensed into the phonemes.
It is a work that bears the burden of continuous play with the commencement of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and other winds,
and which provides a definitive determination of the meaning through its correspondence with other scriptures.

I shall compose the *Kuladīpikā*, a commentary on the latter six chapters [of the *Tantrāloka*], concerning the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*)—who is the very essence of the Lord Triyambaka Bhaṭṭāraka in His nature as Consciousness; who consists of the vibration of manifestation; whose supreme sport is the eternal creation, maintenance, and withdrawal of the universe; who kindles the triad of cities consisting of the Universal, the Individual, and the Deep-Sleep states (corresponding to the Moon, Sun, and Fire); and whose divine form is composed of a multitude of phonemes.

The commentary entitled *Kuladīpikā* on the *Śrī Uttaraṣaṭka*, preceded by the grace of the venerable supreme guru Śrī Brahmānandaprakāśabhaṭṭāraka, is now commenced. This work is intended for those unfortunate ones, impoverished by the tradition of the glorious Kāśmīra Siddhas, who—due to a lack of authentic knowledge regarding the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, which is the means for the supreme worship and was proclaimed in the ocean [of scriptures] by the glorious Dakṣiṇa and Uttara [traditions] for the protection of the entire world—have been led astray by false teachers through their own intellectual fabrications and perverted instructions. First, here is its opening verse:
In that thousand-petaled lotus of the sky, crowded with white filaments,
Kulanāyikā questioned Mahādeva as he sat there.

In that context, "the sky" (*vyoman*) refers to the lotus situated within the cavity of the skull, above the head known as *kodaṇḍa*, which is located at the station of the Command (*ājñā*). That lotus, whose nature is the Kula and which is conjoined with the supreme point (*paramabindu*), is the "sky-lotus. Within that [lotus], the rays of the point are its "spokes"; thus it is called "the thousand-spoked" (*sahasrāra*). By the word "spoke," he intends the petals; it is said to be "filled with white filaments. There, the filaments consist of the sixteen digits (*kalā*); because they are composed of nectar, they are described as "white. And it is stated in the venerable *Nirguṇḍa-śrīmata*:
"In the great sixteen-petaled lotus, upon the pericarp at the top of the head..."
Knowledge resides in the pericarp; the vowels beginning with 'a' reside on the petals of action.

"And these powers are proclaimed to be of sixteen kinds. In that context, "seated there" means that for one who is situated there, the unsurpassed nature of one's own self is perceived through the power of the stainless (*nirañjana*) samādhi;
that is to say, when such power of samādhi has been attained by the yogin.
Yoga arises when there is an excellence in the realization of the meaning of the supreme secret.

Such is the meaning of the sentence: the Kulanāyikā questioned the God of gods, the Lord of Mātṛkās. Here, there is merely a description of the questions in the Tantras, arranged in verses corresponding to the commencement of the subsequent exposition. But in reality, the Supreme Goddess, being the disciple, constantly interrogates the God, the Teacher. Indeed, in the supreme nature of the venerable Paraśiva and the supreme Power (Parā Śakti)—who is the perfected Mātṛkā and the substratum of all knowledge—there is no possibility of even a mutual difference; how much less, then, can there be the relationship of teacher and disciple, or the revelation of that which is not already fully known? Thus says the Upaniṣad: [The text continues with the citation from the Upaniṣad.]
Abiding in the roles of teacher and disciple, the Lord Sadāśiva himself brought down the Tantra through words and phrases consisting of preceding and succeeding sections.
How did he inquire? [He said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, Bhairava, destroyer of worldly existence!
O Lord of gods, I wish to praise the determination of the mantra of the Goddess. By "of the Goddess," the meaning is "of Tripurā. Herein are the matters to be investigated.
He summarizes by way of a question:
"Likewise, the Great Lotus Grove is endowed with the three genders."
And another is the Kadambagolaka, specifically the Brahmarandhra.

"Tell me the seventh [topic]: the fivefold union of mudrās, the three seats (pīṭhas), and the distinction between Kula and Akula. Although the word "endowed with" (*samāyukta*) is used here in connection with the "three marks" (*liṅgatraya*) and the "Great Lotus Grove" (*mahāpadmavana*), it should be understood that both are separate subjects of inquiry; otherwise, there would be an inconsistency in having only seven questions. Furthermore, by employing the term "endowed with," it indicates the proximity of the Great Lotus Grove to any one of the three marks. This same principle should be understood in subsequent instances as well.
The linga facing west is proclaimed to be situated in the yoni;
it is self-manifested (svayambhū) and denotes the arrow (bāṇa), residing in the place of the seed-syllable within the knot of the heart.

"And for this reason, [the syllable] *visarga* (: is situated in the intermediate space, meaning it is 'stationary' (*sthāvara*), which signifies facing westward. 'The Yoni' refers to a specific arrangement of phonemes, characterized as will be described by the passage beginning with 'between the anus and the penis. Located therein is a single *liṅga*, and that is called the 'Body' (*piṇḍa*). Regarding the phrase 'the state of the seed-syllables of the heart-knots': there, the knots are fourfold, known as Vāmā, Mudrā, Maṇḍala, Mantra, and Vidyā. These are to be understood in order as the names of the *mātṛkā-cakra*, divided into four parts consisting of twelve phonemes each, starting from the beginning. And so it is stated in the *Śrīmat-śrīcakra-nirṇaya* by the Lord."
On the garland of the Maṇipūraka, four kinds of knots have arisen:
the Mudrā, the Maṇḍala, and the Mantra, as well as the fourfold Vidyā-knot.
Furthermore, each one [of these] exists within the interior of the machine of Māyā with twelve subdivisions.

Mahāmāyā, perceiving herself as having the form of a forest due to the continuous sprouting of thousands of [lotuses], speaks of it as "the forest. Here, although there is a general reference to the "surrounding area" (*parisara*) of the aforementioned supreme *liṅga*, it should be understood as being "above that. In this context, the "Great Lotus" (*mahāpadma*) is known as the *visarga*. *Akula* is beyond form; it is the nature of the supreme seed-syllable (*paramabīja*). That very thing is designated as the "Yoga-pīṭha," because it is the station of Viṣṇu-Īśanātha, the venerable Lord Paramabhairava. Now he speaks of the "Golaka" (the sphere) within the Kadamba: "That Kāma, in the form of a seed, has the shape of a Kadamba-golaka; one should know it as the Kadamba-golaka. This is the specific point. By the word "that" (*tat*) in "that Kāma" (*tatkāma*), the Great Forest (*mahāvana*) is referred to. In its center is the position of the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Contained within is a triangle and a hexagon in the form of the expansion of Kailāsa; above that is the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*), consisting of the machine of the principle of Kāma. Because it has the shape of a Kadamba-golaka, it is called by the word "Kāma"; thus, the meaning of the sentence is: "one should know it as the Kadamba-golaka. Accordingly, in this Tantra, he will designate fire by the word "Kāma": "Having meditated on Kāma, situated between the eyebrows, resembling a Bandhūka flower, with a subtle crest above it"—by "in the form of a seed" (*bījārūpiṇam*), the meaning is that it possesses the nature of the encompassed supreme seed-syllable (*parabīja*).

(p. 23) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the nature of reality as it is (tathatā-svabhāva). Among these, Mahāmati, the imagined nature refers to the various characteristics of objects that are grasped by ordinary people through names and signs, which do not exist as such in reality. The dependent nature refers to the manifestation of the mind (citta) and mental factors (caitta) arising from the habit-energies (vāsanā) of false discrimination. The perfected nature refers to the non-existence of the imagined nature within the dependent nature. And the nature of reality as it is refers to the equality of all phenomena, which is the realm of the Tathāgatas. [End of excerpt]

And it is said in the *Śrīmad-uttarakaula*: "The pervasive, supreme seed-syllable (*bīja*) is established in that which transcends dissolution (*layātīta*). By the term "transcending the dissolution of the son" (*putralayātīta*), the *brahmarandhra* (the aperture of Brahmā) is designated; and that is the center of the pericarp of the forest of great lotuses (*mahāpadmavana*). Immediately thereafter, he describes the *brahmarandhra*: "The *brahmarandhra*, however, is right there the mandala that is the support of the *suṣumnā*. "Right there" means precisely in the *kadamba-golaka*. The mandala that serves as the support for the *suṣumnā* is the *suṣumnādhāramaṇḍala*; it is indeed the lunar mandala. Taking that as its support, the *suṣumnā*—which is a certain subtle power (*kalā*) called *suṣumnā* that has followed the body—is known as such. And so it is stated in the *Śrīmata*: "In the single hand, at the end of the resonance and light within the space between consciousness and the unconscious, that which is requested is the supreme consciousness, the illuminator ending with Śiva; she is to be known as the *Brahmasūtrā*, and for that reason she is called a 'thread' (*sūtrā*). Now, he will explain the five mudrās: "The principles (*tattvas*) beginning with Earth are the marks of the mudrās. This means that the principles are the expressive forms (*vācaka-rūpa*) of the mudrās of essential nature (*svarūpa-mudrā*); they are not the expressed forms (*vācya-rūpa*) such as Earth and the rest. These [principles] reside in the locations known as the *ādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *maṇipūraka*, *anāhata*, and *viśuddhi*, and are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) known as *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ghoṣa*. For practitioners who meditate upon the syllables *la* and the others residing in those respective locations such as the *ādhāra*, whatever supernatural powers (*vibhūtis*) are accomplished, those are designated as "mudrās. As it is said in the *Śrīkrama-nirṇaya*: "The sequence belonging to the Heroes (*vīraga*) has been declared; now I shall speak of the essential nature of the mudrās."
p.

24) There, the designators of the stages (*bhūmi*) are situated as *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha*. From the support (*ādhāra*) up to the purification, there is the pentad beginning with the support.
It is stated that this is the locus of the designators of earth and the other elements.
In the *Śrīratnadeva*: "In this world, the pentad beginning with earth, from the support (ādhāra) up to the purified state (viśuddhi), [is established]."
Naturally existing, moving and radiant, it is the stable root joined with space.
This seed-syllable, which is of the nature of Parā, is enriched with Māyā at its beginning and so forth;
it is joined with Bhaya and Varada, and is further endowed with Māyā below.
The subtle mudrās are said to be natural when they have reached the station of Brahmā;
they are called "moving" when in the station of Viṣṇu, and "blazing" when they have reached the station of Rudra.
Having established a firm consciousness in Īśvara, which is constant like Rudra in the state called Sādākhya, these [mudrās] are of equal nature;

thus, through the means of contemplation (*bhāvanā*), the letters beginning with *la* become the cause of specific supernatural powers (*vibhūti*) for these mudrās. In this way, these mudrās are superimposed upon the *mā* [of Māyā]. Now, he describes the three seats (*pīṭhatraya*):
"The reality known as Pūrṇa is the *bindu*, situated between the two bows."
Above that is the place named Ānāha, and beyond that is Oḍyāṇa.

"Kāmarūpa shall be the resting place of Śakti, and beyond that [is the next]. Here, the elision of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is to be understood. The principle of the Bindu consists of light; it refers to the sacred seat (pīṭha) named Pūrṇagiri, located between the eyebrows. Above that is the sacred seat named Nāda; above that is the second Oḍyāṇa, known as Nāda. (p. 25)

The *pīṭha* is the nature of the vibration (*sphuraṇa*) of that *bindu*, which is of the nature of light and consists of the crest (*śikhā*). "From there" means that above the second *pīṭha*, the third *pīṭha* named Kāmarūpa is the Śākta, whose nature is the repose of light; that very thing is called *Śakti*. Having thus described the three *pīṭhas*, he divides [them] into *Kula* and *Akula*: "O Dear One, *Visarga* is *Akula*. The thousand-petaled great lotus, adorned with red filaments, is located there; it is clearly perceived as raining down drops of blood."

One should perceive—that is, one should contemplate—the lunar light, which consists of an outpouring of radiance, as a specific star called *visarga* (emission), which is *akula*. This is what is meant. And so it will be said: "Having drunk the divine nectar of the *kula*, which is red, intensely radiant, and pouring down like a torrential rain, that *akula* is eternal; and one should contemplate it as emission (*visarga*), for from it the wheel of *kula*—consisting of the *mātṛkā* ending with the letter 'Ya' and the group of powers beginning with Will (*icchā*)—is extended. And it is stated in the *Śrīkulamūlāvatāra*: "She is called Will, Knowledge, and Action; she is Kuṇḍalinī and likewise Mātṛkā. From her everything has arisen; therefore, the manifold *kula* [proceeds] from that. Having thus taught the specific mantra called *visarga*, which is *akula*, he describes the nature of *kula* as the womb (*yoni*).

"I shall now explain the binding of that mudrā previously indicated, which is known as the Secret and consists of nectar, by means of which one attains realization. This refers to what was previously stated in the section explaining the three signs (*liṅga*), beginning with "facing west," and so forth.

(p. 26) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature as the basis of worldly convention (loka-vyavahāra-svabhāva)."

By virtue of being the locus of the primary *liṅga*, the *mudrā* known as the Secret (*guhya*) and the Womb (*yoni*) is indicated. She is the entire *mātṛkā-cakra*, the progenitress, the essence of the power of all mantras, whose nature is the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), and who consists of resonance (*ghoṣamayī*). I shall explain the attainment of her bond through heedfulness and constant contemplation, by means of which—becoming one with the yoga of Sarasvatī—the attainment of supreme consciousness occurs; such is the meaning. Now he explains the method of the bond: "In the beginning, one should join the mind to one's own substrate (*svādhāra*) by means of the yoga of inhalation (*pūraka*). First, having performed the yoga of inhalation, one should join the mind to one's own substrate. Immediately thereafter, he speaks of the own substrate, and it is said in the *Viśvāsakāriṇī*:
That which is the seed at the beginning of the Veda, the single source ending with *kṣa*—
through the union of the correspondence between these two, it is to be known as the imperishable syllable (*akṣara*) of the Veda.
One should contract and bind that source located between the anus and the penis.

Thus one should bind it; having done what? Having forcibly drawn upward from the source—that is, from the seat of the anus which serves as the foundation—by contracting [the muscles]. And it is said in the *Śrīmad-Uttara*: "It vibrates from the contraction of the foundation (*ādhāra*)," and in this tantra, the foundation is stated to be the anus.
This is also stated in the *Piṇḍayoga-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīmata* known as the *Rakta*.
Thinking, "Having ascended this, one should set it in motion," he asks what should be meditated upon by the mind through its connection with its own support. He says:

"Having meditated on that which resides in the source of delusion—desireless, resembling the bandhūka flower, like the blazing fire of time (kālānala), and possessing a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning."

27) "Wandering" means vibrating. The word *kāma* is established in the secret scriptures (*rahasyāgama*) as referring to the fire (*jātavedas*) located within the body; that is designated as the principle of *kāma*. Having meditated upon this specific kind of light situated in one's own support (*svādhāra*), which is the nature of the wheel (*cakra*) about to be explained, he says that one should likewise meditate upon oneself together with its crest-flame (*śikhā*).
Above that, however, is the subtle crest (śikhā), the supreme digit whose nature is consciousness.

One should contemplate oneself as united with it, having become one with it. The meaning is this: one should meditate upon oneself as having attained oneness with that crest—the digit consisting of consciousness which is an integral part of Jātavedas (the Fire)—and as being joined with it. Having thus cultivated this state of being, he asks what else is to be meditated upon, and says: "Ascending by the path of Brahman through the sequence of piercing the *liṅgas*, [one reaches the state] resembling ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons."
The nectar situated at the point of emission, characterized by supreme bliss,
is molten blood, rich in radiant luster, and raining down in a continuous stream.

"Having drunk the divine nectar of the *kula*, one should enter the *kula* once again; one should go back to the *akula*. Here, the accusative case (*gacchantīm*) is used in the sense of the nominative. Regarding "the path of Brahma":
the sequence of locations beginning with the *ādhāra* and ending with the *viśuddha* is being described.
But by means of two, both paths [are attained]; however, the group of five is joined together.
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna— these are to be known as the pure [faces]. The western is Viśuddha, and the northern is Anāhata.
The southern one is named Maṇi, while the eastern one is Svādhiṣṭhāna.
The face below has the form of a tortoise, and the Ājñā [cakra] has the form of Īśāna.

The previously mentioned *liṅgas*, beginning with the *svayambhū* and so forth, constitute her own self as the Lord. Having successively abandoned those *liṅgas*, that crest (*śikhā*) ascends through the path of Brahma (*brahmamārga*). It reaches the Supreme Bliss (*paramānanda*), whose characteristic substance is the form of the Visarga situated in the center of the aforementioned [space], which is red, radiant, and possesses the nature of a torrential downpour of a stream of blood-red drops. Being born from the supreme sky (*paravyoma*) of Akula, it drinks the divine nectar (*amṛta*). Having leaped up and returned by that same path, facing upwards, she enters the Visarga, which is the equalization of Akula. This occurs through the union of the measures (*mātrāyoga*), and not otherwise. "Measure" (*mātrā*) refers to the triad known as Bindu, Nāda, and Śakti. These sequentially connect the three seats (*pīṭhatraya*) located in the station of the Command (*ājñāsthāna*), the forehead, and the middle of the heart. As it is said in the *Śrīmata*: "Bindu, Nāda, and likewise Śakti—these are declared to be the three measures. Therefore, the meaning is this: ascending upwards in the manner described, that crest, being joined by the three seats named Bindu, Nāda, and Śakti—which are above the root of the nose at the station of the supreme *liṅga*—enters Akula in due order. Having entered, she then descends by that very same path, facing downwards, and enters the support of the Yoni (*yonyādhāra*). By this, it should be understood that the entry into the path of Brahma results solely in the non-differentiation (*abheda*) of the *liṅga*. Although only the word "she should enter" (*viśet*) is stated here, one should contemplate the crest in this very manner.

(p. 29) [The text continues: ...the Bodhisattva, having generated the thought of awakening, trains in the six perfections for three incalculable eons. Having trained in these, he attains the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Therein, the perfection of giving consists in the relinquishing of all internal and external things to all sentient beings without attachment. The perfection of morality consists in the restraint of body, speech, and mind through the observance of the precepts. The perfection of patience consists in enduring harm from others and reflecting on the nature of phenomena with equanimity. The perfection of vigor consists in the application of effort toward wholesome qualities without slackening. The perfection of meditation consists in the one-pointed concentration of the mind upon a single object. The perfection of wisdom consists in the thorough discernment of all phenomena as they truly are. These six perfections are the path by which the Bodhisattvas proceed to supreme, perfect enlightenment. Thus it is said: "By means of these six perfections, the sons of the Conqueror traverse the stages and purify the Buddha-fields. [End of page 29]

In its essential sense (*tātparya*), that which is to be reached is designated as *prāṇa* in this Tantra, O Supreme Goddess. That [state] is called *udghāta*, and it arises at the end of *prāṇa*. By saying "that," she refers to the *śikhā* (the crest). In this Tantra, it is designated as *prāṇa*; the reason for this is that it is an *udghāta*. *Udghāta* means the upward-moving wind; it is the severing of the knots (*granthiccheda*). Because it effects that [severance], the *śikhā* itself is expressed by the word *udghāta*. The end of *prāṇa* is the phoneme *kṣa*. By this, he intends the *saṃvarta-maṇḍala* known as *visarga*, which serves as the respective locus. Thus, the meaning is this: when that *śikhā* enters from the support of the *yoni* into the end of *prāṇa*, the locus of *visarga*, then—because it effects the severing of the knots—it is called *udghāta*. Therefore, in this Tantra, it is designated as *prāṇa*. Even *prāṇa*, being upward-moving and having the nature of *visarga*, is not capable of effecting the severing of the knots in the form of *udghāta*. This has been stated by the venerable Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka: "Above the *prāṇas* and below the *jīva*, that which has the nature of *visarga* is called supreme. The *Kālatantra* also describes the Great Yoga (*mahāyoga*), which has the nature of binding both *visargas* and is designated as the sleep of the *yoni*: "When the *apāna* is pressed because the *prāṇa* is being impelled, and having gone upward, it returns—this is the definition of *udghāta*. And it is said in the venerable *Bhagavadgītā*: "Others offer the *prāṇa* into the *apāna*, and likewise the *apāna* into the *prāṇa*; others, intent on breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), [suspend] the movement of *prāṇa* and *apāna*; still others, restricted in their food, offer the *prāṇas* into the *prāṇas*."

And it is said in the Upaniṣads: "We offer speech into breath; we offer breath into speech. Thus, she who extends the coming and going [of the breath] is described as the "Tuft" (śikhā). In the venerable *Ratnākhyatantra*, it is stated: "In the midst of that, O Dear One, is the Goddess Kuṇḍalinī together with Śiva; moving through the piercing of the stations, she drinks the nectar of Ambikā. Therefore, the yoga of the head of the practitioner, consisting of the practice of burning and flooding during the coming and going [of the breath], should be understood in this way.
Practicing thus day after day with certainty, he is liberated from the bonds of existence by the floods of suffering such as old age and death.
By this, he demonstrates the excellence of the fruit of binding the *yonimudrā*:
"The fourfold creation which proceeds from that womb dissolves back into it,
beginning with Kalā and Agni and ending with Śiva."
"The binding of the supreme *yonimudrā* is proclaimed to be within her.
Within her, who has become the womb (*yoni*), the fourfold creation of the world proceeds;
and within her, the collection of principles (*tattva*) beginning from Kālāgni and ending with Śiva dissolves."

That *yonimudrā* belongs to the Supreme (*parā*) and is endowed with unsurpassed excellence; its binding has been described as such. What on earth cannot be accomplished by the mere binding of this *mudrā*? Thus, this is a praise of the binding itself. Otherwise: "O Goddess of Gods, he who performs this mantra in one way and performs it in another way does not attain success—this is the truth, the truth again and again. The meaning is that one who mutters the collection of mantras without [proper] recitation, or performs the entire range of rites such as attraction (*karṣaṇa*) and so forth without the binding, does not succeed and is not joined with the fruit.
Therefore, those who desire merit must practice constantly;
from practice comes perfection, and through practice one attains liberation.
Through practice one attains realization; yoga proceeds from practice.
The mastery of mantras comes from practice, and the control of the vital winds comes from practice.
"Through practice, there shall be the deception of time and likewise the conquest of death.
This explains the necessity of practicing the binding of mudrās and their fruits.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Kuladīpikā*, a commentary on the *Uttaraṣaṭka*.
Now he begins to explain the extraction diagram (*uddhārayantra*) of the *Tripurā* Vidyā:
"Henceforth, I shall fully proclaim the great Trailokyadaṃmara mantra, which expresses the essence of Tripurā, together with its traditional transmission."
Now, the word "atha" (then) signifies auspiciousness.
On a perfectly level plot of ground, free from depressions and elevations,
strewn with heaps of flowers and perfumed with fragrant blossoms;
Adorned with a tilaka mark upon his forehead, his eyes colored with collyrium,
his mouth filled with the fragrance of betel, and his consciousness delighted by wine;
His limbs were smeared with saffron and the sun;
he was adorned with a mark of lac, clothed in red garments, and graced with red garlands.
With his limbs smeared with camphor powder, free from anger and malice,
he should invoke the goddess Tripurā, who bestows both seen and unseen fruits upon being beheld.

One should draw an eight-petaled lotus, rich with filaments and possessing a pericarp; at the tip of each petal, it should be joined with a fragrance, and at the end of that [tip], there should be three prongs.

Then, on the aforementioned plot of ground, the preceptor should draw a lotus with eight petals, rich in filaments and possessing a pericarp; the tips of the petals should be joined by circular knots, and at the tips of those knots, it should be provided with tridents arranged in groups of three.
On all sides of the eight tridents, O auspicious lady, he should follow the sequence as I shall describe it.

“O Blessed One” (bhadre) is an address to the Supreme Goddess (parameśvarī). Here, with three peaks for each petal—thus eight peaks in total—one should place [the letters] upon those petals and knots according to the stated method; this is the meaning of the statement, “I shall describe the Mātṛkā-cakra associated with the Tripurā-vidyā.

The phrase “eight peaks” (aṣṭau śṛṅgoṇi) is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for both the knots and the petals. One should arrange them on the petals and at the peak-like knots in the manner previously described.

Having carefully drawn this wheel, the most excellent practitioner should subsequently arrange the *mātṛkā*. Thus, having drawn this wheel in the form of a lotus, the preceptor should afterwards arrange the *mātṛkā* upon its petals and nodes according to the method taught in this Tantra. To explain how this is done, he says: "The *pīṭhas*, *bhairavas*, and *yoginīs*. The *pīṭhas* are Kāmarūpa and so forth; the *bhairavas* are Asitāṅga and so forth; the *yoginīs* are Brāhmī and so forth. These he should first arrange there. He explains this very point [as follows]: (p. 35)
One should draw Kāmarūpa in the east, Kollagiri in the south, Cauhara in the west, and Aukaṇa in the north.
Malaya is in the south-eastern direction, Kulāntaka in the south-west;
Jātāndhara is in the north-west, and Koṭṭaka, O Goddess, is in the north-east.

Thus ends the section on the consumption of the petals. Here, since it is impossible to arrange the seats (pīṭhas) such as Kāmarūpa and others upon the petals of the eastern and other directions, one should understand that those very petals are to be meditated upon as being of the nature of the seats of Kāmarūpa and so forth. The phrase "one should place the lords of the seats there" means within those petals. [One should place] the Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga.
One should arrange them starting from Brahmāṇī and ending with Caṇḍikā:
Asitāṅga, Ururudra, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmattabhairava.
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra are remembered as the eighth;
likewise Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Caṇḍikā.
The passage ending thus is easy to understand.
One should assign long vowels to each of the Mothers, and one should assign short vowels to the Yamalas known as their respective Bhairavas. Thus [it is said].
This is the meaning: the writing of the eight long vowels beginning with *ā* and ending with the *visarga*; the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Yoginīs beginning with Brāhmī;
and the writing of the eight short vowels beginning with *a* and ending with the *anusvāra*.

The placement (*nyāsa*) of the Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga: by this, it should be understood that the long vowels are Brāhmī and the others, while the short vowels are the Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga. One should arrange them as pairs on each petal. Thus, on the petal named Kāmarūpa, one should write the letter *a* called Asitāṅga together with the letter *a* called Brāhmī. Having thus shown the placement of the Bhairavas and Yoginīs on the other petals as well, he describes the placement of the Mātṛkās on the knots (*granthi*). "In the auspicious [lotus], the letters of the *ka*-group and so forth, ending with *kṣa*, are located at the knots. Thus, the letters beginning with *ka* are the "group-letters" (*vargākṣara*). There are five: the *ka*-group and the others; the semi-vowels (*antaḥsthā*) and the sibilants (*ūṣman*) make seven groups; and *kṣa* is one group, making eight groups in total. Of these, the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*—namely *ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa, kṣa*—are to be placed at the knots starting from the east. "All other groups of letters are situated at the tips of the prongs (*śṛṅga*) and corners. Thus, the other groups of letters—consisting of four types excluding *sa* and *ha*—twenty-four in number, are to be written at the ends of the prongs starting from the east. "One should place the letters from *ka* to *kṣa* at the knot, and the remaining ones should be placed on the limbs. By this, he clarifies what was previously stated: "One should place the letters beginning from the south, which bestow the fruits of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). The intention is that through placement starting from the right (south), the letters become conducive to accomplishment. He describes that placement starting from the south: "One should arrange them from the direction of Indra (east) to the northern prong by way of the south. Starting from the eastern quarter up to the northern prong, the arrangement according to the rule is the "southern placement" (*dakṣiṇanyāsa*).
"Then the wise practitioner should place those [syllables] at the beginning here according to the path.

By this, he confirms exactly this: beginning with the syllable *ai* (Aindra), one should arrange the phonemes in the manner of the sun’s southern transit (*dakṣiṇāyana*). "The two called *jīva* are in the center of the pericarp, situated upon the station called *haṃsa*."
The meaning is that within the pericarp (karṇikā) there are two syllables resting in pure consciousness (cinmātra).
To the question "What are they?", he says: "The letter *ha*, which arises from the recitation of the letter *sa*, is called the vital breath (prāṇa)."

"Both are renowned throughout the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving. "Kula-kulapaddhati" is indeed the name of the *cakra* itself; one should meditate upon this at the end, O Blessed One, O Goddess, [saying] "the practitioner. Having meditated upon the *vāgbhava* [syllable] in the center of this *cakra*, one should worship it; by this, it is shown that this is the *vāgbhava-cakra*. Thus, having revealed the *vāgbhava-cakra* here, he then extracts the *vidyā*: "Then one should extract the mantra that bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. This is easy to understand. "Taking the seed-syllable of Indrāṇī, adorned with *saṃhāra*."

In this regard, the great vidyā of Tripura Mahāsundarī possesses two forms, namely the general and the particular. Therein, the "general" refers to the sweet [form] consisting solely of three feet, while the "particular" consists of those known as Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Rudra, Bhūta, and Kulīśvara; he demonstrates that both of these are conjoined with those three. Among them, the seed-syllable (bīja) of Indrāṇī is the twelfth vowel (Ū). "Adorned" by the "destruction" (saṃhāra), which is the anusvāra (ṃ), means accompanied by it. (p. 38)
Therefore, the twelfth vowel accompanied by the *anusvāra* constitutes the mantra known as Vāgbhava; this is its general form.
Now, he states its specific form:
"O Goddess, the Vāgbhava [mantra] is worshipped when it is pervaded by that very [twelfth vowel]."

Some explain the meaning of this [verse] as follows: "That" (*tat*) refers to the seed-syllable of Indrāṇī. "Bhava" is Śrīkaṇṭha; "overpowered by him" (*tenākrāntam*) means accompanied by him. Thus, the very seed-syllable of Indrāṇī becomes the Vāgbhava syllable, which is a specific form occurring after Śrīkaṇṭha. This interpretation, while being explained, will indicate that even the eleventh vowel possesses the nature of Vāgbhava, in accordance with the subsequent aphorism on the literal meaning of the letters beginning with "Śrīkaṇṭha is Vālīśa. Therefore, there is another meaning: "Overpowered by its own birth" (*tadbhavenaivākrāntam*). That is, the seed-syllable of Indrāṇī is overpowered—that is, presided over—by Śrīkaṇṭha, who is heard [as the final element] in the *saṃhitā* form. For in the *saṃhitā* form of the seed-syllable of Indrāṇī, Śrīkaṇṭha is contained within and is heard [therein]. Setting aside that [interpretation], by the expression "as if overpowered," the seed-syllable of Indrāṇī—which is essentially the *saṃhitā* form of the letters born from Śrīkaṇṭha—is made to be joined with Śrīkaṇṭha as he is actually heard, once the swallowing of that *saṃhitā* form has been abandoned. Thus, it is stated that the three letters, consisting of the anusvāra which is the essence of the seed-syllable born from Śrīkaṇṭha, constitute the specific form of Vāgbhava. And so, the fact that such a mantra possesses the nature of Vāgbhava is revealed in the *Śrīvyomacakravivaraṇa* of the Śrīmata: "The triangle is the manifestation of the letter E."

(p. 39) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna-svabhāva). "Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is the grasping of names and characteristics (nāma-lakṣaṇa) based on the dependent nature, just as one perceives a snake in a rope or water in a mirage. This is called the imagined self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the dependent self-nature? It is the manifestation of various objects through the power of false discrimination (vikalpa), which does not exist as it appears. This is called the dependent self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the perfected self-nature? It is the state in which the dependent nature is completely free from the imagined nature; it is the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena, which is eternally unchanging and beyond conceptualization. This is called the perfected self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of the Great Vehicle? It is the realization that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature, that they are originally quiescent, and that they are the realm of the Tathāgata-garbha. By entering this, one transcends the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and attains the stage of the Tathāgata. This is called the self-nature of the Great Vehicle. "Mahāmati, if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understands these four kinds of self-nature, he will not fall into the views of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but will swiftly attain the stage of the Tathāgata."

Regarding the phrase "in the form of a *bindu*": even in the *Siddhayogeśvarīmata*, it proclaims that the eleventh vowel alone constitutes the *vāgbhava*. It says: "The first horn is proclaimed as the letter *a*; its seed-syllable (*bīja*) is the *vāgbhava*, celebrated together with the *bindu* and *nāda*. And it is said in the *Laghuvāda*: "O Thou who knowest the state of the subtle essence, that creeper which is a mere measure (*mātra*) and resembles a *trapusa* fruit, abiding in the first *vāgbīja*, we constantly offer our salutations to Thee, the Giver of Existence. Here, in the word *amātra*, a pause (*vicchitti*) in the phrasing is to be made. Having thus demonstrated that this *vāgbhava* possesses both forms, he states that it must not be given to one who is unqualified: "This supreme seed-syllable, the source of the great creation, should not be given to other disciples, especially to those devoid of devotion. Now follows the *kāmarāja*. Taking up the *kāmagranthi*, he begins by taking the right horn of the *kūṭa*.

Having joined it with Māheśvarī, one unites it with Saṃhāra. The syllable *ka* is the "Kāma-knot," the peak (*kūṭa*) of the Wheel named Vāgbhava. O Goddess, this is the specific northern petal of the Wheel named Koṭṭa. Because it is situated on its southern prong, it is the letter *la*; thus, the southern prong of the peak is so described. Māheśvarī is the letter *ī*, and Saṃhāra is the anusvāra (*m*). The sequence beginning with *a* indicates the excellence of the fruit obtained from extracting the Kāmarāja-mantra. "The agitator of all principles, the life-force of all, the highest of the high"—the meaning is that one should recite [this mantra] which causes agitation (great passion) in all principles and all souls. [It is] the three worlds...
"O Goddess, this Kāmarāja, which brings about creation and destruction, is worshiped; O Goddess,
it bestows the accomplishment of desires"— this is easy to understand.
Immediately following this, he states the specific distinction of this King of Desire.

"Having unified the division of the *para* and *apara*, the practitioner, with one-pointed mind, should perform the recitation (*japa*) for the attainment of the subterranean realms (*pātāla*) and so forth. *Para* means superior; *apara* refers to the letter following *a*, namely *ā*. That which is both *para* and *apara* is *parāpara*. This itself is the "division" (*vibhāga*), meaning the specific distinction. The meaning is that one should recite [the mantra] having joined this as previously described with the extracted *Kāmarāja*. And it has been stated by the venerable Laghupāda: "In the *Nityā*, the *Kāmarāja* is the supreme, partless (*niṣkala*) syllable of the mantra. Here, *ikāra* is the first, and *apara* is the subsequent letter, which is the letter *ā*. This is the sequence of letters. Likewise, in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, it is shown in the form of the *kīla-vidyā*: *klā īm maddravye*; *a eṃ kliṃ netralesauṃ*. It has also been stated by Laghupāda: "In the form of the partless *vidyā*, *ā ī pallavitaiḥ*. And it was said by the venerable Jyeṣṭhanātha: "*Ā ī* is known as *masaṃjñā*, the immortal, the infinite, the three-syllabled *Kuṇḍalinī*, the three-cornered. "With one-pointed mind" refers to the method of visualization (*bhāvanā*). "For the attainment of the subterranean realms and so forth" means the practice beginning with the seed-syllables (*bīja*). Now, he extracts the *Śakti-bīja*.
The individual soul (jīva) situated on the seat of breath (prāṇāsana), again pierced by Cāmuṇḍā and restrained within Caṇḍikā, is the seed-syllable that fascinates the three worlds.

*Prāṇa* is the letter *ha*. That itself is the seat; thus, it is the "seat of breath" (*prāṇāsana*). That which is situated upon that is "situated on the seat of breath" (*prāṇāsanasthitam*). *Jīva* is the letter *sa*. *Cāmuṇḍā* is the vowel *au*; by her it is "pierced," meaning distinguished or conjoined. *Caṇḍikā* is the visarga (*ḥ*). By those two it is "accompanied. This is what is meant: having mentally placed the letter *ha* in the pericarp of the Vāgbhava [cakra], one performs the placement of the letter *sa* above it. By this, he expresses the letter *sa* as "the living soul (*jīva*) situated on the seat of breath. Having joined it with *Cāmuṇḍā* (the letter *ca*) and [the visarga], one should extract it from the wheel in the form of the seed-syllable of Śakti; this is the general rule. Having extracted the supreme seed-syllable in this manner—having obtained it through the grace of the gaze of the venerable Lord of Teachers—one should either recite it separately or rotate the *jīva*. Having thus demonstrated the seed-syllable of Śakti consisting of these forms, he states the specific detail.
One should indeed perceive [the deity] seated upon the throne of Sadāśiva by means of the upward utterance (uccāra).

*Sadāśiva* is the sound *ghoṣa*. That itself is the seat; thus, *sadāśivāsana*. "Seated upon that" means *sadāśivāsanastha*. The meaning of the sentence is that one should first utter the sound *ghoṣa*, and immediately thereafter utter the previously mentioned seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Śakti. And it has been said by the venerable Laghupāda: "That which is ever-present," and "I bow to that Tattva which is the seed-syllable of *māsa* (the month), shining like the moon, whose power is seen by the wise in bringing about the activity of words. In that context, "whose power is seen in bringing about the activity of words" refers to [the aforementioned]. (p. 42)

He explains that the syllable of sound (ghoṣākṣara) is the seed-syllable of the vital breath (prāṇabīja). Likewise, according to the Śrīmata, the function of the vital breath is the support for the manifestation of Vaikharī speech.

It is also stated in the Kalātantra: "The letter Ha is remembered as the vital breath. Having thus taught the Vidyā which possesses both forms, he describes the procedure for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇavidhi) for its accomplishment.

"One should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvassevā*) by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while remaining motionless with the *yonibandha* posture, having resorted to the entrance of a cave, with a single-pointed mind and senses subdued.
Here, "preliminary service" means the *puraścaraṇa* rite; "having resorted to the entrance of a cave" refers to taking refuge there.
Having bound the *yonimudrā*, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times as a preliminary practice (*puraścaryā*).

The meaning is that one should perform the recitation (*japa*) for thirty days. And it is said in the *Śrī Haṃsabhedatantra*: "A hundred thousand [recitations] per month is prescribed. Subsequently, in order to demonstrate the initiation (*dīkṣā*)—which bestows upon the practitioner of the mantra (*sādhya*) the state of authority, which consists of the threefold knowledge (*trikavidyā*), which is both common and supremely secret—he introduces the question concerning the *kāmatattvayantra*, which is its primary constituent part, as mentioned in the section on the binding of the *yonimudrā* with the words, "the desire [is] resembling the *bandhūka* flower," by stating: "Even now there is doubt regarding the means of accomplishing the *kāmatattva* of the Deity."
"Grant me the attainment of pure consciousness, O Destroyer of Tripura!"— this refers to the *kāmatattva*,
which has "hṛllekhā" and so forth as its internal name, beginning with the king of desires (*kāmārāja*), and which is a specific yantra to be described later.
It is called "the attainment of pure consciousness" because it brings about the fruit through mere consciousness alone.
The illustrious Bhairava said: I shall describe in brief the characteristics of the principle of desire (kāmatattva).

"Listen to the supreme, divine attraction in brief, O Śeṣa"—this is easy to understand. "The wood (kāṣṭha) situated in the middle of desire (kāma), enclosed within the womb of desire (kāma)—one should accomplish desire by means of desire; this is called Hṛllekhā."

By the term "middle of desire" (*kāmamadhyam*), it means the King of Desire (*kāmarāja*) is without distinction; "made into the belly of desire" refers to the triangular arrangement (*trikoṇa-vinyāsa*) named "belly of desire," which consists of the twelve vowels. The sense is: "by what is it encapsulated? That is to say, that which resides in desire (*kāmastham*)—namely, the state of being in the middle of desire (*kāmamadhyasthyam*)—this second [element] must be encapsulated within the "belly of desire. This is the grammatical connection. By the mention of "encapsulation" (*saṃpuṭita*), he indicates the arrangement of the second "belly of desire" facing each other. Therefore, because of its triangular form, when the two 'E's (the vowel *ai*) are arranged facing each other in an upper-lower relationship, it becomes a hexagon (*ṣaṭkoṇa*); this is how it should be understood. Although not explicitly stated here, the commentary (*vivaraṇa-grantha*) will be explained later, so the point designated as the "Bindu" (*bindu-saṃjñita*) should be inserted in the middle. He himself will explain the nature of the "Hṛllekhā" and others among the "residing in desire" (*kāmastha*) etc., in the subsequent passage beginning with "kāmaṃ dambhu... [referring to the *Kāmadambhu*]. Regarding the phrase "one should accomplish by means of desire" (*kāmena sādhayet kāmiti*), there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) to be supplied there: "by this desire" (*anena kāmanā*). Thus, the fourfold group beginning with Hṛllekhā, which has the aforementioned form, is the essence of desire (*kāmatattva*). As it says in the *Śrīrudrayāmala*: "Hṛllekhā, Kāmarāja, Vāgbhava, Bindu, and Trīṃ."* *Note: The text contains several lacunae marked by asterisks where the original manuscript was likely damaged or illegible.*

(p. 44) The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive a dharma that is the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive a dharma that is enlightenment. Since he does not perceive these dharmas, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not dwell upon them. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of wisdom, become one who has set out for full enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a dharma that is a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive a dharma that is the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive a dharma that is enlightenment. Since he does not perceive these dharmas, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not dwell upon them. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of wisdom, becomes one who has set out for full enlightenment. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of wisdom, become one who has entered the fixed course toward enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a dharma that is a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive a dharma that is the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive a dharma that is enlightenment. That which is called *kāra* is proclaimed as the "fivefold desire" (*kāmapañcaka*), namely Kāmarāja, Manmatha, and so forth. It should be understood that the fifth [syllable] is the designation for *hṛllekha*. And thus it will be stated there: "O Dear One, by means of the conjunction of those situated in reverse order from the two hundred thousand [syllables], this extraction (*uddhāra*) is to be understood through instruction during the vow. This awakens all the principles (*tattva*). O Goddess, this is the mouth of Parā, the abode of the activity of radiant energy (*tejas*). O Dear One, Manmatha is born from the form of their conjunction. I shall speak of Kandarpa... [which is] preceded by *Ā*, situated on the path of the elements (*bhūtamārga*), and joined with the first [vowel]. O Goddess, Kandarpa is declared to be the practice born of yoga."
Formerly, there was Kṣabha; his son was Tejas, who had eleven sons.

"O Dear One, the two hands [are] 'Aḥ' in the east, and 'Manohū' comes [thereafter]"—by this, the meaning is as follows: by means of this arrangement prescribed by the order of recitation, one should write the syllable *strīṃ*, known as the *kāmatattva*, together with *kāma*. This is the essential meaning: for when it is done thus, the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the *kāmatattva* occurs; therefore, one should practice it. Having established the word *nihita* (placed), the term *kāma-tattva* will be explained here. "One should propitiate the *kāmatattva*"—from this, one must understand that this sequence of arranging the diagram (*yantra-vinyāsa-krama*) is intended by the one speaking thus. How so? First, the *hṛllekhā*; then the *kāmarāja*; and surrounding that *kāmarāja-hṛllekhā* on all sides, the form of a hexagon (*ṣaṭkoṇa*).

The syllable born of speech (*vāgbhava*) is designated as the *yoni*; in its corners, one should write the syllables designated as *bindu*, namely *bḷṃ*. Then, having formed the abode of Kandarpa, which is divided into two, one should draw the encapsulation of the hexagon and the form of the woman (*strīkāra*). For it is said in the *Śrīmata*: "One should place the King of Desire (*kāmarāja*) situated in the center of Manmatha. Having made the temple of Kandarpa, which has become twofold, one should bestow [the syllables] upon the six corners. Those four are the Great Desires; one should cast them into the belly of the fifth. One should cast desire by means of desire. The meaning is that one should cast this *kāmarāja*-yantra into the *yoni* of Kāma and contemplate it as being contained therein. "Having made [her] desired by means of desire, one should certainly cause the one situated in desire to tremble. Thus, having made the soul of the target by means of the *kāmarāja*-yantra, one should certainly cause the one situated in desire—that is, the one situated in the *yoni*—to tremble, meaning the nectar situated in the *visarga*. And it is said in the *Śrīmata*: "That which rises from the place of birth is the eternal mandala (*dhruvamaṇḍala*). This will be clarified by the commentary beginning with "by *huṃ*" and ending with "then one should certainly cause that to tremble. In this wheel, one should meditate on the King of Desire, who is worshipped by the world; this is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "situated in desire, to be known in the world" and so forth: "world" (*bhuvana*) means the place of existence. "The body in the middle of desire."

By the phrase "in the midst of desire" (*kāmamadhye*), he will state the previously mentioned term "situated in the midst of desire. One should understand that "situated in the midst of desire" refers to the *vigraha* (the formal body or configuration). One should know the nature of desire (*kāmasvarūpa*). Regarding the nature: the mantra known as Kāmarāja is the belly of desire; the womb (*yoni*) is Vāmā, which is Vāgbhava. The sequence is: "that which is at the end of the two folds (*puṭānta*) shall be known as the Bindu. "At the end of the folds" refers to the six corners [of the triangle]. "Known as the Bindu" means one should accomplish the turning by way of the turning of the Yantra. One should accomplish it with desire. This is the explanation of the word "desire" (*kāma*). Indeed, this very desire is to be projected into the womb of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya-yoni*). This is the explanation of "one should cast desire into desire. From "the churning of the name of the Bindu" up to "one should agitate," it is the explanation of "having made it desired by desire, one should certainly agitate that which stands in desire. By the word "Bindu," the self of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is spoken of; and thus it is said in the *Śrīmata*: "The Bindu is declared to be the Self; this man within is awakened. By the first word... *(Note: The provided source text contains numerous ellipses (* * *) indicating missing portions. The translation above reflects the available Sanskrit fragments and their logical connection based on standard tantric exegetical conventions.)*
This indicates the excellence of constant practice; thus it is said in the *Śrīmata*:
"Furthermore, one should repeatedly perceive the form of the Self within that [space];
for this is declared to be 'churning,' which destroys the impurity of ignorance."
That which is called *visarga* refers to the Moon-Island (*candradvīpa*) at the end of the sixteenth [digit].

That which is called the Path of Power (*śaktimārga*) is the Suṣumnā; likewise, it is said in the Śrīmata: "One should agitate that which is situated in the womb, known as the Path of Power, the Suṣumnā."

This is an adverbial modifier of the action (*kriyā*). Here, one should also recall what was stated in the *Saṅgrahasūkta*: "having performed the desired act through desire. By that very [statement], it is said: having fashioned the "instrument of desire" (*kāmayantra*) in the form described for the womb of the object (*sādhya*), and having constrained the self of the object with that very instrument of desire, one should cause the nectar situated in the emission of the object to be stirred by means of the practitioner's own self. In such a way that, being emitted through the path of its power (*śaktimārga*), it reaches the womb of the object; thus, this very "secret initiation" (*rahasyadīkṣā*), though introduced first as belonging to the world of the object, is so designated. What need is there for much speaking here? It is easy to understand that it is "fashioned," O fair-faced one. Immediately thereafter, he states the instrument of the seed-syllable of Power (*śaktibījayantra*).

"Having drawn the previously mentioned great Yantra which denotes Tripurā"—that is to say, having first drawn the Tripurā Yantra as previously described. "Vāgbhava" is now being designated; that is to say, it should be written in the place of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the Great Lotus Yantra which is about to be described. One should write it on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*) together with *gorocanā* (yellow pigment) and with the *svayambhūkusuma* (spontaneously produced flower) arising from the *kuṇḍa* and the *gola*.
Here, by the word *kuṇḍa*, the female sexual organ (*yoni*), which serves as her sign, is denoted.

By the word *gola* (ball), he intends the male organ (*puṃcihna*), and by the word *kusuma* (flower), he intends the menstrual flow (*ārtava*). Here, "self-born" (*svayambhū*) refers to that which has first arisen. Thus, by the term *kuṇḍagolodbhava*, the semen and blood produced from the union of a woman and a man, in their combined form, are designated. By the word "flower," [he refers to] the self-born [organ] of the woman.

"First, the seasonal [menses] have arisen; by those two and with yellow pigment (gorocanā), one should draw"—this is the meaning. "A great lotus with sixteen spokes, but twelve spokes on the outside; again, sixteen petals, and thirty-two on its outside. Thus, it should be understood that one should draw a sixteen-spoked lotus surrounding the Vāgbhava-yantra which occupies the position of the pericarp (*karṇikā*). By the word *ara*, the petals (*dala*) are designated. One should draw twelve spokes on the outside of that, and thirty-two spokes on the outside of that as well. "In the pericarp, however, the Vāgbhava; above that, the Kāmarāja. By the word "pericarp," the previously mentioned sixteen-spoked great lotus situated at the edge of the Vāgbhava-yantra is indicated through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), because it resides in the center of the yantra. Indeed, this [lotus], being a collection of petals, cannot primarily be considered a [single] part. But the pericarp is the Vāgbhava-yantra itself as first established. Here, by the word "Vāgbhava," the sixteen vowels are denoted. And so, when he himself explains it later: "In the first, the groups of vowels. Regarding "above the Kāmarāja": since it will be explained later that "one should place the Kāmarāja, having divided the Kāmarāja according to the twelve vowel-distinctions," the seed-syllable (*bīja*) intended here for "Kāmarāja" is indeed without vowels (*anacka*). "Above that" means on the twelve-spoked [lotus]. "Above that, one should write the Śakti-seed, the Great Yoni, a hundred times"—"above that" means on the sixteen-spoked [lotus] situated outside the twelve-spoked one. By the term "Śakti-seed," he intends that very [Kāmarāja]. The name "Great Yoni" occurs in the subsequent sūtra.

(p. 49) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna-svabhāva). "Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is the grasping of names and characteristics (nāmalakṣaṇa-grahaṇa) based on the dependent self-nature; it is like seeing a rope in the dark and perceiving it as a snake. This is called the imagined self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the dependent self-nature? It is the manifestation of various appearances (nimitta) arising from the habit-energy (vāsanā) of false discrimination (vikalpa); it is like a dream, a mirage, or a reflection. This is called the dependent self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the perfected self-nature? It is the state in which the imagined self-nature is not perceived within the dependent self-nature; it is the realization that all phenomena are devoid of the duality of grasper and grasped (grāhyagrāhaka). This is called the perfected self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of the Great Vehicle? It is the realization of the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena, the entry into the gate of the Tathāgata-garbha, and the attainment of the stage of the Tathāgata. This is called the self-nature of the Great Vehicle. "Mahāmati, if one does not understand these four kinds of self-nature, one will fall into the views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) and fail to distinguish between the nature of the mind and the nature of external objects. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should cultivate wisdom through skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) and enter into the realm of the Tathāgatas. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati, along with the assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had taught. (p. 49) *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Chapter on the Characteristics of the Dharmas (Dharmalakṣaṇaparivarta).

That which is about to be described is figuratively called the "thirty-two-petaled [lotus]" because it is to be arranged upon the yantra. "Situated therein" means desiring to enter into its interior. By this, the meaning is as follows: one should write the seed-syllable of Śakti within the sixteen-petaled [lotus] situated inside the thirty-two-petaled one. Regarding the verse: "The Great Yoni (mahāyoni), known as the mother of the three worlds, consists of three staffs (tridaṇḍa) joined with a bindu, and is distinguished by the twelve vowels. The aggregate of three staffs is *tridaṇḍa*. These are any one of the letters from *ha*, *sa*, *au*, etc., up to *sa*; the *bindu* is the *anusvāra*; and the "twelfth vowel" is *ai*. Therefore, the meaning is this: the sequence consisting of any one of the letters from *ha*, *sa*, *au*, etc., up to *sa*, together with *ai* and the *bindu*, is designated as the "Great Yoni. In this context, although not explicitly stated, it is understood by implication that the forms beginning with *ka* and ending with *sa* are to be arranged on the outer circle of the yantra, on the thirty-two petals; for the author will later state: "Outside of that, all the Mātṛkās [are to be placed]."
Then, having divided the *svarasaṅghāta* in the first [position] and the *kāmarāja* in the second by means of the twelve vowel variations, one should install them.
In the great sixteen-petaled lotus, one should cause the vowel to pierce through the divisions beginning with Śakti;
outside of that, O Supreme Goddess, one should cause all the Mātṛkās to be provided with the primordial bindu and the creeper, mounted upon the seed-syllable Haṃsa.
This supreme, divine machine is difficult to find even throughout the three worlds.
"One should envelop everything within the interior of the temple by means of a hollow space.
Now, because the method of arranging these [syllables], beginning with the Vāgbhava, has not been clearly stated, he clarifies that very point.
