The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, do you see that dharma which, having reached the stage of non-retrogression, will attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, do you see that dharma which, having attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, turns the wheel of Dharma? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, do you see that dharma which, having turned the wheel of Dharma, establishes beings in the three vehicles? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, do you see that dharma which, having established beings in the three vehicles, causes them to enter parinirvāṇa? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, since you do not see any such dharma, how could you say, ‘I have set out on the bodhisattva path,’ or ‘I am irreversible,’ or ‘I shall attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,’ or ‘I shall turn the wheel of Dharma,’ or ‘I shall establish beings in the three vehicles,’ or ‘I shall cause beings to enter parinirvāṇa’? Subhūti, it is because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature that they cannot be apprehended. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas.”

In the first [verse], by the phrase "the collection of vowels" (*svarasaṅghāta*), he describes the manner of arranging the first circle, explaining that the previously mentioned *vāgbhava* word denotes sixteen repetitions. Regarding the phrase "the Kāmarāja," etc.: by excluding six groups of four, there remains a selection of twelve vowels; with intent, one should arrange the *kāmarāja*—consisting of the letters *ka* and *la*—along with any one of those twelve vowels. This is the arrangement of the second circle. Regarding the phrase "sixteen-spoked," etc.: the term *śakti* refers to the letter *sa*. One should write that very letter joined individually with the sixteen vowels. This is the arrangement of the third circle. Regarding the phrase "outside of that," etc.: although the word *mātṛkā* here encompasses all phonemes (*varṇa*), since the vowels have already been employed in the previous circles, only the thirty-two consonants from *ka* to *sa* are taken, as their employment has not yet been prescribed. *Bindu* is the *anusvāra*. *Nāda* is the prolonged resonance of that very [bindu]. The vertical line is the placement of the *bindu* and *nāda*; these indeed are the *kalās*, and the phonemes are the constituents of the *kalās*. Here, it is understood from what was stated before that each of the consonants from *ka* to *sa*, accompanied by the *bindu* and *nāda*, is to be differentiated by the twelve vowels along with the *mekāra* (the letter *ma*). By the term "Haṃsa-seed" (*haṃsabīja*), he intends the letters *ha* and *sa*. This is the arrangement of the thirty-two-spoked circle. Regarding the phrase "this yantra," etc.: the word "temple" (*mandira*) denotes the *saṃvarta* syllable. Thus, it is said in the *Śrīmata Manthānabhairava*: "The letter *ka* is declared the temple; the Mistress is the goddess of the phonemes. The word "aperture" (*suṣira*) is the seed-syllable of space (*ākāśa*).

This is the meaning of the term *ghoṣavarṇa*: having placed this kind of yantra in the center of the syllable designated as *mandira* (the letter *ma*), one should cast this yantra, together with that letter *kṣa*, into the center of the letter *ha*, which is designated as *suṣira*. Here, by means of the letters *ha* and *kṣa*, he indicates the Great Mother (*mahāmātṛkā*) consisting of seventy million syllables, wherein vowels and consonants are intermingled. Therefore, the arrangement of the yantra of the seed-syllable of Śakti (*śaktibīja*) should be understood. First, having drawn the previously mentioned *vāgbhava*-yantra in the place of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should arrange four mandalas around it, having sixteen, twelve, sixteen, and thirty-two spokes respectively. Therein, in the first mandala, one vowel should be placed on each petal; thus, the sixteen vowels are to be arranged. Next, in the second, the twelve-spoked [mandala], there is the sequential arrangement of the twelve vowels—excluding the group of six and four—each joined with the form of the digit known as *kāmarāja*. In the third, the sixteen-spoked [mandala], the sixteen vowels are also to be placed, each conjoined with the letter *sa*, which is designated as *śakti*. In the fourth, the thirty-two-spoked [mandala], there are thirty-two letters from *sa* to *ha*, each conjoined with the letter *e*, the bindu, and the nāda, and associated with the *mahāyoni*. Having written such a yantra, one writes the encircling letter *kṣa*, and then one should write the letter *ha* encircling that as well. "In this wheel, the best of practitioners should indeed meditate upon the seed-syllable of Śakti. This protection has been declared by me under the name *Tripurabhairavī*; it is easy to understand.
p.
52) One who is endowed with the name Kanyā, having resorted to the entrance of a cave,
should place [the substance] below the *yonikuṇḍa* and perform the fire-oblation (*homayet*) with handfuls (*puṭaiḥ*) of black mustard seeds (*rājikā*).

This is the meaning of the "womb-shaped" (*yonyākāra*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*): he who desires the daughters of the *nāgas* should, while mentally reciting their names, resort to the entrance of a cave, dig a certain pit in the shape of a womb, place a mechanical device beneath it, and satisfy the carrier of smoke with mustard seeds. After seven nights, O Great Goddess, they become agitated, intoxicated by passion, tormented by the fire of separation, and their bodies overcome by fainting. Then those women fall before the practitioner, weeping. Thus it is easy to understand, O practitioner, O great being, O Lord of the Golden Form (*Hāṭakeśvara-vigraha*): having entered, perform your duty as a practitioner over the object to be accomplished. "O practitioner!"—this is the speech of the *nāga* maidens, drawn by the power of the machine; having entered [the cave], he too sports there until the dissolution of all beings (*ābhūtasamplava*). This is clearly understood.
Thus ends the second chapter in the commentary on the latter six chapters.

Now, within the venerable Trika-vidyā, which is divided into gross and subtle aspects, having described the gross vidyā— composed of Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti— together with its specific details such as the yantras and so forth, [the author] now begins to explain the subtle form of pure vidyā, which consists solely of specific [inner] distinctions. In this context, he proceeds to expound the *Śrī-mṛtyuñjaya-sāra*, the convention of the words and so forth, the convention of the meaning of the syllables, and the *Kulacakra* composed of the venerable Great Mātṛkā, as it arises from the essential nature of the deities of the *Merukrama* and the venerable Circle of Great Gurus (*mahāgurumaṇḍala*) as taught in the *Amṛtodyota*.
O Goddess of the lords of knowledge, what is the specific nature of the Kula-sphere?
What is the meaning of its syllables, and likewise, what is the nature of its feet and so forth?
"O Lord of the Kula, tell me, what indeed is the *kulacakra*?
Thus [ends the question]. Now, the answer to these four questions is explained in sequence:
"O beautiful one, listen to the extraction of the *vaiṣika* and the triad."
"O Queen of the Gods, that knowledge which [is not known] by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, and the others"—
this is easy to understand.
It is indeed both the lower (aparā) and the higher (parā), as well as the intermediate (parāparā).

"These supreme powers are said to belong to the sequence of the Trika-vidyā. Thus, because they constitute the vital energy (*vīrya*) of the sequence of the Trika-vidyā, these powers are described as having this specific form. "The supreme phoneme in the form of sound (*nāda*), the supreme, the Brāhmī, and the supreme-non-supreme (parāparā)—the Trika-vidyā extracted from these should be known through the teacher’s instruction.
This vidyā, when devoid of [ordinary] expansion (*prastāra*), brings about the destruction of the multitude of sins."

The resonance of the *nāda* is that Supreme (*parā*) whose nature is soundless and whose nature is beyond all phonemes; she is the form of Brāhmī. Known as both Supreme (*parā*) and Intermediate (*aparā*), she is devoid of the three seed-syllables beginning with *vāgbhava*. She alone is the *trikavidyā* (the triple knowledge). She is to be understood solely through the instruction of the Guru. And she is the essence of the mantra-form of the ancient seat (*pīṭha*). The ancient seat is called Oḍḍiyāna; its mantra is the *praṇava* (OM). She is established therein as its vital potency (*vīrya*). By this, [she is] Brāhmī, who is beyond the phonemes beginning with the resonance (*ghoṣa*).
p.

54) It indicates that the form of the *praṇava* when conjoined [with the other syllables] is called *sādākhya*. Having thus described the specific knowledge (*viśeṣavidyā*) in general terms, he begins to explain its divisions: "Now, O Bhairavī, mistress of the lords of heroes, listen to the specific knowledge and the divisions of knowledge as they truly are, O Queen of the Gods. This is easily understood.
[The goddesses are] Parāparā, the Goddess Parā, and Aparā, respectively.
"She is called Vāgvādinī and is considered the supreme among all vidyās.
Thus, Brāhmī is the vidyā whose nature consists of sound, color, and the form of the cakra; that is to say, she is Vāgvādinī.
And so it is said: "The world says of one who has spoken [well], 'He is Vāc'."

"Brāhmī, Māheśī, Parāparā, Parākramā, Vidyeśvareśvarī, and Bhairavī—thus have I proclaimed her. This is the proclamation of the Supreme (Parā). The letters are the Lower (Aparā), and this sequence beginning with Brāhmī is the Intermediate (Parāparā). Bhairavī is the Vidyā; she is a wondrous manifestation, a mass of throbbing bliss, and the direct realization of that marvelous nature of the Self. She bestows that [realization]. Furthermore, because the world, through the excess of joy born from perceiving such a wondrous object, speaks of her as being under her very sway, she is thus honored as Bhairavī, the Queen of the Vidyā of Transcendent Order (Vyutkrama).
"Killing is praised as common [to all], yet it is accompanied by Yama.

This means that the *vidyā* known as Yamārājñī—the reverse sequence of the *Bhairavī-vidyākrama* taught immediately following in the *Sūpravarasūtra*—is indeed the opposite [of that sequence]. Having made the first sound of the *Brāhmī* [mantra] the starting point according to the order of recitation, and having placed the "sisters" (*bhātṛvya*) in a state of exhaustion, this is the perfected *vidyā* of Yama’s sister; such is the meaning. And thus, the *darvī*...
A person afflicted by poison cries out in distress; O gentle one,
the knowledge that reveals one's own self is indeed called the "Ah" (the exclamation of pain),
while the solar [knowledge] is said, O Goddess, to be the means for accomplishing the Supreme Self.
In this case, there is a reversal of the sequence for Vāg-vādinī, who is the sound of the first syllable.
O Goddess, the Vidyā is fourfold and bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
indeed, this Vidyā is accomplished through knowledge alone, and not without the Command (ājñā).
He alone should be known as the bestower of the fruits of the fourfold aims of life.

The meaning is as follows: by "knowledge" (jñānena), it is intended that the command (ājñā) consisting of mantras and so forth—which bring beings under control—once deliberated upon, is accomplished merely through the recognition [of its nature] due solely to the wondrous power of *vidyā*. Regarding the statement: "He declares the potency (*vīrya*) of the *vidyās*, mantras, mudrās, and those whose essence is the *maṇḍala*: 'This *vidyā* is Parā, the supreme command of the Supreme Lord,'" the word "here" (*atra*) is used primarily to conform to the requirements of the verse composition. It intends that the practitioner desires to seize for himself the specific realization of the powers beginning with Parā; it does not, however, intend a specific sequence of verbal recitation. The essential point is this: she alone is the inherent potency within the respective functions of all *vidyās*, mantras, mudrās, and *maṇḍalas*. Once the lord of practitioners has been empowered merely by this realization, he becomes capable of accomplishing those various tasks and actions effortlessly, even through other means such as *vidyās* and the like. The reason for this is stated: "Because she is this command of the Supreme Lord."
Now, in order to explain the meaning of the syllables as it has come in due order, he says:
"O Beloved, listen; I shall tell you the instruction on the meaning of the syllables.

Even the gods do not know, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas, the meaning that is revealed through the transposition of the syllables known as Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti—the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the Traipura-vidyā—which take on the forms of deities such as Agni and others. That is the "meaning of the syllables" (*akṣarārtha*). Therein, first, he sets forth the mantra that expresses Jātavedas (Agni) by means of the transposition of the Vāgbhava syllable.
Śrīkaṇṭha and Vālīśa, and immediately after them Mahākāla.

"The mantra of the innate [sahaja] is indeed the divine [divya] *jātavedasaḥ*. Here, the letter *a* is Śrīkaṇṭha; the letter *ya* is Vālīśa; and the letter *ma* is Mahākāla. By means of these, this becomes the mantra-form of the word *jātavedasaḥ* in its nominative singular case-ending. In this context, the sequence of the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable] consists of the vowel *a*, the source (*yoni*), and the nasal drop (*bindu*). Therein, between the initial and final letters, the middle term—which is called the "source" (*yoni*)—possesses a dual nature, like a phoneme (*varṇa*), by virtue of being composed of both vowels and consonants (*arṇātmakatva*), as it exists in the form of a *saṃhitā*. Having thus attained the state of a phonemic sequence consisting of those elements, and making the middle letter *ya* the central part of that *saṃhitā*-form, when it is uttered in this manner, it becomes the mantra. Regarding this, there is a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*): "This Agni is the first-born of Truth," "He is this world, he is this Agni," and "This Agni is Vaiśvānara."
Now he states the exchange for Kāmarāja:
"Mahokāla, then Ṇḍīśa, Pīnākī, and Krodhabhairava—
this is the mantra of Paramāna, which bestows union with the Yoginīs."

Mahākāla is the letter *ma*; Jhaṇḍīśa is the letter *ya*; Pinākī is the letter *la*; and Krodheśvara is the letter *ka*. By this sequence, the mantra signifying the Purifier (*pavamāna*) is revealed. "Bestowing union with the Yoginīs" means that it brings about the union—that is, the state of aesthetic resonance (*sāmarasya*)—of the lord of practitioners with the Yoginīs, such as the Mistress of the Sacred Seats (*pīṭheśvarī*). Here, one should understand that a transposition has been made: having placed the nasal (*anusvāra*), which constitutes the end of the Kāmarāja mantra, at the beginning; having removed the vowel *ā* from the third and fourth [letters] in their respective order and applied it to the seed-syllable of the Yoni (*yonībīja*); and having manifested the second and third positions of the first letter *ka* as the fourth. For the Purifier indeed functions in two ways: as the upward breath (*prāṇa*) and the downward breath (*apāna*). The upward breath is Fire, and the downward breath is the Sun. Through the union of these two, the mantra becomes one whose very form is "union" (*melaka*). Now, he demonstrates the meaning of the letters of the Seed-syllable of Power (*śaktibīja*).
"O fawn-eyed one, Śrīkarṇa, Bhṛgu, and Anugraheśa have themselves been declared to you as belonging to this Mārtaṇḍabhairava. Here,
"Śrīkaṇṭha" refers to the syllable *su* (the sound of a good musical instrument), "Bhṛgu" is the letter *sa*, and the vowel *o* is "Anugraheśa."

Here, in place of the word *ghoṣa*, there is the arrangement of the first letter. Thus it is said in the venerable *Niśvāsakārikā*: "The letter *a* and the letter *ha*, when elided, become one in form. By this, the form of the word *pulliṅginodaḥ* in the nominative singular case becomes the mantra. For this very reason, due to the elision of the case-ending, there is no pronunciation of the *visarjanīya* here. This is the solar mantra. And so says the Śruti:

That which rises glowing is the Sun (Āditya). Now, having described the statement of the Bhaṭṭārikā—who consists solely of the twenty-first [letter] of the supreme power (*parā-śakti*), and who kindles the three cities of the Prājña, Taijasa, and Viśva, composed of Soma, Sūrya, and Vahni—he begins to demonstrate the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*) of the mantra of the Supreme Śiva, the *Haṃsa*, in accordance with its subject matter: "Mahākāla, Ha, Visarga—these are the letters of the immeasurable splendor; this mantra of the pervasive one, whose light is threefold, is most powerful. *Mahākāla* is the letter *Ma*. *Ha* and *Visarga* are the sounds *Ha* and the *visarjanīya*. Here, keeping in mind the structure of the verse, he intends to omit the sequential order and simply includes the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Indra (*Ha*) in their entirety. He does not, however, show that this is the actual sequence of the letters of the mantra being explained. Thus it is seen in the *Śrīmūlāvatāra*: "Establish the form *īhaṃ*. Therein, the sequence of the mantra is *bhrū-mati-bhi-mantra-kramaṃ*. [It says: "O fair-faced one, *śrīmate īraha īlakaṃ caiva īrastaṃ ca*. Here, the sequence of the mantra is *hīṃ klīṃ strīṃ*. And so, because it is established as the literal meaning of the letters—the immeasurable splendor (*amita-tejas*) that is the pervasive one of the three lights (Soma, Sūrya, etc. and has become Brahman—it is impossible for there to be any other sequence of its demonstration except for that which consists of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and the controller (*viniyāmaka*). Therefore, a corresponding sequence of letters must be envisioned. This is indeed the sequence established for the extraction (*uddhāra*) of the *Haṃsa*: the first is the sound (*ghoṣa*), the second is *Bhava* (*Bha*), the third is the letter *Ma*, and the fourth is *Bhṛgu* (*U*).

(p. 59) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. [The text continues: "Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is that which is grasped by ordinary people and Śrāvakas as having the characteristics of form and so forth, based on the appearances of objects such as earth, water, fire, wind, mountains, trees, palaces, and forests. This is called the imagined self-nature. [The text continues: "Mahāmati, what is the dependent self-nature? It is the manifestation of the mind (citta) and mental factors (caitta) appearing as objects due to the habit-energy (vāsanā) of false discrimination from beginningless time. This is called the dependent self-nature. [The text continues: "Mahāmati, what is the perfected self-nature? It is the state in which the dependent self-nature is seen as being eternally free from the characteristics of the imagined self-nature; it is the realization of the non-duality of subject and object, and the attainment of the wisdom of the Tathāgata. This is called the perfected self-nature. [The text continues: "Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha? It is the storehouse of all the Buddha-qualities, which is pure from the very beginning, yet obscured by the adventitious defilements (āgantuka-kleśa); it is the basis for the arising of the three bodies (trikāya) of the Tathāgatas. This is called the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. [The text concludes: "Mahāmati, these are the four kinds of self-nature. If one does not understand these, one will fall into the views of eternalism or nihilism. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should cultivate the insight into the non-arising of all phenomena through the wisdom of the Tathāgata-garbha."

Regarding the fifth [syllable], "bhava": its *makāra* is "bhava," which is Śrīkaṇṭha in the form of Bhṛgu; this should be understood as a transposition in the sequence of the mantra. In that regard, the visarga of Bhṛgu must be removed from the beginning because it belongs to the end of the mantra. By this sequence, when the mantras are uttered, the Kula deities become angry with the practitioners and seize their vital constituents (*dhātu*s), O Bhairavī. Regarding the phrase "by this": the meaning is as shown by the measure of the syllables. For a practitioner who accepts such a sequence, there arises an adverse consequence (*pratyavāya*) caused by the improper manifestation of the deities, Agni and the others. If so, what [should be done]?
He said, "Let the sequence be received. The reversal of the names of the energies (tejas), as taught from the mouth of the Guru, is established:
Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, Śakti, Haṃsa, and Trīśvara.
Those great-souled ones who live thus attain swift accomplishment,
and the deities bestow their grace upon those who take refuge in the wheel of the lineage.

The meanings of the syllables have been demonstrated as follows: *vāyu*, *savitra*, *tejas*, and *tejaḥ* are the terms denoted by the word "splendor" (*tejaḥ*). Their names, in order, are *ayaṃ*, *melakaḥ*, *asau*, and *mahaḥ*—these four. The reversal of these has been shown according to the sequence of extraction. These are the seed-syllables of Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, Śakti, and Haṃsa. By adopting these and breaking down the previously mentioned names, for those who recite [the mantra], there arises the attainment of the highest good. For deities, when worshipped with their names pronounced exactly as they stand, attain satisfaction; likewise, even common people, though not yet fully grown, respond to their own names being clearly articulated by an adult, just as a child does.

(p. 60) They are seen to be delighted by conversations in which the syllables are not clearly articulated or are somewhat distorted, as uttered by the common people. And thus says the Śruti: "One should say 'Indra' instead of 'Indra'; one should say 'Indra' instead of one who is actually Indra; and one should say 'Indra' even when he is wounded. For the gods, like those who prefer the cryptic, favor the indirect. [The Śruti continues: "O Rudra, one should say 'May we procreate with offspring,' and not 'O Rudra,' because that is his very name. And also: "For the sake of avoidance. Having thus taught the convention regarding the meaning of the syllables, he states the convention regarding the words and so forth.
O Bhairavī, listen as I declare the convention of the initial syllables of the words,
which brings about the attainment of the fruit in the investigation of all mantras.

In this context, the Vidyā consists here of three quarters in the form of seed-syllables (*bīja*), namely the forms of Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti. Therefore, it is these very seed-syllables that are designated by the term "quarter" (*pāda*); their initial letters are known as Śrīkaṇṭha, Krodhanātha, and Lakulīśvara. Among them, the Supreme Lord abides as the convention (*saṅketa*) for grasping the entire Mātṛkā, according to the possibility, through the inclusion of the individual phonemes. That is the convention of the initial letters of the quarters; thus, its nature consists of the initial letters of the quarters which grasp the entire Mātṛkā. The essential meaning is as follows: by contemplating Me and also practicing this Vidyā, since the entire collection of mantras is composed of the Mātṛkā, the fruit of contemplating all the mantras is attained.
O Kuleśvarī, by means of Śrīkaṇṭha, who is beginningless, the entire seed-syllable of Vāgbhava has been acquired; it is the great Sārasvata-cakra.

Regarding the phrase "the seed-circle" (*bījacakram*): the sixteen vowels do not exist there [independently]; rather, as Śrīkaṇṭha states on page 61, the inclusion of the other vowels is shown by means of the first syllable and so forth.

O beautiful one, by the first Lord of Wrath (*krodhanātha*), that Yoni-cakra—which bestows the fruit of all desires—was extracted from the seed-syllable of Kāma. Here, "Lord of Wrath" refers to the consonant; by means of the first letter, which is the second of the labials (*vādi*) and ends with the letter *s*, the Yoni-cakra is known as being comprised of thirty-two syllables ending in *s*. By the first [teacher], Lakulīśa, [the extraction] of the seed-syllable of Śakti was performed, O beautiful one...
The science of the feet (pādavidyā) has been fully taught; it is the science of all things (sarvavidyā) transmitted through successive lineage.

Beginning with the third quarter, by means of the syllable *Ha*, which is Lakulīśa in essence, he grasps the Great Mātṛkā known as Saptakoṭīśvarī, who consists of a mixture of vowels and consonants. That very [Mātṛkā] is the Pāda-vidyā, consisting of the syllables of the *bhakṣas*; that is to say, it is the Caraṇa-vidyā. And so it is stated in the Śrīmata: "The name of the quarters is established in the *bhakṣas*. Thus, the state of being composed of the Mātṛkā through the mixture [of elements] in the Pāda-vidyā, and the corresponding nature of the Caraṇa-vidyā belonging to the venerable Saptakoṭīśvarī, are not elaborated here due to their supreme secret nature. Furthermore, the Meru-order and the divine nature of those three syllables beginning with the *pada* as deities are not demonstrated here for fear of violating the lineage of the divine [teachings], owing to their supreme secret nature.
"The definition of pervasion"—thus the Pādavidyā explains the *Śrīkuladdhaka*. Now, listen to the definition of the pervasion of the Kula-cakra;
the Kula-cakra is the armor of the Mothers (*mātṛ*).
In this very context, it was stated previously: "One should worship the lineage-path (kulapaddhati).
And that [lineage-path], which takes the form of a triangle, has begun to be revealed here through its expansion.

Therefore, its pervasion is that of the Vidyā. Its characteristic is the characteristic of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Regarding "of the Rudras, Bhairavas, and Vīras": the phoneme (*varṇa*) distinguished by the sequence from *A* to *Kṣa* [is the Mātṛkā]. The Rudras are those distinguished by the reverse order; the Bhairavas are the twenty-five phonemes beginning with *A* and ending with *Sa*. The Vīras are those measured by the [phonemes] beginning with *Kṣa* and ending with *Na*. This very *Mātṛkā*-wheel is indeed the entire essence (*sarvasva*) of them. Because it is the root of those various permutations of sequence, he calls it the "entire essence. "Yoganīkula" is the designation for the collection of the *Mātṛkā*s.
One should always contemplate [the deity] here within the hollow center of the heart-lotus, in its corner.
All the lines, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the visarga, have been clearly manifested.

Herein is the arrangement (*prastāra*) consisting of triangles. Thereupon, the sixteen vowels are to be placed upon the leftward line. Regarding the nature of their visualization, it says: "Well-worshipped by the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable], resembling ten million moons. By the phrase "well-worshipped by the *vāgbhava*," he shows that the mantra for their worship is the *vāgbhava*. "O Dear One, the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ta*, resting on the rightward line, are like many suns; the letters resting on the middle line are the *kāmarāja* [seed-syllables]. The procedure for this is as before. "The letters beginning with *tha* and ending with *sa*, resting on the frontward line, are like a mass of lightning; these excellent ones are associated with the *śakti-bīja* [seed-syllable]."

The meaning of this is the same as that of the previous [verse]: "In the center, the goddess Kulākula resides; the islands are established as Vidyā. Caṇḍī, possessing the luster of a rainbow, is the one who manifests through the Haṃsa-mantra.
She is to be known from the instruction of the Guru, and not by those who have not studied millions of scriptures. (p. 63)

In the center of this triangle—which consists of the lines of the left and right [channels], whose nature is Soma, Sūrya, and Agni, which is of the essence of Mantra, and which is worshipped with the three-footed Mantras of Vidyā—the Vidyā of the feet and so forth should be deposited. Its name is both *Kulākulā* and *Caṇḍī*, the Vidyā of the Mistress of seventy million [mantras]. By taking a single portion of that, even the Vidyā of the feet reveals its status as being that very Mantra. And the Mantra of this [Vidyā] is *Haṃsa*. Thus, by teaching that *Haṃsa*—which pervades the three [worlds], whose syllabic meaning has been demonstrated in the section on the feet, and which exists within the three rows of Mātṛkās worshipped as the three feet beginning with *Vāgbhava*—is the Mantra for worship, he indicates its preeminence even over the *Vāgbhava* and the others. Your own form consists of the *Kula-cakra*, and your rosary is likewise; similarly, the lotus and the book favored by the second [form] are also composed of you alone. "In this way, O Dear One, it should always be meditated upon in the center of the heart-lotus, as the supreme means for the attainment of Vidyā by yogins and yoginīs."
O Great Goddess, O Beloved, the Kula-cakra has been described by me through your grace;
O Goddess, Mistress of the Kula, for him who always contemplates it within the seat of the Command (ājñā),
the entire world— whether moving or stationary— becomes subject to his own power.

But he who is always of the *kula* lineage, with a mind intent upon the *yoni*, for him the *yoginīs* arise, afflicted by passion (*madanāturā*). In this manner, when one meditates sequentially upon the three supports— the heart-lotus of the *kula-cakra*, the station of the *ājñā*, and that known as the *mūladhāra*— the accomplishment of Sarasvatī arises in the world.
The Yoginī Prabhūtā demonstrates the state of fruition through her venerable qualities.
One should know that the Kula-cakra is indeed the divine body of Śiva;
one should abandon other scriptures and mantras like the dust at the feet [of the true teacher].
O fawn-eyed one, this most profound secret has been told to you;
it should be transmitted from ear to ear and must not be written in a book.
O beloved, this should always be given to a hero of great prowess who is joyful.

"To the devotee, to the exalted one among the lords of teachers, who is firm in his resolve"— thus, describing the pride of the Wheel in detail, he concludes. Thus ends the third chapter in the commentary on the *Uttara-ṣaṭka*.

Thus, having incidentally elucidated the specific knowledge (*viśeṣavidyā*) beginning with the syllables (*akṣara*), he now proceeds to explain the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) known as the Tripurā-yoga.
**The Tripurā-yoga**
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme Tripurā-yoga:
"That which resides in the center of the heart-space-lotus, known by the name Haṃsa.

Thus, [the compound] *hṛdvyomapadmamadhyastham* means situated in the middle of the two lotuses, the heart-lotus and the space-lotus. The "space-lotus" (*vyomapadma*) is that which is located above the station of the *bindu*, designated as the Yoga-pīṭha, and is called the Great Lotus Forest (*mahāpadmavana*). The word "name" (*nāma*) indicates its well-known status. This is the meaning: indeed, it is called by the name "Haṃsa" from that [station].

65) And it abides in the center of that heart-lotus. Furthermore, the intended meaning is that the place of the *haṃsa* is not only the heart-lotus, but also the space-lotus (*vyomapadma*). Thus, both of these—the *haṃsa* and the *paramahaṃsa*—are proclaimed as its stations in the venerable *Kubjikāmata*: "The *haṃsa* is beyond ninety-six; those who know the tradition (*āmnāya*) know it thus."
The Siddhas and Kaulas have attained [this state]; it is not within the sight of others.
There, having performed the worship according to the divine sequence, the yogi should proceed on foot;
by that means he shall go to that supportless state, the supreme state.

Regarding the statement "the twelve supports are the locus of the form" and "this supreme seed-syllable called Haṃsa is situated in the heart," by the term "Haṃsa," the two phonemes beginning with the letter *ha* (i.e., *haṃ* and *saṃ*) are understood. [He is] seated upon the throne of Yoga, accompanied by Cāmuṇḍā and Caṇḍikā.

Although this [mantra] called *ahaṃsa* has both as its substratum, nevertheless, having seated it upon the Yoga-pīṭha-throne, one should cause it to be joined with Cāmuṇḍā, the syllable *oṃ*, Caṇikā, and the visarga; this is the meaning.
As for what is called the Yoga-pīṭha, it is the seed-syllable of space (*vyomabīja*); one should fashion [the seat] by means of that very [syllable].

"One should conceive of Sadāśiva as the Supreme Lord, the *preta* (corpse)," means that one should conceive of Sadāśiva, the Supreme Lord, as the *preta* by means of the mantra mentioned immediately thereafter. This is the meaning: having subsequently uttered the seed-syllable of Śakti (*Hrīm*), one should then fashion the seat of the *preta* with the words "to Sadāśiva, the Great Corpse," ending with *namaḥ*.
66) "Upon that, one should place the form consisting of Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā."

The word "his" refers to the preta. "Donāma" is Lakulīśvara. "Bindu" is Saṃvartanātha. Of these two, [one should take] their *kalā*, which consists of the fifty phonemes—that is to say, the sixteen vowels are the *kalās* of the letter *ha*, and the consonants from *ka* to *ra* (excluding *la*) up to *kṣa* are those of the other. One should fashion the faces and limbs by means of that very mantra.
One should meditate on the form of Maheśānī with an unwavering inner self.
Resembling the rising sun and crowded with many rays.
The Goddess, whose complexion is like the hue of the bandhūka flower, whose form is as red as vermilion,
who is clothed in red garments, and adorned with all ornaments;
She wears a mass of matted hair, is serene, has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament,
is endowed with all auspicious marks, and is seated upon a lotus throne.
Her hips were full and rounded, her breasts were elevated and fleshy;
she was situated amidst waves of folds and adorned with a line of body hair.
The supreme Goddess who is the consciousness of the bliss of wine, the producer of supreme delight,
the enchantress of the three worlds, with a slightly smiling countenance.
The supreme Goddess Śivā, possessing a divine form, having two eyes,
endowed with all ornaments, and seated upon a lotus-throne in the sky.
"By that which rests in the left hand, consisting of divine knowledge, and not [otherwise]"—up to this point, the meaning is easy to understand.
With her right hand, she holds a rosary of beads (*akṣamālā*) which possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns;

"with the hand joined in the mudrā" means together with that which is known as the *vyākhyāna-mudrā*. She is bound together by severed heads (*muṇḍa*) resembling ten million suns, bearing flickering garlands of flames;
she is of divine form and emits red drops.
A garland composed of fierce vidyās, hanging down as far as the soles of her feet.
One should meditate upon the goddess Vibhūti, the mother of the worlds, as being like black antimony.

Having meditated thus upon the Great Goddess—she who is indeed endowed with a brilliance like that of the sun and so forth, who is the garland of severed heads (*muṇḍamālā*), who is Consciousness (*cit*), Caṇḍikā, consisting of the Vidyā, known as the Caṇḍividya, composed of a mixture of vowels and consonants, and who is the Great Mother (*māhāmātṛkā*)—for she, having transformed into the form of a garland of heads, has resorted to the supreme form of the Lord and exists as Caṇḍikā, "dwelling in the midst of the Kadamba forest. In this context, her seat is the interior of that sky-lotus known as the "Great Forest" (*mahāvana*). Regarding that which was previously called the "Kadamba-globule," he expresses it here by the word "Kadamba. The sense is that because it is surrounded by a forest and is continuous, it is a "forest. And it is said in the *Śrīmatottara*: "She who dwells in the Kadamba forest, filled with many rays of light."
"Situated on the upper path, filled with a thousand-petaled lotus,
raining down a flood of nectar with a luster red like molten lac—
one should bathe the Goddess with that very supreme nectar. Here, "upper..."
By the word *mārga*, he denotes the twelfth [tattva] situated above the Mahāpadmavana forest;
from that, it is revealed as the illustrious Kamanninne Śrīmat.

The supreme [state] is said to be at the *dvādaśānta*, indeed subtle and reaching the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). Therein, the flow of nectar is also shown in that very place: "The beautiful one, twelve finger-breadths in extent, situated around the great aperture, flows upward from the *dvādaśānta*; she is remembered as flowing there with the luster of liquid lac. Having meditated upon the lotus of this nature, the meaning is that the practitioner should bathe the Goddess with the supreme nectar arising therefrom.
For the high-souled practitioner who practices in this manner:
The three worlds are thoroughly agitated; it cannot be otherwise, O goddess praised by heroes!

This is easily understood. Here, that *trikavidyā* (the science of the triad) is twofold: consisting of speech (*vāṅmayī*) and consisting of light (*jyotirmayī*). Among these, the one consisting of speech has the nature of *vaikharī*, which is manifested by the places of articulation and efforts (*varṇasthānaprayatna*), and is bound to the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇapravṛtti*). That very [speech] is indicated according to its form as having three quarters (*pāda*). The one consisting of light—known by the names *uccāra*, *ṣmāmāṇā*, *aparā*, *madhyamā*, and *paśyantī*—is the science (*vidyā*) that is spontaneously arisen and innate, belonging to the inner self (*adhyātmahāratī*). It takes the forms of arising, dissolution, and rest, respectively, within the triad of secret abodes known as the *ādhāra*, the heart, and the *brahmarandhra*. Thus says the Śruti: "There are three voices; the foremost is the shining light. And: "Speech is measured in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them."

"Three [quarters] of speech are hidden in the cave, not moving; humans speak only the fourth. Regarding this very [speech], he begins to describe the manner of its cultivation and the locations for its arising and resting:
"How is the meditation on the mantra taught, and how does its emergence occur?"
O Goddess, in what does dissolution occur, and how does rest come to be?
"O Great Lord, please tell this out of compassion," [he said]. This is easily understood.
In that regard, because the mantra-meditation corresponds to the resting places of the ocean, he first describes the sites of emergence (udaya-sthāna) even at the outset of the primary section.

"Arising in the *ādhāra*, the divine state in the center of the heart, and rest in the *brahmarandhra*—this is proclaimed as the three lakhs. Thus, arising is the initial manifestation of the vibration (*spandana*), which constitutes the potency of all mantras; it is the dissolution and the specific abiding. By means of that very form of mere arousal, while remaining in a state of oneness, there occurs manifold existence through the teaching of the *ciṇi* and *ciṇyā* suffixes. And it is said in the *Śrīmata*:
"Ciṇi" is the first sound; "ciṇi" is the second;
the third is the cry of a hero; and the fourth is the sound of a conch.
The fifth is the sound of stringed instruments, the sixth likewise the conch shell;
the seventh is the bronze cymbals, and then the eighth is the sound of thunderclouds.
The ninth is Vahninirghoṣa and the tenth is Dundubhisvana;
that which arises without actual killing is here called Mahāhata.
70) Rest (*viśrāma*) is cessation (*virāma*); the threefold utterance of the venerable Vidyā consisting of light is thus revealed.
The instruction, arising from the pure couple and their mixture, is established in three ways.

"In emergence (*udbhava*) it is called 'pure' (*śuddha*); in the dual (*dvandva*) it is known as 'particular' (*viśeṣa*); and in the mixed (*saṃkīrṇa*) it is 'dissolution' (*laya*). Even in its established state (*saṃsthā*), instruction is threefold; thus the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are proclaimed. Thus, having stated the sequence of utterance (*uccāra-krama*) for the Vidyā situated in the light, he describes its essential nature:
"The foundation is said to be the anus, adorned with red filaments;
in its center is the Vāgbhava [syllable], vibrating with intense radiance."
"In the heart is Kāmarāja, with the luster of molten lac;
in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) is that called Śakti, resembling liquid mercury.

Thus, in the venerable *Trika-vidyā*, the light-filled Vidyā known as the *Vāgbhava*, *Kāmarāja*, and *Śakti* seeds—arising, resting, and dissolving respectively in the *ādhāra*, heart, and *brahmarandhra*, possessing the splendor of lightning, lac, and mercury—is to be meditated upon. O Great Goddess, even a slayer of a Brahmin attains perfection through this meditation on the mantra. Out of affection for you, I have declared it; it must not be given to just anyone.
Thus is this praise of mantra-meditation:
"One should recite the most excellent and supreme mantra, well-established in the *yoni*-posture.
With the body held motionless, slightly bent, neither too rigid nor too slack—this is called the *yonyāsana*.

Having joined the two palms one over the other, the body is thus positioned. Having made the body "bent" (*kuñcita*), the term "bent" is applied to the body thus prepared. One should recite the stream of syllables without doubt in the mind. This means: one should recite in such a way that there is an uninterrupted continuity of one syllable after another. Being absorbed in that, with a single-pointed mind, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) as prescribed.
Having performed one hundred thousand recitations before the Goddess, one should then recite three hundred thousand.
O Goddess, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should then offer oblations into a fire-pit shaped like a womb, using red Aśvamāra flowers mixed with molasses, clarified butter, and milk.
The preliminary service performed by him will certainly bear fruit; there is no doubt.
One who is joined with this ritual procedure attains success even if he is of meager fortune.
One is liberated from all diseases and may even accomplish that which is otherwise incurable;
now listen, O beloved, to what happens when a practitioner recites [the mantra] beyond this point.
He who, having conquered his senses, recites this one hundred thousand times,
shall cause all women to be agitated by passion at the mere sight of him.
Free from shame and fear,
all the people dwelling within this region, numbering two hundred thousand, fall before the practitioner.
Just as those from various lineages and factions come to a sacred ford,
they surrender all their possessions to him, remaining devoted to that very best of men.
When that mandala has been recited three hundred thousand times,
all those belonging to the mandala will be brought under control; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
O protector of the earth, by six hundred thousand recitations he draws in [the spirits] along with their forces and vehicles;
and by twelve hundred thousand recitations, the lords of the hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas are summoned.
O fair-faced one, when fifteen hundred thousand recitations have been performed by the practitioner, they come under his control and constantly carry out his commands.
All the accomplished Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, Apsarases, and others—all of them come under one's control; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Through the knowledge gained from hearing [the teachings] with difficulty, omniscience is born;
it brings about peace, nourishment, and satisfaction, and through oblations, it bestows contentment in an instant.
Likewise, by means of eighteen hundred thousand [recitations], the practitioner,
rising up and leaving this body behind, becomes possessed of a divine body.
By the power of his own will, he sees the world and the earth as if they were open spaces;
then, with twenty lakhs [of recitations], he becomes a lord of the Vidyādharas.
O Goddess, the practitioner shall become one who can assume any form at will and possess great strength;
by reciting [the mantra] three million times, he becomes a lord of the Siddhas and Yoginīs.
Through forty lakhs [of recitations], one attains Brahmahood; Viṣṇu is eternal. Through sixty lakhs, one attains the state of Rudra, and through eighty lakhs, the state of Īśvara.
O Goddess, by ten million lakhs (one billion), one is absorbed into the supreme state.
But the practitioner, O Goddess, shall become invincible even to the three worlds.
The splendor of Tripura is Bhairava, Śiva, the supreme cause;
imperishable, unborn, peaceful, immeasurable, and incomparable.
"O Goddess, one whose doubts have been dispelled attains the desired state of omniscience (*sarvatva*).
This much is easy to understand. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the commentary on the *Uttara-ṣaṭka*.
"O Lord, how is there a place for the deity in nine hundred thousand [yojanas], and what is that place like?
O Wielder of the Trident, you ought to explain this doubt of mine. This is easy to understand.
Immediately thereafter, he begins to describe those nine hundred thousand locations.
It is the most essential of essences, the primary [reality] devoid of external enumeration.
O Goddess, that which is established within the body is difficult to attain even in nine hundred thousand [recitations];
this is the intended meaning of the phrase "devoid of external numbering" (*bāhyasaṃkhyā-vivarjita*).

In common worldly usage, the word *lakṣa* is well known as a specific number; however, here it does not have that meaning. Here, the word *lakṣa* refers to nine locations. These are the forms of light—described below as having the shapes of lamp-flames and so forth—belonging to the syllables of the threefold vidyā without pillars, such as the Śrīkaṇṭha-vāgbhava and others.
[These are located at] the penis, the base, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the uvula.
And likewise: "The ninth is the cavity of the eyebrows, reaching to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
The meaning of the term *ādhāra* is exactly as previously stated. The "cavity" (*bila*) refers to the root of the throat.

The place of the palate is like a large hanging [membrane]; the rest is easy to understand. O beautiful lady of the Kula, the Self is like the flame of a lamp at the penis, while the youthful solar disc is situated at the navel.
In the heart, it has the form of a flame of light; above that, the form of the sun;
at the throat, the form of a lamp-flame; and at the uvula (lambikā), resembling the moon.
"Between the eyebrows, resembling a jewel, possessing universal splendor at the end of the nine.
By this, the specific light residing in the foundation is explained; as a consequence of the discussion on knowledge, the five characteristics of all mantras are [stated]:
"Contact" is the sudden connection of the practitioner with the name-mantra.
Its sign is trembling, and that first arises in the heart.
Furthermore, there is the mantra "Avaloka," if [the deities] look upon the practitioner.

That itself is "beholding" (*avalokana*). Its sign is "shaking" (*dhūnana*), and that too occurs in the ear. Regarding "speaking equally" (*samabhāṣam*): if the mantra speaks to the practitioner, that is "conversing. Its sign is "paralysis" (*stobha*). "The manifestation of the lineage itself" (*sācāsvayaṃ vaṃśasya*) refers to the conceptualization of the entire mantra-science. By the word "drop" (*bindu*), the essence of the mantra is intended. If the mantra reveals its own self to the practitioner, that is "the vision of the drop" (*bindudarśana*). And that occurs between the eyebrows. Its sign is the attainment of qualities such as *aṇimā* and so forth. Regarding "self-penetration" (*svayamāveśanam*): if the mantra causes the practitioner to enter into its own self, that is "self-penetration."
That becomes the *brahmarandhra*. Its sign is the falling away of the body. And it is said in the *Śrīmata*:
"Touching is situated in the heart, while light [is perceived] from the region of the throat."
Speech occurs in the location of the palate, while vision arises from the center of the bindu.
The self-entry [of the deity] is divine; there is no doubt that it occurs through the aperture of the twice-born (the crown of the head).
Trembling upon touch should be known [as the sign], and shaking occurs when gazed upon.
By conversing with him, there may be a sudden paralysis [of the senses], and one comes to understand the meaning of the scriptures;
by seeing him, however, there is the attainment of qualities, namely the eightfold qualities beginning with *aṇimā*.
O Goddess, one will attain self-possessed immersion (svayamāveśana) and fly up; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the commentary on the *Uttaraṣaṭka*.
Now, he begins to demonstrate the method for the invocation of the goddesses and introduces the *Vidyākośa*:
"I shall proclaim the *Vidyākośa*, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments."
O lady of excellent hips, one should worship the wheel of the Goddess with the Vāgbhava syllable.

"Vidyākośa" refers to the eight-petaled lotus described below, which has a corner and a pericarp, is presided over by Sādākhya, and is the seat (pīṭha) of the Pretas; this is what is intended by "the wheel of the Goddess. The meaning is that one should worship it with the Vāgbhava mantra. Having meditated upon the Goddess, who consists of Nāda and Bindu, in the center of that [lotus] as having a divine form and the letters [of the alphabet], [one should worship her] with the entire mantra.
Having assigned the faces and the limbs, one should worship [the deity] above the *prati*.

The *bindu* and *nāda*, whether unmanifest as *Tripurā* or [represented] by the letter of knowledge (*jñākṣara*), should be understood here as being established as the individual vitality (*vīrya*) of the collection of phonemes (*varṇasaṅghāta*). Thus it is stated in the *Śrīmata-kramanirnaya*: "O Goddess, the letter of Mahāmāyā is the Person (*puruṣa*); with the two [others], the Pure One (*amala*) is fourfold. "With the entire mantra" means with the mantra accompanied by the letter *ka*, namely that called *Kāmarāja*. The meaning is: "one should worship above the *preta*. Although not explicitly stated here, one should also conceive of the *preta* as *Sādākhya* by means of the seed-syllable of Śakti. Tripurā, who constitutes the internal sacrifice, is to be known according to the method taught in the Yoga [scriptures]: "The three deities situated in the corners are Rati, Prīti, and Manobhava; Rati is on the left, Prīti is on the right, and Madana is in front. This is easy to understand.

"Afterwards, one should install the Root-Vidyā endowed with its characteristic marks. This means that one should first take the eight long vowels—*ā*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*—which belong to the Root-Vidyās starting from Brāhmī up to Caṇḍikā and Anantā; these are the "moving" (carā) vowels. By joining each of these sequentially with the eight consonants beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *la*, the Vidyā is said to consist of eight divisions. That [Vidyā] is described in this way. One should install that very Vidyā, of such a nature, in the eight petals of the treasury (*kośa*) in due order. The essential meaning is that one should contemplate the installation mentally. Having installed the sequence *ā*, *kṣa*, *ā ī śabdaḥ* on one petal, one installs the sequence *ī*, *la*, *ā ī śabdaḥ* on the other.

In this manner, one should understand [the sequence] for Īśāna and the others as well. Among the eight seats (*āsana*), the names beginning with Brāhma are indeed their designations. Thus, in the *Devatātantra*, the "Eightfold Kula" (*kulāṣṭaka*) is praised. He himself sets forth the sequence of the syllables of the Root-Vidyā, which is endowed with the characteristics of Ananta.
One should everywhere join the letter *kṣa* with the vowel *ā*.
By means of the vowel *ī*, the letter *l* becomes *ū*; by means of the vowel *ā*, [it becomes] *ha*.
The ṛṣā-yoga is thus fully described, and likewise the next is the lṛṣā-yoga;
by means of the letter *e*, the letter *śa* [is joined], and by means of the letter *ai*, the letter *va*.
O Goddess Tripurabhairavī, one should first worship the eight Kulas by means of the syllable *Aṃ* and the name of the eight-petaled root-vidyā.

Having thus presented the extraction [of the mantra], as well as the meditation on the mantra and the yoga, in accordance with the sequence, the author now begins this section to demonstrate that a reversal of such a sequence in the rule for recitation (*japa*) leads to the highest good, and to show the abundance of transgressions (*pratyavāya*) that arise from doing otherwise. "Placed at the beginning and middle, or at the middle and end, or at the end and beginning—this should be recited by practitioners according to this rule for the agitation of the city (*purakṣobha*). In this manner, the sequence beginning with the Vāgbhava [syllable] and ending with the Śakti-bīja, which belongs to the ancient tradition, cannot be the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*), nor the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-krama*), nor the sequence of maintenance (*sthiti-krama*) which consists of both. Indeed, it is not possible for a sequence to occur other than these three sequences. Therefore, the Supreme Lord, intent on guarding the secret meaning and desiring to conceal the eligibility for the speech-mantra (*vāṅ-manda*), performed the extraction (*uddhāra*).

(p. 78) The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a self, nor a being, nor a soul, nor a person; he does not perceive form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor formations, nor consciousness; he does not perceive the eye, nor the ear, nor the nose, nor the tongue, nor the body, nor the mind; he does not perceive forms, nor sounds, nor odors, nor tastes, nor tangibles, nor mental phenomena; he does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor the ear-consciousness, nor the nose-consciousness, nor the tongue-consciousness, nor the body-consciousness, nor the mind-consciousness; he does not perceive contact, nor feeling, nor craving, nor grasping, nor becoming, nor birth, nor old age and death. He does not perceive the limit of past time, nor the limit of future time, nor the present time. He does not perceive the perfection of giving, nor the perfection of morality, nor the perfection of patience, nor the perfection of vigor, nor the perfection of meditation, nor the perfection of wisdom; he does not perceive the emptiness of the internal, nor the emptiness of the external, nor the emptiness of the internal and external, nor the emptiness of emptiness, nor the great emptiness, nor the emptiness of the ultimate, nor the conditioned emptiness, nor the unconditioned emptiness, nor the absolute emptiness, nor the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, nor the emptiness of non-dispersal, nor the emptiness of nature, nor the emptiness of all dharmas, nor the emptiness of own-marks, nor the emptiness of non-existence, nor the emptiness of existence, nor the emptiness of non-existence and existence, nor the emptiness of the essential nature, nor the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor the four grounds of self-confidence, nor the four analytical knowledges, nor the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he does not perceive even the state of omniscience. Subhūti, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma, he is called a ‘bodhisattva. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma, how does he train in the six perfections? How does he enter into the three gateways to liberation? How does he enter into the stages of a bodhisattva? How does he enter into the dharmas of a Buddha? How does he enter into the dharmas of omniscience? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is to be practiced, nor a dharma that is to be entered. Because he does not perceive them, he trains in the six perfections. Because he does not perceive them, he enters into the three gateways to liberation. Because he does not perceive them, he enters into the stages of a bodhisattva. Because he does not perceive them, he enters into the dharmas of a Buddha. Because he does not perceive them, he enters into the dharmas of omniscience. Subhūti, this is the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of wisdom.”

It should be understood that he has prescribed a subversion of the sequence; for this very same [subversion] is seen even in other Tantras. And so it is in the system of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara): having first extracted the sequence beginning with Vāgbhava and ending with the seed-syllables of Śakti, he refutes that [standard order] through the section beginning with "The performance of recitation is to be undertaken as situated in the middle," and so forth. Likewise, by the *Laghupādas*, who demonstrate the sequence starting with Vāgbhava according to the number of syllables in the quarters of the verses beginning with "Like that of Indra" (*aindrasyeva*), and by the *Carccāpādas* who, in their exposition of the sequence of the *Ādhāra*, show Vāgbhava to be situated in the middle—even though they acknowledge the sequence beginning with "Blazing at the crown of the head" (*mūrdhnisphurat*)—this sequence is not to be understood here as being the ultimate reality. This is the meaning of the verse: in the sequence of extraction, Vāgbhava is indeed the first and Kāmarāja is the middle.

In this regard, having placed the *vāgbhava* syllable in the position of the *kāmarāja*, and having made the central *kāmarāja* occupy the position of the *vāgbhava*, one should perform the recitation while leaving the final seed-syllable exactly as it stands. For practitioners who perform this specific sequence of recitation, a "shaking of the city" (*purakṣobha*) occurs. By the word "city" (*pura*), the Buddhas and others are intended. Their "shaking" is the shaking of the city; and by the power of the practitioner's command, this consists precisely in inducing states such as deep sleep (*suṣupti*) in the subject who has fallen into the waking state. The meaning is that the practitioner is able to bring about such a shaking of the city for the subject. Furthermore, the status of the Buddhas and others as a "city" is proclaimed in the *Haṃsabhedatantra*.
They move within the forms of body, life-force, and speech in the three cities;
their essential nature is the sustaining power known as Tripurabhairavī.
In that triad of cities known as the intellect, the vital breath, and the body;
Because his essence consists of the duality of egoism (ahaṅkāra), he is therefore remembered as Puruṣa;
and because he has burnt these three cities, he is known as Tripurāntaka.

"The sequence beginning with Kāmarāja and ending with the Śakti-bīja, joined with the long, short, and ultra-short [vowels], is declared as the order of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama). Next, he states the order of maintenance (sthitikrama): "The first of the first, and the beginningless; the middle of the middle, and the middle; the end of the end, and the endless—this is the swift-granting success of Tripurā. Here, by the first quarter [of the verse] beginning with *ekānādi*, he intends the extraction sequence (*uddhārakrama*) of the first element, Vāgbhava. By the second [quarter], he intends its specific constituent, the initial syllable. The meaning is: "having made that pair—the beginningless and the middle—one's middle. Regarding "the middle of the middle": one "middle" word indicates Kāmarāja, which occupies the central position in the extraction sequence. The second [word] indicates its specific constituent, the word "endless" (*ananta*); the meaning is "having made both of those the middle-beginning. Because of the statement, "the Śakti-bīja, together with its specific [constituent], is situated at the end of the final door of the extraction sequence," the final-middle [syllable] is established here even though it was not explicitly mentioned. This is the order of withdrawal. Regarding "the end of the end, and the endless": as before, by the two uses of the word "end," he intends the Śakti-bīja and its remaining ornament, the sound (*ghoṣa*). The meaning is "having made the endless the beginning. By this, which is intended to designate the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), the short vowels and so forth taught in the forthcoming sūtra are indicated.
The sequence ending with the *pluta* [vowel] has been shown. These two sequences combined constitute the *sthiti-krama*. Thus it is stated in the *Pārameśvara-mata*:

"One should place the first [syllable] in the middle of the 'ma' and join both at the end"—by this sequence, for the best of practitioners who recite [the mantra], the Blessed Lady, who kindles the three cities, grants swift accomplishment (*siddhi*). She reveals the nature of the Self (*ātman*). And it is said in the *Amṛtoda*: "The word 'swift accomplishment' denotes the Self; it is known that 'accomplishment' occurs at the end of 'swift. The heroes constantly behold the Self as the form of the letter *A* situated in the middle of the *Amṛta* (the *m*) and the *Dadhi* (the *a*). Furthermore, the venerable Utpaladeva stated: "Maheśvara is the primordial Accomplished One. This establishes the state of the Krama-vidyā; it demonstrates that if it were taught otherwise than in the manner described, one would not attain success.
But by the first [syllable] it is obscured, by the middle one it is pinned down, and by the last one it is severed; therefore, the vidyā is not accomplished.

The first of the stated sequence is Kāmarāja; if the Vidyā is deprived of this, it does not succeed. According to the methods of extraction (*uddhārakrama*), by means of the venerable *Śrīyāmala*, the first becomes Vāgbhava. Consequently, in the case of Kāmarāja, it is deprived of its beginning by the first [syllable], but it is "pinned" (*kīlita*) by the middle one—meaning it is "separated" (*viyukta*). This is stated in the *Śrīmātṛkātantra*: "Just as mantras do not succeed due to the pinning (*kīlana*) caused by ignorance of the *praṇava*, so too is Sundarī separated by the lack of knowledge regarding *haṃsa*. For here, within the form of the two sequences, in the sequence of maintenance (*sthitikrama*), there is the union of the sequences of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and emanation (*sarga*) in the middle. (p. 81)

Even if this Vidyā were to be deprived [of its letters] by the *Vāgbhava* (the first seed-syllable), it would still not be effective. For in the sequence of extraction (*uddhārakrama*), the *Kāmarāja* (the middle seed-syllable) stands in the middle; thus, if one accepts the sequence of extraction, it becomes "pinned" (*kīlitā*) by that middle one. Furthermore, if it were to be deprived even by the final one—that is, the last letter of the Vidyā mentioned within [the previous discussion], which is the *Kāmarāja*—it would likewise not be effective. For in the sequence of extraction, since the *Śakti-bīja* (the third seed-syllable) is the final one, when it is severed by the final [letter], the Vidyā does not lead to success; such is the meaning. Immediately thereafter, he explains the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).
O fair-faced one, by means of the sequence of short and long [vowels],
and specifically having uttered [the mantra] thus at the end of the prolated (pluta) vowel, one may accomplish even the three worlds.
That which is called "short" is the eighth letter, which constitutes a particular seed-syllable (bīja) of Śakti.

The term "long" (*dīrgha*) refers to the first letter of the *mātṛkā*, which is the essence of the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable]. The "prolated" (*pluta*) is the vowel *ā*, which is the power of the *kāmarāja*. Thus, the short, long, and prolated forms of these are mutually dependent; for instance, midnight is the resonance (*ghoṣa*), and in relation to that, there arise the one-measure (*ekamātra*) short, long, and prolated vowels. For the practitioner who utters these three letters—beginning with the seed of Śakti and ending with the *kāmarāja*—accompanied by these specific qualities of short, long, and prolated nature, even the three worlds will be mastered. The "three worlds" (*trailokya*) are known as the earth, the intermediate space, and heaven.
The meaning is that the three external cities are to be brought under its control;
O Goddess, it becomes manifest and bestows the threefold accomplishment (siddhi).
*Khecarī*, *Bhūcarī*, and *Siddhi*—these are the three *khecarīs*.

By this, he speaks of the triad of accomplishments (*siddhis*). "Khecaratva" means the state of moving through the sky; that is, the ability to travel to distant places in a short time. By the term "supreme *khecarī*," the accomplishment known as the mastery of the space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*) is designated. And that consists of the continuous contemplation within the space of consciousness by means of the dissolved mind. "It likewise bestows other accomplishments upon the lords of practitioners"—it is easy to understand that "the deity of the Kula grants him the eightfold accomplishment."
There is no mantra superior to Aghora; there is no Vidyā higher than Tripurā;
there is no deity greater than the Guru; and there is no Mudrā higher than Khecarī.

In the context of the praise of Tripurā, [the author] points out other even more excellent [teachings] that are useful for the goals of human life: "O Goddess, this very [teaching] is clearly the bestower of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it must not be given to the unworthy—such is the command of the Supreme Goddess.
As it has been stated in the *Tripurāvidyārahasya*: "The secret of the Tripurā-vidyā must not be given to those who are unworthy; such is the command of the Supreme Lord."
The *Kuladīpikā*, which destroys the blindness of those who give false instructions, has been completed with its secret meanings revealed.
I do not worship the earth, nor the abode of nectar (the moon), nor even that which is called the celestial realm, though it be well-named and well-guarded;
for I bow down to Him who is bowed to by all for the sake of perfection, who possesses the noble Uma, and who has manifested great majesty.

O Goddess of Speech, we live our lives with pure and supreme longevity, honoring that form which, by Your grace, has been revealed—Him who wears the crescent moon as His lofty crest-ornament, who scorches the most stubborn darkness, and who is the source of liberation. May we thus make our life meaningful.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Tejonandanātha Viṭambā Śrī.
|| Salutations to the venerable Gurus ||
The Compendium of the Essence of Tripurā.

I worship the Śrīpādukā of Śrī Maheśānandanātha and Maheśvarī Parāmbā. May the auspicious pair of lotus-feet of the Goddess bring you constant welfare—feet that are served by the honey-bees of the sapphire gems clearly set upon the millions of crowns of the foremost gods led by Prahva, Prācīnabarhi, and others; feet whose toenails shine with rays like a mass of golden filaments; and feet whose tinkling anklets are perpetually made resonant by the swans of the goddess’s voice. Having bowed with devotion to the dust-particles of the two lotus-feet of the Guru—the bridge for crossing the ocean of worldly existence—I shall describe the sequence of worship of the Kulanāyikā as instructed by my teacher. Having bathed according to the rules, having washed my hands, face, and feet, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), wearing clean garments and the sacred thread, facing either east or north and assuming a firm posture, I bow to Gaṇapati and the Guru. Then, [reciting] the Saṃ*yojya-jīva and Durga [mantras]...

O Śivā, one should contemplate the world as being entirely submerged in the ash by means of the wind of the Lord of this [mantra], together with the moon (the nasal dot) and the letter *ha* (the *haṃsa*) standing at the tip of the nose, which has gone before the body of the Lord of Men (*Maheśvara*) within the extremely subtle *śiva* situated in the moon of the sky-lotus via the path of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*). Then, having meditated upon the Egg of Brahmā (*brahmāṇḍa*), which is a shimmering circle of light residing in the midst of a vast bubble, one should contemplate these worlds within it, including this surface of the earth. Here, one should intensely visualize on all sides a forest of *kadamba* trees, adorned with blossoming smiles and emerging from a fresh, irreproachable root. Within that, one should contemplate a great golden pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), decorated with clusters of jewels, its brilliance rising like the luster of two gems; it possesses four doors and is joined by four jeweled arches (*toraṇa*), marked above by a white canopy like the lord of autumn stars. At each door stand Gaṇeśa and Kṣetreśa, wearing beautiful garlands of jewels and garments, accompanied by their retinues. At the eastern gate stands he whose vehicle is the bay horse (*hari-haya*); at the southern, Yama; at the western, Varuṇa; and likewise at the northern gate, Kubera. One should meditate properly and without agitation upon that place crowded with groups of celestial women singing within, and even with the leaders of the Gandharvas. In its center, upon a lion-throne, one should conceive a white eight-petaled lotus, radiant as the orb of the rising sun, fierce with reddish-brown eyes. Having placed upon its pericarp the syllable *ka*—which consists of the letter *ma*, the water-element, the fourth vowel (*ū*), the anusvāra (*m*), and the final letter (*kṣa*)—one should, with the intellect, perceive the Lord of the Thirty Gods (*Tridaśeśa*) seated thereupon.

Having meditated upon the Mother of the Three Worlds, the beloved of the Mountain (Himalaya)—who possesses a most beautiful nose, lovely eyes, and palms with auspicious lines; who bears a spotless crescent moon entwined in her mass of reddish-brown matted locks, and whose forehead is graced by a charming eighth-day moon; whose lotus-face is as radiant as the full autumnal moon; whose garment is the luster of Bandhūka flowers and whose teeth are like coral; who has high, rounded breasts and four arms as soft as young lotus stalks; who is illuminated by the three eyes—shining like lotus petals with smiles—that light up the Lord of Stars (the Moon) within them; who wears earrings and possesses eyebrows as graceful as blossoming *cillī* flowers; whose slender waist is highlighted by three folds and a deep navel turning clockwise; who shines with a line of fresh body hair marked by a streak of musk; whose thighs are adorned with a girdle of gems as red as a blooming Bandhūjīva flower; whose pair of thighs are as thick as those of a noble elephant and whose gait is like that of a swan, her soles outshining the filaments of a lotus; whose two feet are reddened by the mass of light from the jeweled crowns of the hosts of gods led by Indra as they prostrate; who eclipses the beauty of the evening clouds with the radiance of her own body, swallowing the surrounding quarters with her splendor; who wears a beautiful single-string necklace (*ekāvalī*) made of pearls released from the belly of a bank of divine clouds, possessing pure and tender luster, and whose neck is smeared with yellow sandalwood paste; whose lotus-hands are raised in the gestures of the noose, the goad, and the granting of fearlessness, and who is delightful with magnificent jewel-ornaments; and whose smiling face reflects the rays of her beautiful teeth—[one should meditate thus].

Having thus meditated upon this Dhṛḍhānī— the Mother of the Three Worlds, whose lower lip is like a fresh leaf of a young tree, who is worthy of worship by the hosts of gods, and who is the wish-fulfilling cow for her own lineage— one should again cause one’s own life-force (*jīva*) to enter the lotus of the heart from the swan seated within the hut of the heart-lotus in the sky. Thus ends the first chapter in the *Tripurasārasamuccaya* composed by Bhaṭṭanāga.
The First Chapter.

One should place the five arrows upon the pairs of fingers, beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger, according to the method taught by the Guru; we shall now describe them here. The first seed-syllable (*bīja*) consists of the face (the letter *i*), the circle (the vowel *u*), fire (*ra*), joined with the "to be tasted" (*sa*), together with the staff (*da*), and the circle (*u*) again—this indeed is the second [syllable] when conjoined with the three forms (*mūrti*). The [third] is situated within the face (*i*), mounted by the king of gods (*na*), with the left eye (*ī*), joined with the preceding face (*i*), preceded by the asterism (*bh*), with the circle (*u*), the enemy (*ṛ*), the half of the sixth vowel (*e*), and the moon (*ca*), joined with the fourth mark of Śaṅkara (*ta*). Having performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*) on the fingers, the best of practitioners should perform the placement of the digits (*kalā-nyāsa*) according to their positions in the hands. He should place the triad of seeds together with the crescent moon upon his head, reaching to the end of his hair. He should place Saṃvartaka upon the circle of the face. The wise one should place the four subtle ones (*sūkṣma* etc. in the four ages (*yuga*). Having placed [the syllables] in the eyes, he should place the two with the half-moon on the ears, the pair of Bhṛgu (*śa*) on the two cheeks, and the pair of Śveta (*śve*) on the two nostrils. After that, the wise one should place the two marked with the half-moon on the chin, followed by the pair on the cheeks, and the head endowed with the moon's orb.

(p. 87) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna-svabhāva). "Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is the attachment to names, signs, and characteristics in accordance with the objects of perception, such as 'form' and so forth; this is called the imagined self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the dependent self-nature? It is the manifestation of the mind (citta) and mental factors (caitta) based upon the causal conditions of the habit-energies (vāsanā) of false discrimination; this is called the dependent self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the perfected self-nature? It is the state in which the dependent self-nature is completely devoid of the imagined self-nature; this is called the perfected self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of the Great Vehicle? It is the realization that all phenomena are non-arising, the absence of conceptual proliferation (prapañca), the non-duality of subject and object, and the entry into the realm of the Tathāgata-garbha; this is called the self-nature of the Great Vehicle. "Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself in these four kinds of self-nature in order to transcend the views of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and other heterodox teachers."

The practitioner of mantra, being attentive, should first place two rows of teeth, then two lips with a curved edge like the crescent moon and accompanied by the letter *i*, then two nostrils, and thereafter two eyes joined with the letter *u* preceded by the face (*m*). Having placed the letter *e* along with the half-moon and the lord of stars (the nasal *m*), he should then place the wind (*ya*) together with the final vowel (*au*) upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*). By always performing this placement according to the prescribed rule, a person lives here for a long time, free from disease and death. Afterwards, either the *Mātṛkā* alone or endowed with the power of Rudra should be placed upon the body. Then the lord of practitioners, having first performed the placement, should contemplate the placement of the Vidyā upon his limbs. This is the placement of the Vidyā.
The wise one should perform [the placement] with the syllables of the root mantra according to the sequence to be described:
he should place the first seed-syllable on the head, the second in the secret place, and the third in the region of the heart.
Then, one should place the three seed-syllables on the forehead with both eyes directed straight ahead, then on the pair of ears and the mouth,
on the two shoulders and the region of the back, on the pair of knees, and on the navel.
With these three seed-syllables alone, the wise one should fashion the six faces, beginning with the upward-facing one.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five arrows upon the limbs—namely the secret place, the navel, the heart, the mouth, and the head—using the root mantra. One should also place the five arrows, whose power is seen to agitate the three worlds, here as they are about to be described: Kāma, Rājaka-ma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, and Makaraketana. These are proclaimed by these names, joined with the syllable *manobhava* in sequence. [The first is] *ka* joined with the fifth vowel (*u*), followed by the end of the word *vinaya* (*na*), then the left eye (*i*), and the hand (*ra*) joined with the quality of wind (*ya*). [The second is] *ra* joined with the sun-sound (*u*), then *ha*, *ri*, *ha*, and *ra*. (p. 88)

In that place, Bhṛgu, accompanied by Upārā, dwells in the forest like Viṣṇu with Śaṣṭhā. May he bestow their heads upon me—those which are indeed declared to be my five Kramas, resembling the crescent moon of the wise. Wherever a man meditates day after day on these within his own body, the three worlds become subservient to his mind. For the sake of the limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*), I shall describe the nature of the triad of seeds belonging to the Mistress of the Clan (*kulanāyikā*). This must be guarded by those who know the Kula-dharma for the sake of longevity and the attainment of qualities.
