The seed known as *Vāgbhava*, situated at the half-moon of the syllable *Gaṅka* (the letter *ha*) preceded by *Kāntā* (the letter *a*), and joined with the letter located at the end of the teeth (*da*) and the preceding water-lily (*la*), is called *Nakhara*. By chanting this, one attains success in the nectar-like essence of sublime speech. That which ends with *Kāntā* (the letter *a*), joined with the fifth of the Clan (the letter *u*), and endowed with the staff (*da*) at the end of the eyes (*i*), is declared to be the *Kāma* mantra. From the recitation of this, it is said to be the direct agitator of the world. When joined with the end of the teeth (*da*) and the staff (*da*), it is the entire *Sammohana* clan; one who constantly chants this attains the eight qualities and the power of moving through the sky (*khacaratā*). The seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra is the Great-Souled Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and its meter (*chandas*) is *Paṅkti*. Its Power (*śakti*) is she whose face is adorned with the ear-ornament of Indra (the letter *ra*) and the half-moon of the heart (the letter *ī*). The seed-syllable of this mantra is preceded by Lakulīśa (the letter *la*), joined with the end of the teeth (*da*) and the staff (*da*). The color of this King of Mantras is white, and its deity is the Sage (Brahmā). Gāndhāra is declared to be its musical note (*svara*). This origin of the root of knowledge has been told; it must be understood in every way by those desiring perfection. This primordial Vidyā of the Goddess was cursed by her husband; thus, at the beginning, it became deprived of life (*prāṇahīnā*).

(p. 89) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. "Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is that which is grasped by the ignorant and ordinary people through names and signs (nāmanimitta) regarding objects that have no intrinsic nature; it is like seeing a rope in the dark and imagining it to be a snake. This is called the imagined self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the dependent self-nature? It is the manifestation of various appearances based upon causal conditions, devoid of the characteristics of the imagined; it is like a mirage in the springtime. This is called the dependent self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the perfected self-nature? It is the state of the dependent self-nature being eternally free from the characteristics of the imagined; it is the realization of suchness (tathatā) and the non-dual knowledge. This is called the perfected self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha? It is the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) which, when purified of all adventitious defilements, is known as the Tathāgata-garbha; it is the dharmakāya of all Buddhas, which is the realm of the noble ones (ārya). "Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself to abandon the imagined self-nature and to realize the dependent and perfected self-natures, thereby attaining mastery over the Tathāgata-garbha."

Therefore, Śambhu has placed the seed-syllable of Śiva-Śakti above those two preceding seed-syllables. Akula is above Para, and Fire (Dahana) is below Madhyamā; from that point on, she becomes powerful. This Bhairavī is declared by the teachers to be preceded by Kula, provided she is preceded by Kula; she alone is called the Vidyā on earth that grants swift fruit, and she must be kept strictly secret among the ignorant (paśu). The eighth [letter] of Śiva is the first seed-syllable alone; the other is the eightfold seed-syllable of Bhaga. The supreme three-lettered Saṅketavidyā, ending with the head (the letter *ha*), is said to be accessible only through the mouth of the Guru. The end of "Kāntā" (the letter *pha*), the end of "Vāntā" (the letter *sa*), the end of "Akula" (the letter *ka*), joined with the "left eye" (*ī*), followed by the staff (*da*) and Kula (*ka*), along with the resonance (*nāda*): this six-peaked [mantra], spoken in the Tripurārṇava, is extremely secret; it is Smara himself in person. He who recites this, having joined the first seed-syllable in the middle of the second, and the last at the beginning and end of the middle one—the hosts of beings within the three worlds will become subject to his will and partake of his sovereignty. Making the first [syllable] the end and the last seed-syllable the beginning, and the middle one in the first, the lord of practitioners who constantly recites this mantra becomes liberated while living and attains all perfections (*siddhis*). One should recite this King of Mantras, the cause of the enchantment of the entire world, interspersed with the Mātṛkās, both forward and backward. A wise man, endowed with the Haṃsa-deity, even if he is a mere householder possessed of divine qualities, attains the aforementioned perfection. He who, with a steady and pure mind, recites this which is joined with the consonants and the Haṃsa, and which enchants the entire world of the dyer and the dyed, quickly attains perfection. The lotus [syllable] with its middle and first vowels elided, joined with Īśa (*ha*) and the rest, together with the Bindu and Nāda.

(p. 90) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna-svabhāva). "Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is the grasping of names and characteristics (nāmanimitta) based on the objects of the five sense-bases (pañcendriya-viṣaya), which are like a mirage or a dream, and it is the attachment to them as being real. This is called the imagined self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the dependent self-nature? It is the manifestation of the mind (cittapratibhāsa) arising from the habit-energies (vāsanā) of false discrimination; it is the non-dual nature that appears as duality. This is called the dependent self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the perfected self-nature? It is the state in which the dependent self-nature is seen as being eternally free from the imagined self-nature; it is the suchness (tathatā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and the ultimate truth (paramārtha). This is called the perfected self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of the Great Vehicle? It is the realization of the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena through the wisdom of the threefold liberation (vimokṣa); it is the attainment of the stage of the Tathāgata by means of the ten stages (daśabhūmi). This is called the self-nature of the Great Vehicle. "Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself in these four kinds of self-nature so as not to fall into the views of the externalists. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the venerable Mahāmati and the assembly of bodhisattvas rejoiced in what the Blessed One had taught. [End of Chapter] (p. 90)

This [mantra] is not to be recited within a village or similar places; it shines upon the earth as ordained by the Heart [of the Goddess]. *Oṃ-klīn-namaḥ*. This Vidyā, which yields all desires, is honored in the three worlds, bestows heaven and liberation, is more secret than the secret, brings about great prosperity, and is known here as the Yoginī. She is declared to be the birthplace of the essence of Sarasvatī, the granter of good fortune and wealth, and she produces immediate conviction even when recited but once on this earth. However, because she has entered into seven states (*saptāvasthā*) by the All-pervading Lord, she does not grant accomplishment (*siddhi*) even if constantly recited. But if the Vidyā is awakened, she bears fruit instantly as an illuminator; therefore, I shall now declare this most profound secret Vidyā here. [The mantra is: *Puṣpaṃ* (the letter *pa*), *vāri* (the letter *va*), *mucāndava* (the letters *ya*, *la*, *ba*, *ra*), and another [letter], those very same vowels (*ta* = *e*, *va* = *ai*, *eva* = *ai*), then the long *vāri* (the letter *vā* = *au*), followed by *sakha* (the letter *sa*), ending with *ambu* (the letter *u*), and likewise the two letters ending in *dhā* (the letters *dha* and *na*), along with the vowel *loka* (the letter *o*). This Vidyā, which illuminates the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava, is the birthplace of Sarasvatī, the manifest wish-granting vine (*pārijātalatikā*), and has been declared by me in eight syllables. [Brahmā] joined with Indra’s eye (*i*), together with Bhaga (*bhaga*) and Meṣa (*meṣa*)—this is Nādinī, ending with Kānta (*kā*), with Bhaga (*bha*), Pūtana (*pu*), and then Dha (*dha*) and Meṣa (*meṣa*) with Sadṛk (*ṛ*). Kāla (*ka*) joined with Ananta (*a*), Viyat (*ha*), Sad-aśana (*da*), Saṃvartaka (*sa*), Bhīṣaṇa (*bha*), Sā-kūra (*ku*), Kamalāsana (*na*), Śiva (*śa*), Vaiśva (*va*), and Naras (*na*)—such is the mantra.
This eleven-syllable mantra is most capable of awakening the seed-syllable of Manmatha;
it suddenly agitates those dwelling in the regions of the Nagas, the earth, and the Rasatala.

Joined with the mouth of Savitri, it is Mahadikali, whose end is adorned by a crescent moon reaching to the edge of the sky. Likewise, this [mantra] is to be placed in the fire-pitcher (agniṣṭhi), joined with the lotus-born (Brahma) and Mohini.

On earth, it shall be the illuminator of another’s seed-mantra. Whichever seed-mantra serves as the illuminator for a particular [mantra], one should first utter that very seed-mantra before it. The excellent practitioner should constantly apply the six limbs of the mantra to the faces and the various deities in the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). By performing the placement of the limbs of the mantra upon his own body, this triple world comes under the control of the man; his sins are immediately pacified, and the *rākṣasas* along with the serpents flee. This form of the mantra has been described by me; it is obtained entirely through the mouth of the Guru. Without the grace of the Guru, this mantra on the surface of the earth does not bestow its fruits.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Sārasamuccaya* composed by Bhaṭṭanāga.
The Second Chapter.

Now, this body is considered by the wise to have an excellent length of ninety-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) measured by one’s own fingers. By the fingers of the Sun (twelve), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), known as "the wind from the vicinity," is held by those who know yoga to be greater than the body. Here, through constant practice, a man brings this vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) into a state of diminution within the limbs; he who attains equality with the body on this earth is considered by the wise to be the foremost among those who know yoga. Fourteen principal channels (*nāḍī*) are situated here; among them, only three are primary. These are the *iḍā*, the *suṣumnā*, and the *piṅgalā*. Of these, the *suṣumnā* alone is the most important. The channel named *iḍā* rests upon the left side of the body, and the channel named *piṅgalā* upon the right. Between the two, resting against the backbone (*praṣṭhavaṃśa*), is the *suṣumnā*.

(p. 92) The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real. He does not perceive the perfection of giving as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of inherent nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-attainment, or the emptiness of nature as real. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive the state of a bodhisattva or the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha as real. Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma as real. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: although all dharmas are empty, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through skillful means, practices the perfection of wisdom and fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, what is this skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, generates the thought of awakening for the sake of all beings, yet he does not perceive those beings as real. He practices the perfection of giving without perceiving a giver, a recipient, or a gift as real. He practices the perfection of morality without perceiving a precept, a transgression, or a moral agent as real. He practices the perfection of patience without perceiving an object of anger, an offender, or a patient person as real. He practices the perfection of vigor without perceiving a body, a mind, or an exertion as real. He practices the perfection of meditation without perceiving a meditator, a meditative object, or a state of concentration as real. He practices the perfection of wisdom without perceiving wisdom, an object of wisdom, or a knower as real. Subhūti, this is the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”

It remains as far as the *brahmarandhra* (the aperture of Brahmā), situated within the *suṣumnā*, joined with the variegated channels (*citranāḍī*) and radiant with five colors, accompanied by the five deities. Within that is situated the extremely subtle *brahmarandhra*, shining like the interior of a lotus fiber. This is the *brahmasūtra* for embodied beings, their very life-force and the sole cause of immortality. Regarding this, the ancient sages say it is the "divine path" for those whose minds are devoted to liberation. The moon, garlanded with cool rays, moves in the *iḍā*; therefore, the left side is declared to be "immortal" (*amṛta*). The sun moves in the *piṅgalā*; therefore, the right side is called "poison" (*viṣa*) by the lords of sages. One should know that the rising and setting [of breath] occurs in the belly of the goddess at the root of men through meditation, in the fingers of the hot-rayed one (the sun) during the morning and evening twilights. One should understand the constant downward movement as night and the upward movement as day; the moon moves upward and the sun moves downward. When the deity has entered the lunar channel (*tuṣārāṃśunāḍī*), one should perform rites such as pacification (*śāntika*). When the wise man enters the solar channel (*mārttaṇḍanāḍī*), he performs fierce rites (*raudrakarma*). When he enters both channels, he performs mixed rites. The wise man should observe the arising of the elements from both; therein, first, the earth arises in the sharp-witted one when the sense of smell touches the burnt [element]. The arising of water occurs when the sense of taste touches the deity; of fire, when it moves upward; of wind, when it touches transversely; and of space, when it is touched all around on the path of the wind. The arising of earth is recommended for subjugation (*vaśya*) and immobilization (*stambhana*); the arising of water is recommended for auspicious rites such as pacification and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*). Furthermore, the arising of fire is for the swift execution of cruel acts against an enemy, such as killing, inciting discord, and expulsion. The arising of wind is for similar purposes.

If a messenger approaches here on behalf of those afflicted by disease, asking about peace or the removal of poison, when the Lord (Īśvara) is situated in the sky (ākāśa), there is benefit; when He is in the earth (pṛthivī), those tormented by illness attain relief; and if He is in the water (jala), the disease reaches pacification. However, if He is in the earth, death occurs. Likewise, when the Lord is in the air (vāyu), the destruction of diseases occurs only after a long time. Now, if the Lord is in the southern part and the sick man stands on the right side and asks, "Will that man live free from fever?", then he lives. But if the Lord is in the left and the man, whose body is distressed by disease, stands on the left and asks, then the disease remains for a long time and he does not live. If the Lord has gone to the left and the man, standing on the right, asks here, it is difficult to cure; the wise say that even a reversal of this results in a class of diseases that are indeed incurable. If the inquirer asks while the Lord is inside, the man lives free from disease; if the Lord has gone outside, he goes to the city of the King of the Dead (Yama) with that very same illness. In all undertakings, when the Lord is inside, auspiciousness prevails; when the Lord is outside, one should know that the fruit of actions, whether good or bad, is determined by Him. Beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight (darśa), the Lord rises in the left nostril for three days; then for three days in the other (right) nostril, until the full moon (pūrṇā). Then, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, the Lord occupies the nostril for three days starting from the fourteenth day (bhūtā).
On the right wing there are three [joints], and on the left likewise as far as the *kahara*; one should always observe them in this manner.
By the reversal of even a single side, a human being here becomes overcome by disease.
The death of both their kinsmen and friends would occur due to the reversal of the two sides.

When, by the power of time, the breath moves in reverse for one’s self, having abandoned its natural course, then, remaining there, it obstructs the garment [of the body] and resorts to the other side. The sun and the moon (the friend of the night-lotus) each govern half the entire duration of time. Suṣumnā is the enjoyer of this entire time, consisting of nights and days. Therefore, the wise man should gradually apply effort according to the rules to restrain the movement of the vital breath through the path of the purified channels. With diligence, he should slowly fill his own belly with air through the path of the cool-rayed moon (the left nostril), free from drowsiness, using measures of the *vikāra* type, with his mental faculties fixed on the root of the Kālāgni. Then, the steady-minded one should retain the wind that has been filled for four *maṣi*-measures; as long as it is outside the bright star (the right nostril), he should hold it slowly for half of those measures, and once it is restrained within, he should do the opposite. The wise man should then perform the reverse, and again the opposite of that. By this method, the well-disposed one should constantly practice the perfect restraint of the vital breath.
That which produces perspiration is declared the lowest;
that which causes trembling in men is the middling; and the highest is that which effects the abandonment of the body's contact with the earth.
The wise person, composed through breath control,
should perform it according to the rules for as long as the qualities described for breath control can arise in this world.

This *prāṇāyāma* (breath control) is declared by the great sages devoted to yoga to be "with seed" (*sagarbha*) when it destroys all evils and yields hundreds of virtues; it is called "without seed" (*agarbha*) when it is devoid of recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*). A self-controlled twice-born man who, being pure, performs sixteen *prāṇāyāmas* accompanied by the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) every day at dawn and dusk, purifies himself from the sin of killing a fetus within a month—these [practices] burn away the mass of accumulated evils. Within six months, they rescue one from the heap of sins acquired in other births; after a year, they reveal that supreme Brahman known as Acyuta. Furthermore, leaving aside the *kapūra* and *kāka* methods, he of steady mind who constantly practices only the *kevala-kumbhaka* (pure retention) attains the speed of thought; such a mortal becomes free from old age and disease. Indeed, nothing in the three worlds is difficult for him to obtain while established in this *kevala-kumbhaka*; surely the eightfold supernatural powers (*aṇimā* etc. are already in his hand for him whose fear of death has been dispelled. Placing the tongue near the root of the teeth and not touching the pair of upper teeth, one should drink the air through the "crow-beak" (*kākacañcu*) method; this is the highest form of breath restraint (*prāṇasaṃyamana*). By slowly inhaling the air through the "cuckoo-beak" (*pikacañcu*) method and drawing it in continuously, fatigue, delusion, poison, bile-fever, and abdominal tumors are pacified. Even for one who drinks [the air] during both twilights for just a single *muhūrta*, [the result is attained] within three months.
(96) When the wind, carrying the scent of the *pikacañcu* flower, blows upon the earth, the success of Sarasvatī shall arise. Hari:
Even the fierce poison of those possessing terrible power is brought to destruction when it reaches the five rivers.
How much more so from drinking the breath from the mouths of scorpions, insects, spiders, crickets, and crows?
The man who constantly draws the wind from the crow’s beak (*pikacañcu*) into the mouth of his own *kuṇḍalī* through continuous meditation, lives free from the disease of consumption (*kṣayaroga*).
The man who, free from desire, drinks the wind from the parrot’s beak day and night,
will certainly, within a year, attain both hearing and sight even from a great distance.

By drinking the wind from the beaks of cuckoos through various methods, the powerful fear of death caused by old age quickly perishes along with it for men. Having placed his tongue at its root and firmly pressing his teeth against his teeth, the lord of practitioners who drinks the fragrant breeze—whether slowly or intensely—with streams of saliva flowing in succession, shall within six months be freed from all diseases and sins. Within a year, having conquered the swift onset of untimely death, he shall live for a long time upon the earth. (100)

By virtue of three years of practice, he who has hair as black as a bee-line knows the past and the future; poison does not take effect in his body even when bitten by the most terrible lords of serpents, nor does artificial or natural (sthāvara-jaṅgama) poison, much less even *kālakūṭa*. Having attained the eight qualities through the power of time, he sports upon the earth like Bhairava, O support of Yāmuṇḍā.

The food and exhalation passing through the aperture between the two pillars (the nostrils) is white; it flows from the moon situated in the hollow of the sky-lotus of the head and descends into the palace of the body. He who causes the bird [the vital breath] to enter the cavity of the belly within that channel called Vajra, for him there shall be the dissolution of the vessel of the universe, a state free from the body yet dense with immortality, and death itself becomes deathless. Bound by practice, he truly removes the multitude of diseases from his limbs and effects the movement of men through the sky. The wind, when mastered, spreads all forms of immortality; indeed, mastery over the breath is easily attained through practice. Now, having restrained the heel with the heel, standing with the left foot's heel placed at the base of the upward-pointing [perineum], with body and neck straight, self-restrained, and the flood of senses withdrawn from sense-objects; having filled the cavity of one’s own belly with winds drawn in like the tip of a crow’s beak, and having blocked the ear-openings with both thumbs, the eyes with the two index fingers, and the nose with the two middle fingers, the man of steady and pure intellect should then firmly close the mouth with the remaining fingers and fix his mind upon the abode of the Lotus-born (Brahmā). Having practiced according to his capacity for a day, he should then, with a concentrated mind, cause the Kuṇḍalinī—the illusory power (māyā) united with the supreme space consisting of consciousness—to rise up along the great path of Brahman, accompanied by the foundational power (ādhāraśakti). Having pierced the three signs (liṅgas), the wise man should lead that power of the Self upward through the Brahma-nāḍī from the station of the Lotus-born to the lotus of the sky, the source of supreme bliss, the root of the universe, the place of emission, where a stream of blood-like nectar flows from the interior of the moon.

Having drunk the divine nectar-essence of the *kula*, one whose self is composed should again enter the center of one's own *kula*. Then, by means of the application of the *mātrā* as instructed by the best of teachers, one should go from the *kula* to the *akula*. That power (*śakti*), which has become the life-force of the entire body, is called "Prāṇa" here in this preeminent Tantra. When that [power], having been led gradually until it touches the end of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is proclaimed by the lords of sages as the "Udghāta" (the upward thrust). The faithful practitioner, established in right conduct, constantly performs this through the power of practice, forever free from all impurities known as the *avadhūta*. Released from the floods of suffering, with old age, death, and disease gone, and endowed with a multitude of virtues, he lives for a long time in his true nature upon this earth. From her, indeed, the fourfold creation proceeds; into her dissolves the entire world, from Kālāgnirudra up to Śiva. This very *yonimudrā* has been described by me; its binding is difficult even for the gods to attain. There is nothing that cannot be accomplished by this binding for that preeminent practitioner; for him, [the obstacles] are severed, obstructed, pinned, paralyzed, asleep, intoxicated, fainted, deprived of potency, burnt, cast down, or situated on the side of the enemy—whether they be children, the elderly, or those arrogant in their youth.

Those beings who are known to be deficient, whose limbs are broken, and who are deprived of their mantras—these mudrās should not be bound at all; otherwise, all mantras become powerless. [Even] the violation of the teacher’s bed, the drinking of liquor, the double murder, and the theft of gold—by this [mudrā], they go to destruction.

By practicing this bond even once, they attain [liberation] immediately. For he alone is the best of ministers, he alone is the yogi established in the state of the perfection of qualities. He who constantly practices here with this bond—the steadfastness in the duties and laws of one’s own appropriate actions—by that constant practice of the bond performed by embodied beings, neither old age nor death, O King of the Ancestors, nor the fear brought about by them occurs. From the constant practice of this very fourfold bond, a human being attains the incomparable *siddhis* such as *aṇimā*, as well as exalted consciousness; and they constantly behold the peerless Yoga, victory over the vital breaths (*marut*), or the fifth, which is the supreme station of Viṣṇu, which the wise ever perceive.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the procedure for binding the Yonimudrā, in the Tripurāsārasamuccaya.

Now, I shall describe here the supporting lotuses situated within the Suṣumṇā, along with their contraction; as well as the deities residing on the petals of those lotuses, and the goddesses of the six supports who possess the colors of those lotuses. The wise here declare that the first support is the lotus at the Ajagranthi which I previously mentioned. It is endowed with four petals of golden luster, accessible to yogis, and a source of great wonder. Upon its four lotus petals, one should place the goddesses whose names correspond to the oceans beginning with Niruddha, or simply the vowels (*a* etc. alone. With the power of the nasal bindu, the deity Ṣoḍākinī shines here with a blazing, radiant light.

Through the yoga of perfect practice at the *mūlādhāra*, six qualities arise perfectly for men: paralysis (*stambha*), levitation (*utpluti*), the power of a frog (*dārdurī*), the ability to move through walls (*bhramitvāga*), the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*), and the excellence of physical luster. There is the manifestation of sound (*nādavyakti*), the blazing of the digestive fire, lightness of the limbs, sharpness of the senses, health, and freedom from dejection. Having made the mind steady here in this wheel (*cakra*) and constantly practicing with devotion, a person burns away the past, present, and future, as well as the scriptures themselves. Immediately abandoning the lotus-face of the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā), Sarasvatī, in her divine form, dances within the interior of his lotus-like mouth, joined by waves of joy. Having attained mastery over mercury and mantras, having conquered invincible Time, and having reached the state of agelessness and immortality, they finally attain the noble station of supreme bliss. In the beginning, the entire world was submerged in the waters of a single ocean; then, that primordial light-form became the *liṅga* within the heart. With his soul presided over by the six Siddhas, possessing the bodies of all the gods, endowed with six faces and six sheaths, Maheśa is the swan who destroys the darkness of the fear of worldly existence. The body of the Lord who bears the *liṅga*-form is the deity Dviranda. Mahākāla was the eastern face of Śiva; then [the face] facing upward; the southern face is Agni himself, the wielder of the Pināka bow; the western face is the venerable Chagalaṇḍa; and the northern face belongs to this [Lord].

At the base of the banner (the penis), there is a lotus called *svādhiṣṭhāna*, possessing six petals, shining like the rising sun. Upon its petals are placed the letters of the alphabet starting from 'k' (the first letter of the *ka-varga*) up to 't' (the last letter of the *ta-varga*), with a *bindu* (dot) illuminating their heads. This is the station of the Lord who is the Liṅga-ātman, the wielder of the trident, accessible only to the most excellent of yogis and to those who have transcended the senses (*pārākin*). In this *svādhiṣṭhāna*, by the power of dissolving his own mind, the best of practitioners—his heart stilled by a flood of intense bliss—whether standing on the ground or united with a woman, experiences the group of emotions filled with beauty and the side-long glances of deer-eyed women, smiling with passion. Here he knows the practice being performed, his own nature, and the entire web of scriptures without depending on them. Having shaken off old age and disease, this mortal man lives for a very long time, free from the fear of death. He constantly effects the supreme purification here for men whose bodies are otherwise vessels of impurity. Just as the moon, though obstructed by thick clouds in the world, attains firmness upon reaching autumn and the water-lily; and just as the great lord of chariots (Arjuna) was suddenly stopped from departing from the celestial lotus (the sky) by the glance of Kamalā (Lakṣmī); even so, the wise and steadfast, indeed the best of men, restrain the mind here. Just as a mighty lordly elephant, even when intoxicated, comes under control slowly through skillful means; and just as the powerful moon, though it is the maker of nectar, necessarily becomes subject to the wind of the breath (*saukama-rut*); in this same way, through the dissolution of the elephants that are the senses and passions such as attachment, the dissolution of the thunderbolt and the lotus (the *mūlādhāra* and *svādhiṣṭhāna*) is produced, and even the powerful *saṃvarti* fire arises. For men who partake of the mercury of the great nectar dissolved within, through the dissolution of the flickering mind, the rising of the moon of bliss manifests suddenly and gently.

Those people who constantly meditate upon the Maṇipūraka at the navel—possessing ten petals with the hue of blue collyrium, endowed with the ten syllables beginning with *ṭa* situated on the petals and topped by shimmering *bindus*, and presided over by Lākinī—they perform the compulsion of men, the neutralization of poisons, the shaking of the earth, and so forth. For the virtuous one whose self is fixed in this place, there is the supreme attainment of Pātāla; the mastery of the peerless sword is also seen by the eye. There is the power to assume form, to leave the earth, to enter another's body, the destruction of old age, the pacification of all suffering and disease, and the eluding of Time (Death). In the heart, the wise desire a lotus the color of a fresh cloud, vermilion, or gold, struck by the rays of the mouth and adorned with petals shining like the sun. It is decorated by the eleven Bhairavas, Krodhīśa and the rest, who possess fierce valor and are joined by their consorts. That [lotus] is presided over by Kākinī through her divine power, and is eternally graced by the Goddess Haṃsā. In this place, those yogis whose minds are perpetually settled remain unshaken even while standing in celestial chariots, accompanied by divine women endowed with wondrous and divine splendor. They possess knowledge regarding the incomparable Mantra and the three times, the shaking of cities, the hearing and seeing from afar, the power of flight, and union with the Yoginīs. Now, in the throat, there is the lotus called Viśuddha, possessing sixteen petals with the luster of a row of smoke, surrounded by the vowels beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha. In this place resides the Goddess Sākinī, whose own power is incomparable—the eternal Goddess who pacifies the distress of those who seek refuge.

(p. 103) The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the sensation born of eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive the sensation born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as real. He does not perceive the stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real; he does not perceive the once-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning as real; he does not perceive the non-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of non-returning as real; he does not perceive the arhat as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of arhatship as real; he does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the awakening of a pratyekabuddha as real. He does not perceive the bodhisattva as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of giving as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as real. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or great compassion as real. He does not perceive omniscience as real, nor does he perceive the state of all-knowledge as real. Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive these things as real that he is called a ‘bodhisattva.’”

With his lofty peaks covering the expanse of the sky, the mountain ranges adorned with various jeweled ridges; likewise, the delightful forest lands with their deer and antelopes, and the vast earth endowed with various fields beneficial to me. With its high waves filled with crocodiles, elephants, and sea-monsters, and formidable with clouds like excellent mountains; likewise, the ocean with its green waters from the pure rivers, the rows of swans, and the banks of lakes frequented by cranes. With its surface of foam and water-birds, its interior waters blue and terrifying with thundering sounds; likewise, the skull-like mass of new clouds accompanied by favorable winds and travelers. In this supreme, most wonderful, immutable, and sole source of great bliss, the yogi of steady mind should fix his own consciousness upon that highest station through the *mudrā*. Gradually, the mind attains identity with That through supportless concentration (*nirālambayā*); thereafter, the great bliss of the "Blue" (*nīla*) arises within from the state of dissolution. When the mind has dissolved here in the abode of the universe, first sparks like those of fire are seen, and immediately after, shimmering lamps and sprouts of light appear. Then, there shines a dense radiance like that of the rising sun, or rather, a splendor filled with moonlight within the hollow of the space between earth and sky. "The Lord of the glory of the treasure of eternal bliss," thus [is he called] the Person Śrī Vāsudeva; "He is not the self, He is Acyuta of inconceivable majesty"—thus is He meditated upon by yogis. In this supreme station, that very Blessed One, the immutable, becomes manifest.

Moving through the midst of the sky like Rāhu himself, it eclipses the orbs of the moon and sun; this is the great abode of the Lord, the sanctuary of the universe, the supreme station where virtuous men, at the time of death, having fixed their vital breath (prāṇa), enter the pervasive, eternal, primordial Person—the one to be known by the wise, the poet among poets, the source of all, the constant root of singular great bliss. Below the point of emission (visarga) lies the thousand-petaled lotus, facing downward, with its mass of filaments slightly reddened. Within it rests the moon, devoid of its deer-mark, possessing three peaks, with a network of rays shimmering from within, full of nectar. Inside that is the subtle aperture called the *brahmarandhra*, which serves as the support for the channel named Suṣumnā. This is the supreme, divine, secret place, inaccessible even to the gods, which must be guarded with effort. This is the station known as Kailāsa, the seat of Akula, the form of the Bindu and the form of the Sky (Kha). There dwells the God of gods, the Swan (*haṃsa*) who destroys the darkness of the fear of worldly existence (*bhava*). He is the primordial being of all beings, the ocean of nectar, emitting a continuous, pure stream of light within the inner self, bestowing desired fruits upon yogins and accessible through yoga. By the mere knowledge of this place, men shall never again be born in this cycle of transmigration. Through the yoga of constant practice, one gains the complete power to create and sustain the entire aggregate of elements. With his mind fixed on this supreme station named Kailāsa, the abode of the Swan, the yogi—freed from disease, having cast down mental afflictions, and liberated from death—lives for eternity. In this place resides the eternally risen [fire], free from the states of decay and growth, facing downwards.

The sixteenth digit (*ṣoḍaśī-kalā*) of the Moon, whose splendor resembles the rising sun, is like a single part of a hair-tip divided a hundredfold; because of its subtlety, it bears a stream of nectar flowing without interruption. Beyond this stands the Blessed Lady, the sovereign of the elements and the lord of the gods, known as *Nirvāṇa*, curved like a half-moon, reaching to the end of the sixteenth. Because of its subtlety, it is like a single part of a hair-tip split a thousandfold; she who is the mother of the three worlds possesses the luster of twelve suns. Situated above the great digit called *Nirvāṇa* is the supreme power (*parā-śakti*), known as *Nirvāṇa-śakti*, whose brilliance is equal to ten million suns, profound, and like a portion of the tip of a hair. The Mother of all beings, who is equal to a ten-millionth part [of that], is eternally risen, stainless, eternal, vast through the state of bliss, the gateway to the city, and without support. Beyond this is the station of the power of Nirvāṇa, the Śaiva state, which is more supreme than the supreme, eternal, beyond measure, stainless, eternally risen, and free from desire. Wise men call that the "station of Viṣṇu," some the "station of Brahmā," some the "station of the Swan" (*haṃsa-pada*), and others the "stainless station" (*nirañjana-pada*) or the "unsupported" (*nirālambana*). Having repeatedly projected the power from the abode of the Lotus-born (Brahmā) through the stages and places up to the limit of the Command (*ājñā*), and having meditated with a concentrated heart in due order, one should lead her to the end of Sound (*nāda*) and meditate upon the primordial Power in the form of consciousness—residing within the Great Lotus of the Heart of the Bird-family (the *Haṃsa*)—for the attainment of desired fruits. She is directly like lac-dye, situated in the Great Lotus of the Heart located in the sky, emerging from the Swan.

Having drunk the flood of divine nectar, one should again enter the center of the *kula*. In each and every wheel (*cakra*), by means of the spreading essences of nectar in due order, one should satiate all those deities, beginning with Hākinī, who reside in the lotus-born feet; one should then inundate that Kuṇḍalinī.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Foundation" (*Ādhāranirṇaya*).

Within the central cavity of the *svayambhū-liṅga*’s own source, inside the lotus of the heart, the wise say that one [seed-syllable] is called *Bāṇa*, while others are in the space between; others say they are in the sky-lotus. Having meditated upon that seed-syllable known as *Vāgbhava*, resembling molten gold, in the place of the self-manifested *bhūta-liṅga*, and having meditated on the second, the one called *Kāma*, possessing the luster of a *bandhujīva* flower and the brilliance of the autumnal moon, within the *bāṇa-liṅga* situated in the hollow of the heart-lotus, one with a tranquil mind should contemplate the third seed-syllable surrounded by the others. Those who, having fixed their vital breaths (*prāṇa*) within the source, meditate with their minds on the Goddess Bhāratī—known as the Seed-syllable—residing in the cavity of her own source, arisen from the cavity of the navel, whose splendor is like the rising sun, and who has the form of the *siddha-liṅga*—for them alone there is the wealth of poetic talent that distills the nectar of the scales. Those who, with undistracted minds, meditate on the divine women who illuminate the entire *kula* with their splendors red as vermilion, residing within the heart-lotus in the form of the *bāṇa-liṅga*, arisen from the point (*bindu*)—they [attain the goal].
The desires of those who worship the form of the Liṅga as Gaurī or by other names with their own inner luster fall upon the earth at their very feet.

May that stream of yours, the abode of all prosperity—resembling the crescent moon situated at the point of the bindu, radiant with the beauty of the rays of the moon, emerging from the great lotus of the visarga, and consisting of nectar as pale-red as coral—protect us. 1.

The excellent practitioner, having fixed his intellect steadily upon these three locations—the three *liṅgas* which possess exceedingly intense splendor—should perform the recitation of the mantra one hundred thousand times with fresh flowers from the *brahmataru* tree; thereafter, he should offer oblations at night with those same flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), while moving according to the [prescribed] course. || 2 ||
Having fearlessly stepped upon the deer and reached the base of the mountain rising from the earth,
the wise one, while stationed on the mountain slope, enveloped the sun with his hands and, having composed himself,
began the prologue for the performance of the *Kapālika* dance before Rahu.
One should perform the oblation in the sacrificial pit with the hand using *kuraṇḍaka* flowers; this is a most wonderful rite for Yama.
A mortal who, with a mind thus disciplined, offers oblations for even a single year,
immediately conquers death and bestows upon his body a pervasive nourishment;
like the god of love, he shatters the pride of gazelle-eyed women, becoming as it were a female bee to them.
He whose beautiful, curly locks are adorned with three [marks] shall live for many years. || 4 ||

She bore a lower lip lovely with a splendor like that of the Bandhūka flower or an evening cloud, made radiant by the rays of her gentle smile; and her pair of cheeks, adorned with beautiful earrings, was as white as the full moon.

She possesses high, well-knit breasts, and her beautiful waist bends under the weight of her pearl necklace; she is adorned with the three folds of skin that ripple like waves; she has a deep navel-cavity and thighs resembling the massive trunks of plantain trees; her lotus-feet are ruddy. She bears upon her head the crescent of the moon from which flows a stream of pure nectar, and wears a crest-jewel fashioned from the blossoms of the *santāna* tree. Clad in garments as white as the rays of light, she stands upon the great lotus that is as white as ten million moons.
With her two hands, she holds a crystal rosary and the auspicious vessel of wisdom (*jñānabhadrā*).

She bears in her two right hands a jewel-encrusted crown, a book, and the gesture of fearlessness; in her two left hands, she holds a jeweled girdle and a conch. She is adorned with jeweled armlets, necklaces, and divine garments, and is anointed with divine perfumes. Though she is the mother of the three worlds, she is completely filled with the splendor of her own radiance, even while she constantly upholds the entire web of scriptures.
Her lotus feet are colored by the pollen from the garlands on the crowns of the gods and asuras who bow down in reverence.

Having meditated upon that Vāgīśvarī, who resides in the sky beyond the Great Bindu (mahābindu) seat and even beyond that place, one should lead her from there to the station of oneself. Beyond that which is beyond the end of "sa" (sāntātīta), she possesses incomparable majesty; from there [emerges] the Solar Wheel (sūryacakra). From that—
Then, having brought the sky-lotus from there, one should bring it to the realm of the departed (pretabhūmi), which is praised by all the worlds.
From the location of the *preta* one should draw a half-moon, and from there one should begin the construction of the bridge;
from that very immeasurable space, one should contemplate reaching the abode of Īśvara.
Therefore, one should lead the Goddess of gods from the abode of Rudra to the station of Viṣṇu;
from the station of Viṣṇu to the station of Brahmā; and from the station of Brahmā, one should lead Kuṇḍalinī to the center of the house.
She is seated upon that lotus of the body, which is adorned with a thousand petals, possesses a beautiful pericarp and filaments, and abides in the radiant light of the *kuṇḍalinī*.
Then, one should consecrate the Blessed Lady with an uninterrupted stream of nectar dripping from the *bindu* at the end of the syllables known as *ga* and *kha*.
By this meditation constantly practiced, O Goddess, death goes to its destruction;
and those perfections that are accessible to divine beings also come to men before long.
Those of pure intellect who meditate within upon the Goddess Bhavānī— who dwells in the Akula state from the Base (Ādhāra) up to the Great Lotus (Mahāpadma),
whose form is radiant with the luster of nectar through the Brahma-nāḍī,
and who exists in the form of the Liṅga— become wise men, cleansed of all sins and endowed with every virtue, accessible through the Mother of Contemplation.
Those whose pores shine with the radiance of a mass of intense luster white as cow’s milk, frost, or a pearl necklace, who possess the form of the entire body of Śeṣa as their insignia,
and who drench the white Goddess of Speech— who is like a stream of nectar flowing from a choice lotus—
with showers [of that nectar], are themselves death unto Death.

Those who on this earth constantly sprinkle with the stream of divine nectar this Goddess— who bears the form of the *liṅga*, is praised by gods and asuras, and resides within the *suṣumnā*— with a splendor like a mass of collyrium, [attain] the dissolution of the form of men at the end of time.
For those whose lower lips have been seen by closing their eyes, how could there be any decay?
He who remembers Tripura within his lineage— she whose slender body is like a stalk of lotus fiber bathed in lac-dye.
Afflicted by love, they remember him— the lord of Rati and the equal of the god of love— whose left thigh was gazed upon with eyes that were dazed and charmingly motionless with wonder.
The sky appeared as if covered by heaps of vermilion powder,
and the circle of the earth seemed drenched with liquid lac.
Those lovers who, casting aside their modesty, meditate upon the various charms of the beloved of Hara, surely attain her on this earth;

for from the interior of the thunderbolt-like channel of the one whose abode is the lotus-born (Brahmā), they slowly extract a multitude of nectar-drops from the lunar orb, joined with the *haṃsa* [vital breath] and the power (*śakti*).

Having led [the mind] there, he who constantly remembers his own primordial power residing in the sky— by that [power], the dissolution of the vessel of the cosmic egg becomes the bodyless [state], which is the dense [cessation] even of death itself.

One should meditate on her as having a yellow luster for rites of immobilization (*stambhana*) and the like; as white as the moon for rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and the like; as smoky for rites of eradication (*uccāṭana*) and the like; and as red as a hibiscus flower for the attraction of the people of the three worlds and for magical operations (*kārmaṇa*).
For the attainment of sky-faring (*khecarī*) and other such powers, one should constantly meditate upon her, day after day, as resembling a pure crystal gem.
One should meditate upon that which is directly present in both accomplishment and liberation, free from conceptualization, resembling the sky and serpent, and accessible through devotion.

On this path, the wise one should observe nine *lakṣas* for the sake of attaining the imperishable state, by which the fivefold incomparable success (*siddhi*) is achieved here. At the base, the flag, the navel region, the heart, the belly, the throat, as well as the uvula, between the eyebrows, at the abode of the Lord of Beings (*bhūtanātha*), and finally at the end of the nine: One should meditate on [the deity] at the base (*ādhāra*) as having a golden luster, radiant and blazing; at the place of the six faces, with a splendor like that of a fresh sun; at the navel, within the lotus of the heart;
and within the chest, in the form of a lamp, with a light shining like the rays of the sun.
In the throat, it has the form of a lamp-flame; between the eyebrows, it is the radiance of a multitude of jewels;
and at the end of the nose, it is light—skillful in destroying the darkness of the fear of worldly existence, known as the universe, and the generator of waves of unsurpassed bliss.

That which is difficult for sinners to attain, which supports the three worlds, known as Traipura, and which stands above all principles— that is the Supreme. Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Liṅga."
Now I shall describe the external worship of Ambikā, whose teaching is honored by the three worlds;
by performing this worship on the surface of the earth, a human being attains the state of being worthy of worship by all people.
In a temple or a house that is pure, pleasing, and free from the gaze of animals,
one who has performed self-purification according to the previously mentioned method should thereafter perform the purification of the site.
The sky [of consciousness] of the Supreme Lord, previously joined [with the breath], is likewise situated with the *sānalā* (fire-accompanied) left eye.
By sprinkling it with water from *kuśa* grass, one may be purified entirely through this conciliatory rite;
the seed-syllable of logic (*tarkabīja*), which is without lineage yet possesses lineage,
is joined with the syllable preceding *Śiva* (i.e., *Ha*) and the crescent moon.
With this mantra, one whose mind is composed should perform the sprinkling of the ritual substances with water.
Puṣkara, conjoined with Śiva, Mukha, and so forth—this is proclaimed as the mantra for the purification of the vessel.
Then, with that very [water], the person should wash the collection of vessels with nectar-like water; thereafter,
he should smear the pedestal, which has been rinsed with water.
[He was adorned] with naturally occurring flowers, induka flowers, and turika flowers.
One should draw this yantra all around with Kashmiri gorocana; then, having drawn a triangle followed by a circle for the petals, as will be described hereafter.
Then there is a pentagon, and outside of that, a circle as well.
Furthermore, one should draw a six-petalled lotus outside of that,
and subsequently an eight-petalled lotus outside of that;
then, on the northern side of the pedestal, one should worship the lineage of gurus according to the prescribed rite.
Beginning from the northwestern direction and extending as far as the northeast,
one should worship Ādhāraśakti, Āsana, and Mūlamantra, as well as Ananta.
Above that, the mantrin should worship the Tortoise and the Earth with scents and other offerings;
he should worship them in sequence in the four corners of the pedestal, beginning from the southeast.

Having worshipped the four [deities] beginning with Dharma with the four [substances] beginning with fragrance, and likewise those beginning with Dharma in the cardinal directions, and having worshipped the triad of sattva, rajas, and tamas upon the pedestal (pīṭha).
Above that, one should worship a lotus; upon it, one should worship the eight [petals] and the orbs of the sun and moon.
One should worship the *preta* situated in the center of the triangle within the middle of the lunar orb.
Following that, having invoked the beloved of Śaṅkara from the depths of the heart-lotus, one should place her above that.

Having established [the deity], restrained [the senses], and prostrated, one should display the mudrā; being exceedingly secret, it is called "Secret," and one should perform the offering of arghya and so forth according to the ritual rules.
In the left corner of the triangle, one should worship Rati, who holds a noose in her hand, resembles molten gold,
and possesses a captivating appearance, using her own seed-syllable.
One should worship the delighted [deity] in the southern corner with her own seed-syllable— she who resembles the moon,
holds a goad in her hand, has a beautiful face, and is resplendent in her attire— with fragrances and other offerings.
The practitioner of mantras should worship the flower-armed god (Kusumāyudha) seated before the Goddess,
having the hue of the bandhūka flower, and holding a bow and arrow made of kārṣmarya wood.
The seed-syllable of Kāmarāja is taught as the seed of desire for passion; the Vāgbhava is likewise declared. That which is called Sammohana is proclaimed as the seed of delight.
Having worshipped those five deities of the arrows with their respective mantras upon those five petals,
[one should meditate on] the young women who resemble the moon, gold, twilight clouds, a blue lotus, and madder.
Drāviṇī and the others, adorned with all ornaments and full of passion,
hold arrows in their right hands while making gestures of salutation with their remaining hands.
Then one should worship the goddesses named Bhagā, Bhagajihvikā, Bhagāsyā, Bhagasarpiṇī, and Bhagākṣī on the six petals, as well as the Bhagāhlādanikās in sequence.
They are smoky-grey like autumn clouds, resembling the twilight sky, water-laden clouds, fruit-bearing trees, the night, and gold in color;
they are beautiful with ornaments, blazing, youthful, their minds delighted by wine, and enchanting.
With his own hands, he bears a sword, a trident, a scimitar, a staff of Vetālas, spears, and a shield.
Wondrous to others,
I shall here describe the parts of the skull, such as the *bhaga* and so forth, along with the body, the *dundubhi*, the *nāda-bindu*, and the *mudrās*, pertaining to the deities.
The seed-syllables also consist of the Vāgbhava [syllable] together with the staff (daṇḍa).
In the sky situated in the southeast, preceded by the Kula [direction] and joined with the moon [digit] that bestows wealth, one should meditate on Brahmāṇī in due order:
seated upon a swan, resembling molten gold, possessing four faces and five eyes, holding in her lotus-hands the *brahmakūrca*, a water-pot, a radiant staff, and a clear rosary.

One should worship her—who wears beautiful garments, whose limbs are lovely, who always bears a fine mass of matted hair and a necklace—at the base of the leaf that points toward the direction of Hari, using perfumes and other offerings.

One should worship that Māheśī, who holds a skull, a skull-topped staff, a hand-drum, a trident, a sword, and a chisel in her long, pillar-like arms; she is radiant with three eyes at the base of her matted locks, which are like the fire and the quarters of the sky, and she bears a charming crescent moon; she rides upon the bull, who resembles the moon, and dwells eternally [in the heart].

One should worship Kaumārī, who possesses the radiance of youth, with a most beautiful countenance and the luster of saffron; she is exceedingly lovely and holds in her right hands a spear, a noose, and a goad, as well as the gesture of fearlessness.
Playful and graceful, with a pair of large, languid eyes, adorned with all ornaments, and seated at the base of a leaf in the southeast direction, one should honor her with perfumes and flowers.
In the southwest direction, at the base of the leaf, [one should worship] her whose limbs are dark like a water-laden cloud, who possesses beautiful hair,
and who holds with her staff-like arms a conch, a skull, and a discus.

One should constantly worship with perfumes and other offerings that Vaiṣṇavī, who is mounted upon Garuḍa, resplendent with a jeweled crown, her eyes ever-fluttering and delighted by the intoxication of wine;
and Vārāhī, who has the face of a boar, wields a shield, a sword, a formidable plow, and a mace,
and whose cheeks shine with jeweled earrings at the base of her ear-lobes.

One should worship with perfumes and other offerings that Indrāṇī, who is eternally worthy of universal honor, who sits upon the peak of the mountain like a fierce female serpent in this world, whose face is most beautiful, whose body’s luster is smoky-grey,

whose own face resembles the orb of the moon, whose complexion has the hue of sapphire, whose eyes roll to the corners of her ears, and who wears a crown of jewels— at the base of the leaf belonging to the direction of Vāyu.
One should daily worship that Cāmuṇḍā, who holds a vajra, a conch, a trident, and an arrow in her four lotus-like hands; she is adorned with perfumes, flowers, and incense,
and she possesses a terrifying mouth within a fierce and formidable brow that blazes with intense radiance— the consort of the Lord of the Gods.
She bears a sword, a trident, a skull-cup, and a shield with her own lotus-like hands.

One should worship Kālī, who is fleshless, red-eyed, and a source of terror to the three worlds; she dwells at the root of the leaf of the Saumya direction, wears a crown of skeletons, has upward-pointing hair, and resides in the abode of the ancestors (the cremation ground).
Afterwards, one should worship Āmavayyarūpā, whose face is most beautiful and who has the luster of pure gold.
In her lotus-hands she holds a protection-thread, the gesture of fearlessness, a radiant lotus, and a citron fruit.

One should worship Lakṣmī, who is herself worshipped by the people of the three worlds, who is rich in youth, and who is supported at the base of the petal in the direction of Īśa (northeast) by the weight of her lofty, full breasts. Then, one should place these seeds: Ananta at the beginning of the wick, Dīpa [the letter 'ra'] at the end of the wick, and Indra at the end of the eye [the letter 'i'].
[The sequence] ending with *prāṃśu*, *udra*, *gantā*, and *anta*, followed by *kulānta* joined with *anantarudra*;
then *tithīśa* with *sānanta*, *bhṛgu*, *atha*, and *hara* together with *ananta*.
The Lord of Wealth (Dhanada) with Bakānta (Bakānta), followed by Bakonasta (Bakonasta);
then Ka-pūrva (Ka) joined with Sūkṣmānta (Sūkṣmānta); then Vana (Vana) with Anuvadana (Anuvadana), and then Vadana (Vadana) joined with Śacīnātha (Śacīnātha), and finally Kāntānvita (Kāntānvita).
Then, one should worship Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodhīśa, Unmattakapālin,
the one named Bhīṣaṇa, and the one known as Saṃhāra, in sequence within the Palāśa petals.

Holding staffs, skull-bowls, and tridents that match the dark blue color of a mass of collyrium, they are joined by small drums; they have three eyes and are fierce with staff-like arms, one hand holding an elephant’s trunk, and staff-like trunks.
They wore elephant hides as upper garments, their foreheads knit with frowns, their hair like bees and lotus stalks; though their inner hearts were gladdened, they possessed the vigor of prime youth.
The third [letter] from *ha* (i.e., *ja*), conjoined with *bha* and *bu*, followed by the end of the *kula* (i.e., *la*), joined with the corner of the eye (the vowel *e*),
and having its head marked by the half-moon (*niśākara*)— this is declared here to be their seed-syllable (*bīja*).
He who is Hetuka, he known as Yantripurāntara, those two Vahni and Vetāla whose tongues are like spirits,
Kāla, Karāla, and he who indeed has the terrifying form of Ekapāda and is named Bhīma.
Then, [he visualizes her] whose complexion resembles a dark blue cloud, holding upon the tips of her fingers— in sequence with perfumes and other offerings—
a trident, a skull-cup, and a shimmering snake-noose, borne by her slender, staff-like arms.

The practitioner should worship with the Lord of Spirits (Bhūtīśa), who is joined by the Half-Moon, those of terrifying form who possess vast cavernous mouths formidable with fangs, whose faces are made hideous by three eyes from which blood flows and by knitted brows, who are eager for Kādambarī wine, whose hair stands erect, and who are endowed with youthful vigor.
His body is dark like the *priyaṅgu* flower, his hands are resplendent, he wears a shimmering crest-jewel made of jewels,
and his form is presided over by the face of an elephant.
One should worship this Hari, who bears a thousand lotus-eyes,
in the eastern direction with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings.
Then, one should worship Agni, who has a blossoming *kiṃśuka* flower as his emblem, who is mounted upon a goat, whose hands hold a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) and a spear (*śakti*),
who wears a jeweled crown, and who is adorned with gem-studded earrings, using fragrant flowers of the finest quality.
Thereafter, one should worship on the right side the Lord of the Ancestors (Pitṛnātha), who resembles a dark blue rain-cloud, holding a staff in his hand,
with reddish-brown eyes, seated upon a buffalo, and resplendent in brilliant attire.
One should worship him who is mounted upon a man, who possesses terrifying fangs and wields a well-sharpened sword, whose body is dark like a water-laden cloud,
who is playfully restless, as swift as a flash of lightning, and whose eyes are blood-red.
Then he beheld the lord of the rākṣasas, adorned with various ornaments, according to his custom.
One should worship Varuṇa in his own direction— he who resembles the full autumnal moon, who is seated upon a sea-monster (makara), who is endowed with radiant attire,
whose cheeks are adorned with jeweled earrings, and who holds a boon-granting gesture and a noose.

One should worship Anala in his own quarter according to the prescribed rite, offering flowers and other gifts, while he holds a boon-bestowing staff, a goad, and a red hand, possesses a pure banner, has a body with the natural luster of smoke, and wears necklaces of jewels.
Then [he saw] the Lord of Wealth seated, his color like a mass of gold, surrounded by all the Yakṣas and treasures;
holding a mace in his hand, with tawny eyes, and a pair of lotuses beautifully adorned with flowers.
And one should always worship with perfumes and flowers in one's own direction for as long as one lives.

In the northeast direction, one should worship Hara, whose mass of matted hair is adorned with the crescent moon, who has three eyes, whose body is reddened by vermilion, and who always holds a trident and a skull-cup.

Then the practitioner [should visualize Him] holding with His four arms the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and the one called yoga (*yogākhyamudrā*), His body smeared with ashes, and mounted upon the preeminent bull.

The mantra of the world-protector (Lokapāla) is proclaimed as follows: beginning with the head [syllable] *sa*, followed by the group of water-syllables starting with *ma* (*maskādi*), joined with the final syllable of fire (*ra*) and the syllable *ka*; this is preceded by the subtle [seed-syllable] and joined with the eastern face [the syllable *ya*]. 64.

Thereafter, that lord of practitioners, endowed with devotion, should worship the host of *vaṭukas*, Durgā, and the *kṣetrapālas* in due order with their respective seed-syllables followed by "namaḥ," using sandalwood paste, flowers, and other offerings.
One should worship Bhūtavaha, Piśitāśa, and Īśa in the directions starting from the northeast (vāyu-īśa). 65.
He should offer oblations to the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the powerful Bhūtas; thus has the ritual of sacrifice been described.
Even the wise man who performs this daily, though he be at the very bottom of the ocean, [attains his goal].
Having attained all his desires in their entirety, he rejoices like Giriśa. || 1066 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter.

Those of perfectly pure intellect have declared that for both daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit is recommended; it may be triangular like the house of Smara (the god of love), or circular.

Alternatively, a hexagonal pit, resembling the moon, is praised as a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila); this should be one span in size, raised to the height of a thumb-joint, and made very level with sand.
(119) The wise say that it should be quadrangular, with a height of one cubit, and a width of one cubit.
Then one should perform purification, washing, and drying, and likewise one should also perform inhalation. || 68 ||

There, one should draw three lines rising upwards from the east; then, with sacrificial grass (*barhis*), one should likewise draw four-faced deities with faces turned toward the west. Among them, for the enemy of Vṛtra (Indra), Hari (Viṣṇu) is situated in the middle of the eastern line, while [the others] are in the center, to the right, and to the left of the eastern line.
O Lord, likewise, in this [mandala], the presiding deities of the lines oriented toward the east are Śvīśa, Śrīśa, and Surādhipa. || 69 ||
Having sprinkled [the area] with water containing kuśa grass and perfumes such as sandalwood, and having worshipped its center with the middle [mantra],
one should then meditate upon Vāgīśvarī, who shines like a dark-blue river and is beautifully bathed.
Having placed [the seed] born from the orb of the sun, or from a fire at the time of death, or from the house of a Vedic scholar, into a field or into a vessel— whether a golden vessel,
a copper vessel, or even a clay vessel— the mantra-practitioner, with a mind free from great impurity, should deposit it using the seed-syllable of fire as the mantra.
Abandoning that portion consisting of raw flesh, one should thereafter purify it with the weapon-mantra through meditation.

Then, having armored oneself with the Kavaca mantra, the wise one, having subsequently established the self and displayed the Dhenu-mudrā, should perform the sprinkling (āmratīraṇa) with the fire-seed syllable (Ra) accompanied by the nasal drop (bindu). 72.
Having circumambulated three times in a clockwise direction the Mistress of Speech who is properly situated in the center of the *kuṇḍa*,
the mantra-practitioner should then place his own face toward the *yoni* and [offer] the fire with the root mantra.
Then, composed in mind, one should offer seven oblations of clarified butter with the *hṛn-mantra*;
thus, this rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) will be properly performed here when [the moon] has entered the sign other than [that of] the white [lunar day].
In this manner, the practitioner of mantras should perform the *puṃsavana* rite, and thereafter the *sīmantonnayana*;
he should likewise perform for the fire the *jātakarma* rite according to that same procedure.
Then [he saw] one seven cubits tall, with three feet, two heads,
four tusks, and bound in three ways;
joined with tawny eyes numbering twenty.
That fire has two nostrils and four ears. || 75 ||
Seated upon a red lotus with one leg pendant, he has mounted the back of the lordly bull;
his face is turned toward himself, and he is devoid of four right arms as well as three left arms.
In his right hands he holds a spear, fire, and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles;
in his left hands, a javelin, a palm-leaf fan, a serpent,
and a full vessel of molten gold.
The vessel [is placed] perpetually beneath the seven-tongued [fire].
That which is golden, yellow, and red,
situated on the left side of the face, multiform,
and possessing the beautiful color of well-refined gold.
She stands at the eastern direction of the wielder of the trident, [the quarter] beginning with gold.
That one which is the color of lapis lazuli and is named Kanaka is seated upon Vāsava;
that which is red has the appearance of the color of the rising sun.
That tongue of the fire is well-established as "jihvā-hari."
p.
121) That which is black, with a color like that of a blooming rain-cloud,
is situated in the quarter of the Lord of the Rakṣasas.
Resplendent like a ruby, the goddess Prabha is situated in the western direction;
resembling a red lotus flower, she is Tiraścī, located in the direction of the wind.
The tongue named Bahurūpikā, which possesses its true characteristics, is situated to the south of the northern [tongue];
it is praised when located in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). The tongue called Hiraṇyā is recommended for rites on the ground such as *kārmaṇa* (subjugation).
The one named Kanakā is considered suitable for rites such as *stambhana* (paralysis), while the tongue Raktā is indeed favored for rites such as *dveṣaṇa* (causing enmity).
For the purpose of killing, the dark-complexioned Śākyā is proclaimed here on earth by the best of wise men;
for driving away, the red one is effective, and through the Bahurūpottara [tantra], success is achieved.
O slender one, she grants supernatural power from the south, and she is always auspicious in the center.

Other wise scholars, who have reached the further shore of the scriptures and possess pure intellects, declare that there is the Suprabhā situated to the east of the Lord of the Ancestors (Yama); the Kṛṣṇā and Hiraṇyā to the south;
the Bahurūpikā to the west; the Raktā situated to the north; the Atiriktā to the southeast; and the Kanakā situated in the middle of Kuṇḍala.
The wise [should use] a tongue named Kanaka for rites of pacification;
one that is red for rites of subjugation (kārmaṇa); and one that is black for minor activities.
They say that the tongue uttered as "Suprabhā" brings about liberation;
it is the tongue that is superior in attraction, multiform, and the bestower of all perfections.

The practitioner of mantra should contemplate Citrabhānu as endowed with all ornaments, appearing in this form for all rites; he is joined with the seven tongues of flame that are perfectly delightful, born with his face turned upward and averted.
At the conclusion of the birth-rite, the mantra-practitioner, having honored [the deity] with water for the feet, the arghya offering, and so forth, according to rule,
should offer seven oblations of clarified butter with the heart-mantra over the smoke of the banner of the illustrious name of such-and-such a person.
Then one of sharp intellect should properly strew kuśa grass with its tips pointing northward around the single-girdled sacrificial pits,
placing the girdle below them.
One should spread [the sacrificial grass] upon the girdle; in the case of two girdles, it should be over the upper girdle;
but in the case of three girdles, one should spread it upon the middle girdle.
The wise practitioner should place three enclosing stones (*paridhi*) outside the sand of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*),
on the southern, northern, and western sides of the pit (*kuṇḍa*).
The eastern portion is designated as the front (pūrva), the right side as the south (dakṣiṇā),
the left side as the north (uttara), and the rear as the west (paścima) by those learned in the Agamas and by the wise.
Then, having spread darbha grass on the left side with their tips pointing toward the beloved’s direction,
he should place the vessels above that in pairs.
The wise one does not long for that nirvana.
Vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay are highly recommended here for rites such as *śāntika* and others;
likewise, these trees— the *selva*, *akṣadruma*, and *śigru*— are used for the rites of *vidveṣaṇa* and *uccāṭana*.
For rites such as subduing, killing, and so forth, these vessels are also highly recommended.
Then, having spoken thus, one should fill one vessel among those vessels with water and [invoke] the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) therein.
Having reflected well, he should sprinkle the collection of materials situated on the left side with *darbha* grass from a *kūrca* while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having performed the purification with ghee and possessing a perfectly pure intellect, one should offer seven oblations;
this is the *annaprāśana* [rite], and it is also for the *caula*.
Bestow the object of perception even upon the two eyes.
In all [ceremonies] such as the auspicious Godāna and others, he should offer oblations with his heart;
he should likewise offer oblations during the Samāvartana and Vivāha ceremonies.
And having prepared a fire in the consecrated ground according to the previously prescribed rite,
one should then worship Ambikā there along with her retinue, as instructed.
One should offer ten oblations to each of the deities of the retinue, and one to the Goddess;
thus, having generated the Bhairava-fire, one should then begin the homa.
By means of oblations made with palāśa flowers, the three sweets, white flowers, campaka, pāṭala, and vacakila, a person attains all desires.
One may obtain a kingdom with bilva fruits and their leaves, as well as imperial sovereignty with lotuses;
long life with grass-blades and sprouts along with their leaves, peace with consecrated sesame seeds, wealth with a base [of offerings], and freedom from disease with white mustard seeds.
Through jaggery one gains affection, through leaves sons, and through fruits happiness.
Through this oblation of parched grain, one attains good fortune and prosperity; through oblations of *dhānya* grain, [the same]; and through *kādamba* flowers, lordship over the world of the Yakṣas.
A mortal attains the state of a Vidyadhara through Punnaga trees; through Malaya flowers, he reaches the worlds of the Siddhas and Gandharvas.

The summoning of yakṣiṇīs occurs through oblations of arjuna flowers and mustard seeds mixed with the three sweets (trimadhu). Courtesans come under control through oblations of harihaya flowers and kiṃśuka flowers. Through oblations of karṇikāra flowers, the gods of the earth are subdued; through kāsamarda flowers, the kṣatriyas; through kiṅkarāta flowers, the hosts of vaiśyas here become subject to one's will; and through pāṭala flowers, the śūdras.
By performing a homa with even a small portion of goat or elephant flesh, an entire enemy kingdom shall come under one's own control;
furthermore, even a mighty hostile force shall turn its back in retreat when [the offering] is mixed with honey.
