At night, oblations should be performed with the three pungents, nimba, parakeśa, and nākhalā,
combined with one's own jaggery and mixed with mustard oil.
Let them tear asunder the three [worlds], which act like the days of a sage.
Indeed, a fire-offering performed with *nagnajitasthya*, *aja*, *haridrā*, and pieces of fingernails is a rite that,
for seven days up to every fortnight, brings about the immobilization of even the most powerful armies of kings.
Through oblations of *māṣa* beans one attains testicular enlargement; through *kodrava* grains, affliction by disease;
through *kalāya* pulses, wind-related ailments; through *adakṣaja* fuel-sticks, intoxication; and through [oblations of] *mṛtasañjīvanī* fuel-sticks, death.
Within seven days, [the results are achieved] by means of those made from śālmalī wood.
A human being [should perform the rite] with *kapilā* [cow's milk], clarified butter, barley, wheat, and sesame seeds, using hexagonal sacrificial pits (*ṣaḍaśra-kuṇḍa*).
Having become composed in his inner self through the night vigil, he attains the state of a sky-farer for a million years.
Having kindled a fire with fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood and offered oblations of *bandhujīva* flowers sprinkled with sandalwood water,
all beings become subject to one's will through this *homa*.
And likewise, they may be made with priyaṅgu flowers.
A person, having offered various kinds of food, edibles, drinks,
and sweet substances such as those from the *vaṭa* and *udumbara* trees, shall attain supreme prosperity in this world.
But fame was fashioned by Mallikā, endowed with [all] these qualities.

Through oblations of blue lotuses, contentment is attained; through saugandhika flowers, nourishment (puṣṭi) arises; through white water-lilies (kumuda), affection for the people; and through kaṅkeli blossoms, sons shall be born.
Whatever indeed may be most difficult for men to attain on the surface of the earth,
all that becomes easily achievable in no long time through the oblation of the three sweets.
Regarding the heights measured in *ghṛta* [finger-breadths]: double sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) is the best; here, for the medium [size], it is half of that;
and eight finger-breadths is the lowest. It originates from sesame seeds.
In the same way, honey mixed with the five products of the cow [is offered].
One handful of milk-curds from the cow, and from the forest, one each of wild grains;
and a single cake should be the size of an *akṣa* seed.
One each of plantain, orange, and citron; ten pieces of jackfruit,
and seven pieces of wood-apple fruit.
Karkarikā is a piece of a vegetable stalk; dalapuṣpa is a piece of fruit; akhaṇḍa is that which is equal in size to four thumbs; and there are also side dishes, oil-cakes, and kṛsara.
Indeed, half of half a *culuka* is the measure of a handful (*prasṛti*) of sesame seeds when cooked;
a handful of parched grain (*lāja*) is said to be equal to that, while mustard seeds are declared to be half of half a *kaṣa*.
Mudga and māṣa beans are measured by the *karṣa*, while rice (*vrīhi*) is measured by the handful;
sixteen *māṣas* constitute a *narapati*; wheat and red rice are measured in the same way.
Seven or eight barley-corns [make] a *veṇuyava*; five or six [of these] are said to constitute a *gulā* (half a *phala*). Half a *muṣṭi* is declared to be the measure of rice grains.
Saffron, sandalwood, musk, and ghanasāra should be the size of chickpeas;
the fruit of the kapittha tree should be the size of a large fruit and divided into two parts.

Having discarded the *śleṣmātaka* tree and the *piśāca* tree, one should gather sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) from other trees; having discarded the cow’s tail and the *śīrṣaka* plant, other grasses should serve as the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*).

One should offer fuel-sticks of *edha* wood into a golden vessel, a sacrificial porridge (*caru*) into a silver one, and clarified butter into a multi-colored vessel; furthermore, one should offer *siddhārtha* seeds into a yellow vessel and barley into a red one.
In this world, one should offer parched grain (lāja) to Kṛṣṇā, flour (saktu) to Suprabhā,
sesame seeds (tila) to Atiraktā, and all kinds of substances to Kanakā.
From an oblation into the throat of the fire, there is affliction by disease; from the eyes, blindness; and from the nose, improper conduct.
There may be a loss of wealth at the head;
therefore, the wise man should always perform the internal fire-sacrifice (antar-homa) with that [substance].
The sound of a drum, a rain cloud, or an elephant; a sound in the sky or in fire that is auspicious; one resembling the color of gold, which brings about a favorable outcome;

one like the dust of vermilion; possessing the luster of the rising sun; reddish like the powder of well-refined [mercury] or like the *indragopa* insect; and its fragrance being equal to that of campaka, pāṭala, and vicakila flowers, as well as clarified butter—[these are the signs of a favorable omen].
Resembling the fragrance of the filaments of the *punnāga* flower and of *gulgulu*, it brings about success;
shaped like a parasol, it bestows auspiciousness, and its crest should be motionless and free from trembling.
Smoke resembling fire or like the fruit of the *kunda* flower, or similar to the *kāśa* flower, is auspicious;
however, a sound resembling the roar of a harsh wind brings destruction to the fire.
If it is black with the color of fire, it will cause the sacrificer to die before long;
if it is tawny, it brings about many diseases, and if it is silver-colored, it will even bring about the burning of the king's kingdom.
A smell like that of excrement brings about various sufferings;
one like urine causes the loss of strength; and one resembling sweat brings about the destruction of one's children.
A flame that is broken causes death; one that is well-rounded causes loss of wealth. A flame like a parrot’s feather or wheat quickly destroys the horse and the lord of the house.
A mark resembling a dove at the source of the well causes loss of cattle;
however, a clockwise whirlpool in the sacrificial fire yields auspicious results.
A frog [seen] at a lightning strike on a Viṣṇu-liṅga,
or one that is counter-clockwise and joined with a planetary halo (p. 128).
The fear of "hotu" (be it) is the arising of the assembly of beings.
In these hundred faults, the lord of practitioners should offer oblations exceeding one hundred with the weapon-mantra;
then, he should perform the worship of the wheel for his son.
The lord of the earth certainly becomes submissive by means of a hundred-thousandfold homa;
the ministers and vassal lords [become submissive] by half a hundred-thousandfold [homa], and [the common people] by a quarter-homa.
Sixty thousand queens of kings and their sons shall come under one's control;
and by a single thousand-fold oblation, beautiful women and courtesans shall become submissive.
By ten million [attendants], the foremost leaders of the gods become subject to the will of the sinless ones;
by three million, the wives of the gods, as well as the sages and the minor deities likewise.

Indeed, by means of a single hundred thousand [recitations], the hosts of Gandharvas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Apsarases become subject to one's control; and by means of ten million [recitations], all the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) likewise come under one's sway.
By means of fifty million [repetitions], Sadāśiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā become subject to one's will;
by means of ten million, one attains the eternal abode.
Then, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* and dismissed the beloved of Durāri, the firm-minded practitioner,
with a concentrated mind following that, should dismiss the Lord of Svāhā by means of the mantra.
A wise practitioner should never burn the enclosing sticks (paridhi) along with the ritual grass-covering (paristaraṇa) during a regular fire-oblation;
however, during an occasional oblation, the mantra-master should burn both the enclosing sticks and the ritual grass-covering.
Thus ends the eighth chapter.

Now I shall describe the fire-ritual (agnikārya). One should perform it in the northeast direction of the sanctuary; specifically, in the corner situated within the mandala of Agni, the Lord of the East, who is the Lord of Wealth and the Master of the Quarters.
It should be nine cubits in measure, or as many as the arms of a mountain-dweller, or even equal to the number of the senses;
it is elevated, adorned with four beautiful and unblemished auspicious archways, and graced by a white canopy.
Then, in the center of that [mandala], one should fashion a wise [image] provided with four gates; the altar (vedi) shall be one-third of that [area], with a height equal to three aratnis,
reaching as far as a mirror.
There, one should perform the act of captivating with a luster that is like a shimmering light.
One should construct [the mandala] upon that ground shaped like a lotus, which has four corners, a triangular source, a half-moon, a fire-corner (pentagon), a perfect circle, a hexagon,
and eight corners; and in its center, some scholars say there should be a circle for the Lord of Gaurī and the Lord of the Gods.
In the northwestern direction, there is a five-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and in the northern direction, that of the enemy of Madana (Śiva), there is a seven-cornered one.

Having first laid down the initial line, a person of pure intellect should mark its center with a fish-diagram using half of that length, positioned between the directions of Yama (South) and Kubera (North). Then,
having drawn circles from those two points, one should subsequently mark the four corners.
The sacrificial field (kṣetra) here should be square; from this, one may also produce other types of fire-pits (kuṇḍas).
Having cast one part from the front portion here on the outside of the field,
one of sharp intellect should grasp it and rotate it by half of a quarter;
likewise, there is a radiant corner and the falling of a pair of threads.
One should fashion it from the center; thus this becomes the Manmatha fire-pit.
Having abandoned two parts, the wise man here should sit below that which has been made into a row of parts.
One should rotate it with this measurement; thus, this fire-pit becomes properly marked with a half-moon.
Having divided the area into half-portions of the day-lord, the wise man should place two portions on both sides;
by that measurement, he should lay down two threads.
This pit, O Rudra, should be nine-cornered.
One of sharp intellect should project [the points] outward from the field according to the sequence exceeding the world-elephants;
by this proportion of parts, one should rotate [the circle] in every direction.
Thus, the supreme meter comes into being.
Having placed two parts outside on both sides from the middle of the ground's width, one of pure intellect, using that left side,
should perform the descent of six lines joined with a pair of fish-marks on both sides.
One should construct a sacrificial pit; this one, having four corners, is beautiful and pleasing to the mind.
Having laid out the tenth part and having circled one outer portion with that very [line],
one should likewise draw the petals up to their tips and also form the pericarp within the middle [circle].
A wise man should construct an eight-petaled lotus-shaped bathing pool.

Having cast [the line] here upon the field toward each of the external directions, and having made one part consisting of the degrees of two suns (twelve), the wise man should again form a square with that; then, taking half of a corner from that corner, p.

131) Having cast [the line] here upon the field toward each of the external directions, and having made one part consisting of the degrees of two suns (twelve), the wise man should again form a square with that; then, taking half of a corner from that corner,
From those two corners, one should indeed mark points all around using that same measurement;
thus there shall be an octagon, and one should extend the application of eight lines on all sides.
Having placed the square outside the Bhāyāṃśa and drawn a circle on the ground,
the length of the cloth should be three times the four parts (yugāṃśa) made by the divine measures (īśa), resulting in five threads.
Therefore, by way of application, this is the five-earthenware-vessel [offering].

Having set aside one part from the tenth part of the field's width here on the outside, and having made it a perfect circle by this measurement, and then again dividing this [circle] into sixty-four parts;
the length of those parts, according to this measure of thirty-three parts, is determined by the firm-minded one.
One should fashion a seven-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and this is accomplished through the application of seven lines.
Whatever measurement has been stated for the width of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), that same measurement is prescribed for its excavation as well;
the wise man should make it whatever shape the pit itself possesses.
One should fashion the girdle in such a form.
One should make three girdles in the pit, or two girdles,
or if wise, a single girdle;
above the girdle, it should be shaped like an elephant's lip.
And one should also offer [oblations] to Kāra and Yoni in the direction of the Hotṛ priest here.
p.
132) At a distance of one fist, the girdles should be two finger-breadths wide and one and a half finger-breadths in height.
Gradually, within this space measuring one cubit, there are again stars with heights and distances of three finger-breadths, two finger-breadths, and one finger-breadth respectively.

In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit (hasta), these [altars] should be raised in sequence by two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten finger-breadths (aṅgula) from the eye-line;
however, in a pit measuring two cubits, they should be raised by two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, and eleven finger-breadths respectively.
They should be endowed with a height and width of one finger-breadth.
In this Veda-kara (four cubits), those [measures] are increased by the height of a finger, a tāla, and a cubit from the ocean and the non-mathematical ocean (the Vedas);
in this six-cubit [measure], they are increased by ten, a jar (kumbha), and a limb (aṅga).
Together with the height of the gulatāra, they are combined.
In a *suhasta* (twenty-four fingers), these [altars] should have a width and height of eight, nine, and ten *aṅgulas*, respectively.

One should not draw a great lotus with eight petals and a pericarp here within. The wise have stated that the *yoni* (womb-altar) has a measurement of one fist (*muṣṭi*) and a length, width, and height of six, four, and two *aṅgulas*.
The navel here is endowed with stars (tārā) raised by four fingers (netravedāṅgula); the yoni is one finger (ekāṅgula) at the eighth [position].
This characteristic of the yoni is declared for this [pedestal] measuring one cubit (ratni).
Indeed, that very [measure] of one cubit is to be eaten by me from the sacrificial pit.
One of sharp intellect should increase each of these by one finger-breadth in other sacrificial pits;
here, however, the womb and the navel [of the fire-pit] should be increased by two barley-corns, and likewise the lip of the womb.
One should fashion the navel as circular, or even in a form corresponding to the shape of the pit; here, in the case of the yoni-shape, one should place the yoni and the navel resembling a lotus.
For a pit measuring one cubit [in diameter], they say the *yoni* should be two *aṅgulas* in length and breadth;
it should be provided with a height equal to one-third of its width, and should be made proportionate to the *bodhikṣmā* (the altar-ground) and the sacrificial vessel.
One should fashion the eyes with pupils possessing a height of one digit (aṅgula), and eight petals at the navel and the two shoulders;
the pericarp of those [petals] should be made by a portion of one-twelfth of the diameter.
The wise one should construct it in the middle portion, starting from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The beautiful rim of a single *kuṇḍa* should be one *aṅgula*; from that, starting from the ray of light (*virocanakarāt*),
the wise man should contract it by half an *aṅgula* for each successive *kuṇḍa*, up to the northern *kuṇḍa*.
Outside of that, one should indeed construct three enclosures (mekhalās) according to the prescribed sequence.
For the *śatārdha-homa* (fifty-fold oblation), the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should indeed be one *muṣṭi* in measure; for the hundred-fold oblation, it should be one *ratni*;
for the thousand-fold oblation, one *hasta*; and for ten thousand, two *hastas*.
This [measurement] of four cubits is prescribed for a [mandala] of one hundred thousand [repetitions].

Those who know the Āgamas declare that for a *koṭi-homa*, ten lakhs and eight thousand oblations of clarified butter are required; however, for homas exceeding ten million, they say it should be eight times that amount.
Some [prescribe] a fire-pit one cubit deep for a hundred-thousand oblations, two cubits for two hundred-thousand, and three cubits for three hundred-thousand.
They say that for a home, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring four hundred thousand cubits is prescribed for five lakhs [of coins], and five cubits for five lakhs.
In the case of one hundred thousand *rasas* (six million), the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) shall be seven cubits; in the case of seven hundred thousand, it shall be eight cubits;
in the case of one million, nine cubits; in the case of one million two hundred thousand, ten cubits; and in the case of nine million, nine cubits.

For ten lakhs [of oblations], the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be ten cubits; likewise for ten million (koṭi) homas here. Indeed, on this supreme earth, there is no pit larger than ten cubits, even when measured by the fist.
The southeast corner brings about all accomplishments; the southwest grants sons and possesses the luster of the god of love;
the northwest is like a half-moon and bestows auspiciousness; and the northeast is the cause for crushing enemies.
For rites of pacification, it should be perfectly circular;
for the slaying of enemies, it should be hexagonal;
and here, a lotus-shaped pit brings about rain.
The eight-cornered [mandala] which brings about the pacification of diseases.
The sacrificial pit for Brahmins is square, for kings it is circular,
for merchants it is shaped like a half-moon, and for Śūdras it is triangular.
Some teachers say that for all [rites], the square shape is recommended;
however, that fire-pit which grants the desired fruit bestows worldly enjoyment in this world.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) may be hexagonal, crescent-shaped, or even shaped like a lotus;
the five-cornered pit bestows liberation, while the eight-cornered one is the source that grants sovereignty in this world.
The Ninth Chapter.

(p. 135) Now, I shall describe that Yantra of Tripura, which is the sole cause of good fortune, prosperity, and virtue, and which was held even by the lords of the gods, the lords of the Dānavas, and the most renowned among the Siddhas.

Having just applied collyrium to his eyes, his entire body smeared with camphor and saffron, purified by a stainless bath, wearing a linen garment, and adorned with shimmering decorative patterns clearly fashioned from the paste of Śrīkaṇṭha,
he opened his face wide, filled with boundless joy.
With the cavity of his mouth filled with a red morsel of betel, he should draw the King of Machines.
With musk, agallochum, pieces of moonstone, camphor, and balls of *jāgala* sugar, combined with sandalwood paste, *svayambhū* flowers, and large birch-bark leaves...
One should write it upon a flawless leaf with a needle of refined gold.
One should draw the petals of the earth outside the circle;
outside those, the petals of the months;
and again, the petals of the earth for those [lunar] petals.
The wise one has beautiful outer teeth as its petals.
In the center of that pericarp, within the great yoni, one should write the Vāgbhava; above that, the Kāmarāja;
and above those two, one should place the Śakti-bīja, followed by the Haṃsa.
The god [worshipped] Paristhā, the leader of the world.
Then, on the sixteen-spoked [wheel], one should write the sixteen vowels; furthermore, on the twelve-spoked [wheel], one should write the Kāmarāja mantra.
Having divided this [circle] by the vowels of the lords of the days,
one should write the subsequent seed-syllable (antyabīja) in the outer sixteen-spoked [wheel].
One should write all these letters, beginning with the letter *ka*, which are radiant with the *kalās*, *bindus*, and *nādas* attached to their heads, upon the inner leaves.
The wise man should place [the deity] residing in the temple within his own belly.
Then the mantra-practitioner should wrap the venerable king of yantras all around with a hollow tube,
binding it with a band of very pure gold cloth.
One should perform the *anuhotra* and other rites for this perfected one.
This protection was borne even by the Lord who is the destroyer of Tripura, by the beloved of Śrī, by the preceptor of the gods, and by Hari;
it was also borne by Kandarpa and by the son of Vinatā, whose rays are nectar.
She is constantly cooled even by her own tree-like radiance.
It was held by Gandharvas and Kinnaras, as well as by Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, Siddhas, the hosts of Sādhyas, the best of Pannagas, Vidyādharas, and Guhyakas;

by those longing for good fortune, by others whose hearts were greedy for wealth, by other blessed ones who are auspicious to the world, by the best of men— the kings— and even by Vasu, Īśvara, and the rest.
With many lordly elephants, who were like rutting scent-elephants,
their broad temples smeared with thick ichor.

In tumultuous battle, a lord of men attains the glory of victory through the power of this king of machines; even amidst the grasp of hostile kings and in the midst of legal proceedings, he achieves success by means of its employment.
Indeed, even a human attains victory in debate with opponents through this most excellent machine. For men wandering in forests teeming with buffaloes, tigers, elephants, and packs of jackals,
no fear exists for long once they wear this supreme machine of Tripura.

The best of lords of men become submissive and their respective ministers fall under his control; likewise, women—intoxicated with youth, burdened by the weight of their breasts, and moving with playful grace—become his. That which is like the fierce, deadly Kālakūṭa poison, and which is expert in the act of destruction, certainly becomes nectar for him. Therefore, take up this king of weapons, the Tripura-yantṛ.
Indeed, the fire, with its many flickering flames spread upward within the interior of the excellent yantra,
subsides along with the ocean— the storehouse of waters— of the embodied being; for the practitioner,
having meditated upon the Lord of the Yantra upon the surface of the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
The wise man perceives the coming and going of Śakti within the Suṣumnā;
he who is the eternal abode of innumerable merits is released from the earth by Vāk, Kāminī, and Gominī, through the attainment of their grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
First, one should write the King of Passion (Kāmādhirāja) situated within the hollow of the Manmatha-square;
then, one should enclose that pair with two Kandarpa-syllables.
One should then draw six of its own streams (svadhārās) around the corners of that Fish-bannered God (Makaradhvaja).
In the center, one should place the name of the Mind-born (Manobhava); all of this should be cast within the belly of the diagram.
This [diagram], O Lord of the previously mentioned diagrams, is similar to that; it should also be worn on the head or around the neck.

In his arms he bears the entire three worlds, and they abide under his control. Beautiful women, with lovely tresses, full and firm breasts, and limbs as lovely as bending creepers, their minds agitated by the affliction of desire, would go to him. Having thus meditated upon that King of Yantras within the hollow of the lotus-dwelling at the base of the spine (mūlacakra)—blissful with intense joy, his body radiant with the light of the rising sun—and [having meditated upon] the target situated within the Yantra, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, shining brightly; [The practitioner should perform the piercing.]
The practitioner, being joyful and supported by the mantra, should slowly perform the churning, uttering it according to his own power.

Through this churning, the object of practice (*sādhya*)—even if he be a god of great majesty—will certainly become submissive to the eminent practitioner; what need be said then of a mortal of dull vigor? This occurs within twenty-one nights.
Having drawn a lotus provided with its petals, the wise one should then draw within it two *śṛṅgāṭas* (triangular figures) joined to one another.
In the center, he should write the Heart-mantra of the Goddess, and in the corners, the six Madanas; then, within the six [petals], the name of the desired object to be accomplished.
One should inscribe this mantra, renowned here as *piṇḍāmṛta*, within the hollow interior of the petals of a lotus on a leaf;
when this yantra is fashioned for a person with a strip of excellent gold,
the entire world becomes eternally subject to his control, O Slayer of Bhava.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭanāga.

I worship the venerable sandals of Śrī Puruṣottamānanda Saṃvidāmbā. I worship the venerable sandals of Maheśvarānanda Maheśvarīmbā. Obeisance to Śiva, whose crest is the cool-rayed moon; Hara, Hara, Śiva, Śiva! [To] Mālādharabhaṭṭa.
*Saṃpradāyadīpikā*, page 139.
This is the prostration at the lotus-feet of Gaṇeśa, which he recites,
[feet] that dispel the multitude of obstacles at every step.

The commentary on the *Sārasamuccaya* composed by Bhaṭṭanāga is now begun. Therein, the Teacher, for the sake of completing the work he has commenced without obstacles, and for the sake of the worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and ultimate liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) of those qualified for the Mantra, invokes an auspicious benediction (*maṅgala*) characterized by a prayer for blessings, preceded by a hymn of praise to the Deity who is the means to that end, beginning with "Prahvaprācīra... and so forth. "Prahvaprācīra... etc.: Indra is the one whose outer wall is bowed. *Koṭīra* means a crown. *Mañjīra-jñapura* [refers to the city of the feet]. The *Kulanāyikā* is the Goddess Adhārādhiṣṭhitā. *Jīvam* refers to the individual soul (*jīvātman*). The central channel is the *Suṣumnā*. Regarding "Śiva residing in the moon within the lotus of the sky": in the subtle [level], in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus located at the twelfth [center], which is the nature of the Supreme Guru Śiva consisting of the Moon; [he is invoked] by the *Haṃsa*, namely the *Ajapā* [mantra]. "By Amarendra...": *Amarendra* is the letter *la*. That which follows it is the letter *ra*. The half-moon is the *bindu*. Thus, *ram*. By the wind (*marut*) of Sāsyādinātha: *āsya* is the *visarga*; its beginning is the *bindu*. *Marut* is the letter *ya*. Thus, *yam*. "Bhuvanam" means the world. "By *saka*" (accompanied by *ka*): *valabhid* is the letter *la*. *Ka* is the *bindu*. *Valabhid* is the letter *la*. Thus, *lam*. By the jar (*ghaṭa*) together with the *bindu*: the jar is the letter *va*. Thus, *vam*. "Ājam" means the egg, the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). *Harihaya* is Indra. "The fifth from *ka*, joined with the fourth, and the vowel of *manu* joined at the end": *ka* is the letter *va*. Its fifth is the letter *ha*. [Thus the mantra is formed.]

The letter *ba* is water (*ambu*). The fourth [vowel] is the letter *sa*. The human vowel (*manusvara*) is the letter *au*; that which ends with it is the *bindu*. By means of the letters *ha*, *sa*, *au*, and the *bindu*, there is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) known as Sadāśiva. The teeth are the garment; the lower lip is the cloth. The creepers of consciousness (*cillīlatā*) are the creeper-like eyebrows. The group of gods is the quill-pen; the individual soul (*jīva*) is the life-force (*jīvātman*). Regarding the phrase "the lotus of space" (*ākāśāmburuha*) and so forth, it is clear from the context that it refers to the Supreme Swan (*paramahaṃsa*) residing within the sky-lotus; the rest is self-evident.
The First Chapter of the Saṃpradāyadīpikā.

Having thus performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and having realized the Self as the true nature of the deity, one should perform the series of ritual placements (*nyāsa*) to be described hereafter; so he says, beginning with the words "the thumb," etc. In this context, "Īśa, water, mouth-circle, together with fire, and the vowel *sa*, *da*, *ma*" means: *Īśa* is the letter *a*; *water* is the letter *u*; *fire* is the letter *r*; and the *staff* is the nasal dot (*bindu*). With these, the first seed-syllable is *bāṇabīja*: *a-u-r-m*. "Traversed by the three forms, the mouth, and the circle itself"—here, *trimūrti* is the letter *ī*; "that" refers to the seed-syllable *drāṃ*. By displacing the letter *ā* as directed by that [seed-syllable] and occupying its place, it is joined with the letter *ī*. Thus, the seed-syllable is *drīṃ*. "Situated within the mouth, mounted upon the King of Gods"—here, *mouth* is the visarga (*ḥ*); *King of Gods* is the letter *la*; *left eye* is the letter *ī*; *King of Gods* is the letter *la*; *left eye* is the letter *ī*; *face* is the visarga (*ḥ*); and preceding that is the nasal dot (*bindu*). With the letters *ka*, *la*, *sa*, *r*, *ī*, and the *bindu*, the third [seed-syllable] is formed: *klīṃ*. "Preceded by *bha*, that [is] the circle and the enemy"—this refers to the following.

Regarding the phrase "the sixth vowel, half-moon, lord," and so forth: here, first is the letter *ba*; the enemy of Vṛtra is the letter *la*; the sixth vowel is *ū*; and the half-moon is the nasal dot (*bindu*). With these, the fourth seed-syllable is *blūm*. Regarding the phrase "the fourth [syllable] joined with the preceding": the first is *ka*, which is the letter *va*; its fourth is *sa*; the preceding *ka* is the *visarga*; thus, *saḥ* is the fifth seed-syllable. These seed-syllables should be placed upon the fingers of both hands, from the thumb to the little finger, according to the procedure taught for the placement of maintenance (*sthiti-nyāsa*). One should perform the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) placement on the fingers and the palms of both hands. Indeed, the placement (*nyāsa*) is threefold—creation, maintenance, and withdrawal—according to the distinction of qualified practitioners such as the celibate student (*brahmacārī*), the householder (*gṛhī*), and the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*). As it is stated in the *Vāyavīya Saṃhitā*: "The placement of maintenance is for householders, the placement of creation for celibate students, the placement of withdrawal for ascetics, and likewise for forest-dwellers. One should perform the placement of maintenance starting from the middle finger and ending with the little finger, beginning with the thumbs.
The placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa) is prescribed starting from the little finger up to the thumb;
the placement of withdrawal (saṃhāranyāsa) is said to start from the thumb up to the little finger.
The wise practitioner should perform the placement (nyāsa) by way of maintenance (sthiti), starting from the navel up to the hair and ending at the feet;
the placement by way of emanation (sṛṣṭi) is prescribed as starting from the hair down to the feet.
"The placement from the feet up to the hair is called the *saṃhāranyāsa*.

Thus, having performed the placement according to one's qualification, one should perform the placement of the *kalās* (energies) to be described hereafter. For example: "Having placed the triad of seed-syllables together with the half-moon, ending with the *bhaga*, the supreme *māyā*, and *kula* in sequence, [one places them] on one's own head. Here, *bhaga* is the syllable *Ā*, and that supreme [syllable] is *E*.

May I [worship] Bhuvaneśī. "Up to Akula": *Akula* is the letter *ha*. "Beyond that" is the letter *kṣa*. The "half-moon" is the *bindu*. First, from the letters *e*, *ka*, and *bindu*; second, from *ha*, *re* (*ra*), and *bindu*; third, from *ka*, *ṣa*, and *bindu*. One should place these seed-syllables on the face. "With Ananta, located on the head, and Saṃvartaka": *Ananta* is the letter *ā*; *kaṃ* is the head; "located thereon" means the *bindu* located on the head. *Saṃvartaka* is the letter *kṣa*. One should place the letter *kṣa*, joined with the letter *ā* and the *bindu*, upon the orb of the face. "Having placed the four beginning with Sūkṣma in the pair of eyes, then those with the half-moon in the two ears": *Sūkṣma* is the letter *ī*. Those beginning with it are the "Sūkṣmādis. The "half-moon" is the *bindu*; thus, they are those possessing the *bindu*. *Im*, *īm*, *um*, and *ūm*—these are to be placed in the eyes. In the two ears, one should place the pair of *Bhṛgu*, accompanied by the two *Prāṇas*, and with the head marked by the half-moon. *Bhṛgu* is the letter *sa*. The "two *Prāṇas*" are *ṛ* and *ṝ*. The "half-moon" is the *bindu*. Thus, the letter *sa* with *ṛ* and the *bindu* is one; the letter *sa* with *ṝ* and the *bindu* is the other. One should place this pair on the cheeks. "Afterwards, O Wise One, one should place the pair of *Be*, accompanied by the pair of *Gaṇḍas*, and with the head endowed with the crescent moon": *Śveta* is the letter *ṣa*. The "pair of *Gaṇḍas*" are *ḷ* and *ḹ*. The "crescent moon" is the *bindu*. Thus, the letter *ṣa* with *ḷ* and the *bindu* is one; the letter *ṣa* with *ḹ* and the *bindu* is the other. These two are to be placed on the sides of the chin.

Regarding "the pair of rows of teeth is two cranes (*baka*), and the two lips are a crescent moon and a tooth" (*bakadvayam sendukhaṇḍaradanacchadadvayam*): the crane (*baka*) is the letter *śa*; the crescent moon (*indukhaṇḍa*) is the nasal dot (*bindu*); and the two lips (*radanacchadadvayam*) are the pair of lips. Thus, one should place the two seed-syllables *em* and *aim*, joined with the letter *śa*, upon the rows of teeth. Regarding "then one should place the pair of jars on the lips, and the pair of teeth joined with the face in front": the jar (*ghaṭa*) is the letter *va*; the pair of teeth is *o* and *au*; the face (*mukha*) is the visarga; and that which precedes it is the dot (*bindu*). The remainder is as before. These one should place on the lips. Regarding "joined with the taste (*rasa*), the navel (*nābhi*), and half the moon (*ardhendu*)": the taste (*rasa*) is the letter *ka*; half the moon (*ardhendu*) is the dot (*bindu*). Thus, one should place *vam* at the navel. Regarding "the practitioner should then place the wind (*pavana*), the final vowel, and the crest (*śikhā*) attentively": the wind (*pavana*) is the letter *ya*; the final vowel is the visarga. Thus, one should place *yaḥ* on the head. This concludes the placement of the sixteen digits (*ṣoḍaśakalānyāsa*). The meaning of the section beginning with "afterwards, the body" (*paścāddeha*) and ending with "in the sequence to be described" is as follows: after the placement of the sixteen digits, one should perform the placement of the Mother-letters (*mātṛkā*), either alone or accompanied by the power of Rudra (*rudraśakti*), according to the specific purpose; thereafter, one should perform the placement of the Vidyā. As for the passage beginning with "the first seed-syllable" (*ādyaṃ bīja*) and ending with "the wise one [should place] facing upwards" (*ūrdhvamukhādi vidvān*), its meaning is this: having divided the three seed-syllables of the root-vidyā, there is one placement on the head, the secret place, the heart, and the left [side], etc., and the pair of eyes, and the forehead. There is one placement on the pair of ears and the mouth. There is one placement on the two shoulders and the back. There is one placement on the pair of knees and the navel, etc., and on the upper and lower right faces. There is one placement on the left, the other, and the middle faces.

Thus, one should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the sevenfold root-vidyā. Regarding the phrase "and the limbs with the root-mantra," the meaning is that one should form the limbs using the root-mantra as the seed-syllables. Regarding "the secret place, the navel," etc.: one should place the previously mentioned five arrows in the secret place, the navel, the heart, the mouth, and the head. As for the passage beginning "on the region of the forehead, the face," and so on, its meaning is as follows: "The fifth [letter] of *ka* joined with the end of the eye. *Ka* refers to the letter *ka*. Its fifth is the letter *ha*. "Pure" (*śuci*) refers to fire; that is to say, the letter *ra*. "End of the eye" refers to the letter *ī*. Thus, *ha-ra-ī* constitutes one seed-syllable. "That, joined with the left eye, the wind, and the qualities": here, "left eye" refers to the letter *ī*, "wind" refers to the letter *ya*, and "qualities" refers to the number three. Therefore, it becomes *hrīṃ*. "The hand" refers to the left eye, which is the letter *ī*.

The letter *ya* is Pavana (Wind); it is the syllable possessing that quality (*guṇa*). The third syllable is the letter *la*. *Kara* is the letter *ka*. The letter *la* with the digit (*kalā*) is the letter *ū*; this is called Kāmākhyā. "The twelfth vowel" refers to the diphthong *ai*. "The sixth face of Hari-haya-Viṣṇu": *Hari-haya* is the letter *la*; *Viṣṇu* is the letter *a*; its sixth is the letter *ū*. *Vana* is the letter *va*. The letter *va*, the letter *la*, and the letter *ū* constitute the fourth [syllable]. Then, regarding "Bhṛgu accompanied by *tha*, *la*, *u*, and *pu*": *tha-pūrva* is the letter *ta*; *la-pūrva* is the letter *ra*; *u-pūrva* is the letter *ī*; and *Bhṛgu* is the letter *sa*. These five—*sa*, *ta*, *ra*, and *ī*—[are joined] with the head of each, meaning one should properly place the half-moons (*ardhacandra*). The meaning is that one should assign these seed-syllables (*bīja*) individually with nasal dots (*bindu*), and having conjoined them with the names Kāmarāja, Manmatha, Kandarpa, Makaraketana, and Manobhava, one should assign them to the forehead, face, heart, and so forth. As for the previously mentioned "assignment of the Vidyā" and "the limbs with the root-mantra," [these are to be performed as stated].

(p. 145) The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘a Bodhisattva,’ nor does he perceive ‘the perfection of wisdom. Since he does not perceive these, he does not apprehend them. Because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. Not becoming attached, he dwells in the perfection of wisdom, and having dwelt therein, he transcends the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, transcend the world with its gods, humans, and asuras? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form, nor does he perceive the arising of form, nor does he perceive the cessation of form. He does not perceive feeling, nor does he perceive the arising of feeling, nor does he perceive the cessation of feeling. He does not perceive perception, nor does he perceive the arising of perception, nor does he perceive the cessation of perception. He does not perceive formations, nor does he perceive the arising of formations, nor does he perceive the cessation of formations. He does not perceive consciousness, nor does he perceive the arising of consciousness, nor does he perceive the cessation of consciousness. Because he does not perceive these, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. Not becoming attached, he transcends the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, transcend the world with its gods, humans, and asuras by means of the ten powers of a Tathāgata? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor does he perceive their arising, nor does he perceive their cessation. Because he does not perceive these, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. Not becoming attached, he transcends the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, transcend the world with its gods, humans, and asuras by means of the four grounds of self-confidence? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, nor does he perceive their arising, nor does he perceive their cessation. Because he does not perceive these, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the four analytical knowledges, nor does he perceive their arising, nor does he perceive their cessation. Because he does not perceive these, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, transcend the world with its gods, humans, and asuras by means of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor does he perceive their arising, nor does he perceive their cessation. Because he does not perceive these, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, transcend the world with its gods, humans, and asuras by means of great compassion? Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, transcend the world with its gods, humans, and asuras by means of the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the knowledge of all modes, nor does he perceive its arising, nor does he perceive its cessation. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the emptiness of all dharmas, nor does he perceive their arising, nor does he perceive their cessation. Because he does not perceive these, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, transcend the world with its gods, humans, and asuras by means of the signlessness of all dharmas? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the signlessness of all dharmas, nor does he perceive their arising, nor does he perceive their cessation. Because he does not perceive these, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. Not becoming attached, he transcends the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, transcend the world with its gods, humans, and asuras by means of the wishlessness of all dharmas? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti

*Kagatabinduḥ* (the dot at the end of the letter *ka*). This means "that dot. The sound *a-em* (a-e), when joined, indicates *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) through the rules of euphonic combination (*sandhi*). Thus, there are twelve vowels [in total]. Regarding the term *vāgbhava*: "End of *ka*" (*ka-anta*) refers to the visarga. "End of *danta*" (*danta-anta*) refers to the letter *ka*. The fifth letter preceding that, in reverse order, is the letter *i*. Its end is the letter *ī*. The "staff" (*daṇḍa*) is the dot (*bindu*). With the letters *ka*, *la*, *ī*, and the dot, the one called *Kāmarāja* is extracted. Regarding "end of *danta* joined with the staffed [letter]," which is the entire *Kula* known as *Sammohana*: "End of that" (*tad-anta*) is the letter *au*. The "staff" is the dot. It is "entire" (*sakala*), meaning accompanied by *kāla* (time). With the letters *sa*, *au*, the dot, and the visarga, the mantra called *Mohana* is extracted. The sage (*ṛṣi*) is easy to understand. Regarding this mantra, it is "joined with the end of *rada*" (*radānta-yuk*). The seed-syllable (*bīja*) is preceded by *Lakulīśa* and possesses the staff. "She" (*sā*) is the power (*śakti*), which is the letter *o*. Its end is the letter *au*. *Lakulīśa* is the letter *ha*. The "staff" is the dot. Together with the letters *sa*, *au*, and the dot, it is said to be the seed-syllable of the center of the seed. Regarding "preceded by *Ākhaṇḍala-karṇa*, together with half of *Jaivātṛka*, ending with the face": *Ākhaṇḍala* is the letter *la*. *Karṇa* is the letter *u*. Preceding that is the letter *ī*. "Half of *Jaivātṛka*" is the dot. The "face" (*ānana*) is the visarga. "End of *danta*" (*danta-anta*) is the letter *ka*. With the letters *ka*, *la*, *ī*, and the dot, the *Kāmarāja* seed-syllable is accomplished; it is said to be its power (*śakti*).

(p. 147) The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in all the dharmas of a buddha. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in all the dharmas of a buddha? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the dharma of a buddha as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma. He does not perceive the dharma of a pratyekabuddha as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma. He does not perceive the dharma of a śrāvaka as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma. He does not perceive the dharma of a worldling as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma. He does not perceive the dharma of form as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as a dharma, nor does he perceive them as non-dharmas. He does not perceive the dharma of the eye as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharmas of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as dharmas, nor does he perceive them as non-dharmas. He does not perceive the dharma of form as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharmas of sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental phenomena as dharmas, nor does he perceive them as non-dharmas. He does not perceive the dharma of eye-consciousness as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharmas of ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as dharmas, nor does he perceive them as non-dharmas. He does not perceive the dharma of eye-contact as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharmas of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as dharmas, nor does he perceive them as non-dharmas. He does not perceive the dharma of feeling born of eye-contact as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharmas of feelings born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as dharmas, nor does he perceive them as non-dharmas. He does not perceive the dharma of the conditioned element as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the unconditioned element as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma. He does not perceive the dharma of the past as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the future as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the present as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma. He does not perceive the dharma of the realm of desire as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the realm of form as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the formless realm as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma. He does not perceive the dharma of the dhyānas as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the immeasurables as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the formless attainments as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the eight liberations as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the nine successive meditative attainments as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma. He does not perceive the dharma of emptiness as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of signlessness as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of wishlessness as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma. He does not perceive the dharma of the ten powers of a tathāgata as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the four fearlessnesses as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the four analytical knowledges as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma. He does not perceive the dharma of the path of a stream-enterer as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the fruit of a stream-enterer as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of a once-returner as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the fruit of a once-returner as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of a non-returner as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the fruit of a non-returner as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of an arhat as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the fruit of arhatship as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma. He does not perceive the dharma of a pratyekabuddha as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma. He does not perceive the dharma of omniscience as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the dharma of the knowledge of all modes as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in all the dharmas of a buddha. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive the dharma of a buddha as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; if he does not perceive the dharma of a pratyekabuddha as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; if he does not perceive the dharma of a śrāvaka as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; if he does not perceive the dharma of a worldling as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; if he does not perceive the dharma of form as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; if he does not perceive the dharmas of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as dharmas, nor does he perceive them as non-dharmas; if he does not perceive the dharma of the eye as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; if he does not perceive the dharmas of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as dharmas, nor does he perceive them as non-dharmas; if he does not perceive the dharma of form as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; if he does not perceive the dharmas of sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental phenomena as dharmas, nor does he perceive them as non-dharmas; if he does not perceive the dharma of eye-consciousness as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; if he does not perceive the dharmas of ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as dharmas, nor does he perceive them as non-dharmas; if he does not perceive the dharma of eye-contact as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; if he does not perceive the dharmas of ear-contact

The color is clearly white. Regarding the passage beginning with "the seed-syllable of Śiva and Śakti" and ending with "becomes augmented," its meaning is as follows: the seed-syllable of Śiva is the letter *ha*; the seed-syllable of Śakti is the letter *sa*. *Akula* is *ha*; *Dahana* (Fire) is *ra*. This is the meaning: upon the first and middle seed-syllables of the mantra, the letters *ha* and *sa*, which consist of Śiva and Śakti, are placed one above the other; then, upon the third seed-syllable, the letter *ha* is placed. Below the one called the Middle, the Kāmarāja, the letter *ra* is placed. Thus: first, by means of *ha*, *sa*, the vowel *e*, and the nasal drop (*bindu*); second, by means of *ha*, *sa*, *ka*, *la*, *ra*, the vowel *ī*, and the nasal drop; third, by means of *ha*, *sa*, the diphthong *au*, the nasal drop, and the visarga. *Akula* is *ha*; *Kula* is *sa*. This is the meaning: the Teacher has declared that *ha* is preceded by Bhairavī and *sa* is preceded by Vidyā. The eighth from Śiva is the first seed-syllable alone. Another [seed] is the eighth from the first of Bhaga. The supreme is that which ends at the head; thus the three-syllabled Saṅketavidyā is said to be attainable through the mouth of the Guru. Śiva is *u*; its eighth is *e*. Bhaga is *e*; its eighth preceding it, counting backwards, is *ī*. The supreme is the third. "Ending at the head" means the head is the nasal drop (*bindu*); that which ends with it is the diphthong *au*. The meaning is that the Root-Vidyā, consisting of the twelfth, fourth, and fourteenth vowels along with their nasal drops, is the Saṅketikī, obtainable through the oral tradition. "End of *Ka*, end of *Va*, end of *La*, endowed with the left eye, the staff and the Kula, together with sound"—this refers to the six-peak (ṣaṭkūṭa) mantra.

*Kaṃ* is the *bindu*. Its end is the *visarga*. Within that is the letter *ka*. That whose end is *va* is the letter *la*. *Akula* is the letter *ha*. That whose end is *la* is the letter *ra*. The left eye is the vowel *ī*. The staff is the *bindu*. *Kula* is the letter *sa*. With *nāda*, *nāda* is the letter *ha*. This is what is meant: by means of the letters *ha*, *sa*, *ka*, *la*, *ra*, *ī*, and the *bindu*, the great mantra known as the "Six Peaks" (*ṣaṭkūṭa*) is extracted. Alternatively: *Kaṃ* is the *bindu*. Its end is the *visarjanīya*. Within that is the letter *ka*. *Vaṃ* is water, which is nectar; its seed-syllable is the letter *ṭha*. Its end is the letter *ḍa*. *Akula* is the letter *ha*. Regarding "the end of *la*," this refers to the inclusion of both *la* and *ra*; this is understood through the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*). *La* is taken here in its own form. That whose end is *la* is the letter *ra*. The left eye is the vowel *ī*. The staff is the *bindu*. *Kula* is the letter *sa*, accompanied by *nāda*. The meaning is this: some say the "Six Peaks" consists of the letters *ha*, *sa*, *ka*, *la*, *ḍa*, *ra*, *ī*, *bindu*, and *nāda*. Both these views possess the authority of oral tradition. "One should recite, having joined the first seed-syllable in the middle, the middle at the beginning and the end, and the end at the end. The "first" is that called *Vāgbhava*. Having placed the "seed-syllable" (the middle one) in the position of *Kāmarāja*; having placed the "middle" (called *Kāmarāja*) at the beginning in the position of *Vāgbhava*; and having kept the "last" at the end as it was originally—by those who recite thus, there is the attainment of the stated fruit. "Having made the first at the conclusion, the last seed-syllable in the middle, and the middle at the beginning, O best of practitioners. [This is the second method.]

(p. 149) The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. It should be remembered by you as such. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for which this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar’? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, because it roars like a lion regarding the four kinds of fearlessness, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. What are the four? Here, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, claims before the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among the host of ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans: ‘I am perfectly enlightened,’ he has no ground for fear. This is the first ground of self-confidence. Again, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata claims: ‘I have utterly destroyed all taints,’ he has no ground for fear. This is the second ground of self-confidence. Again, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata claims: ‘The dharmas I have declared to my disciples as obstacles are indeed obstacles,’ he has no ground for fear. This is the third ground of self-confidence. Again, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata claims: ‘The path leading to the cessation of suffering that I have declared to my disciples is the way to the cessation of suffering,’ he has no ground for fear. This is the fourth ground of self-confidence. Because he roars like a lion regarding these four kinds of fearlessness, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well this Dharma-discourse has been spoken by the Blessed One. Indeed, Blessed One, this Dharma-discourse is truly ‘The Lion’s Roar. The Blessed One said: “So it is, Ānanda. So it is, Ānanda. This Dharma-discourse is indeed ‘The Lion’s Roar. For one who hears this Dharma-discourse, Ānanda, there will be no fear, nor trembling, nor horripilation. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is the very essence of the Tathāgata’s teaching. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joyful minds, the Venerable Ānanda and the monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. This is the Lion’s Roar Sūtra, the fifteenth.

The first [syllable] is called Vāgbhava. Having placed the seed-syllable (bīja) in the position of the Supreme Seed (parabīja), one makes that [Vāgbhava], known as Parā, the middle [syllable] in the place of Kāmarāja. Having placed the middle [syllable], known as Kāmarāja, at the beginning in the position of Vāgbhava, for those who recite [the mantra] in this way, there is the attainment of the stated fruit. Thus says the Śruti: "The infinite, the bounded, fashioned upon the earth. Here, by saying "the earth" (mahīm), he indicates the Vāgbhava syllable. Regarding the meaning of: "One should recite this King of Mantras, the cause of deluding the entire world, within the Mātṛkā, both in direct and reverse order": at the time of recitation, having uttered the mantra, one should utter the letter 'a' at the end. Again, having uttered the mantra, one should utter the letter 'ā' at the end. In this manner, up to the letter 'la'. Having performed the recitation with each [letter] interspersed by the mantra, one should again utter the letter 'kṣa' alone, devoid of the mantra, in the position of the Marut (the wind). Then, in reverse order, from 'la' down to 'a', one should recite each [letter] interspersed by the Mātṛkā. The meaning is that for those performing the recitation on the rosary of the Mātṛkā letters in this way, the recitation becomes complete in the number of one hundred in a single round. Regarding "endowed with the Haṃsa deity... O wise one": one should recite the three seed-syllables of the root-vidyā joined with the letters 'ha' and 'sa'; this is the meaning. "The Supreme is 'ka' and 'va'" refers to the root-vidyā. Having first uttered 'ke' and 'va' in the middle seed-syllable, one should recite the final seed-syllable joined with 'ha' and 'sa'. Regarding "the consonants endowed with Haṃsa": having elided the vowel 'a' at the end of 'ha' and 'sa', one should recite them as merely the consonants 'ha' and 'sa' themselves, joined with the vidyā as "hasa".

(p. 150) The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in the perfection of giving, and so forth, up to the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of giving? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the mind of awakening, gives a gift to all sentient beings, and yet he does not perceive those sentient beings as real entities. He gives a gift without perceiving a giver, a receiver, or a gift. He gives a gift without perceiving form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. He gives a gift without perceiving the aggregates, the elements, or the sense-fields. He gives a gift without perceiving the conditioned or the unconditioned. He gives a gift without perceiving the stream-enterer, nor the fruit of stream-entry; the once-returner, nor the fruit of once-returning; the non-returner, nor the fruit of non-returning; the arhat, nor the fruit of arhatship; the pratyekabuddha, nor the state of a pratyekabuddha. He gives a gift without perceiving the bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor even omniscience. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of giving. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of morality? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the mind of awakening, observes the precepts of morality. He does not perceive a self who observes morality, nor does he perceive a being, a soul, a person, or a life-principle who observes morality. He does not perceive the precepts of morality as real entities. He does not perceive form, nor feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the aggregates, the elements, or the sense-fields. He does not perceive the conditioned or the unconditioned. He does not perceive the stream-enterer, nor the fruit of stream-entry; the once-returner, nor the fruit of once-returning; the non-returner, nor the fruit of non-returning; the arhat, nor the fruit of arhatship; the pratyekabuddha, nor the state of a pratyekabuddha. He does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor even omniscience. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of morality. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of patience? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the mind of awakening, practices patience toward all sentient beings. He does not perceive a self who practices patience, nor does he perceive a being, a soul, a person, or a life-principle who practices patience. He does not perceive the practice of patience as a real entity. He does not perceive form, nor feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the aggregates, the elements, or the sense-fields. He does not perceive the conditioned or the unconditioned. He does not perceive the stream-enterer, nor the fruit of stream-entry; the once-returner, nor the fruit of once-returning; the non-returner, nor the fruit of non-returning; the arhat, nor the fruit of arhatship; the pratyekabuddha, nor the state of a pratyekabuddha. He does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor even omniscience. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of patience. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of vigor? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the mind of awakening, exerts vigor for the sake of all sentient beings. He does not perceive a self who exerts vigor, nor does he perceive a being, a soul, a person, or a life-principle who exerts vigor. He does not perceive the exertion of vigor as a real entity. He does not perceive form, nor feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the aggregates, the elements, or the sense-fields. He does not perceive the conditioned or the unconditioned. He does not perceive the stream-enterer, nor the fruit of stream-entry; the once-returner, nor the fruit of once-returning; the non-returner, nor the fruit of non-returning; the arhat, nor the fruit of arhatship; the pratyekabuddha, nor the state of a pratyekabuddha. He does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor even omniscience. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of vigor. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of meditation? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the mind of awakening, enters into meditative concentration for the sake of all sentient beings. He does not perceive a self who enters into concentration, nor does he perceive a being, a soul, a person, or a life-principle who enters into concentration. He does not perceive the entry into concentration as a real entity. He does not perceive form, nor feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the aggregates, the elements, or the sense-fields. He does not perceive the conditioned or the unconditioned. He does not perceive the stream-enterer, nor the fruit of stream-entry; the once-returner, nor the fruit of once-returning; the non-returner, nor the fruit of non-returning; the arhat, nor the fruit of arhatship; the pratyekabuddha, nor the state of a pratyekabuddha. He does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor even omniscience. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of meditation. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the mind of awakening, courses in the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a self who courses in wisdom, nor does he perceive a being, a soul, a person, or a life-principle who courses in wisdom. He does not perceive the perfection of wisdom as a real entity. He does not perceive form, nor feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the aggregates, the elements, or the sense-fields. He does not perceive the conditioned or the unconditioned. He does not perceive the stream-enterer, nor the fruit of stream-entry; the once-returner, nor the fruit of once-returning; the non-returner, nor the fruit of non-returning; the arhat, nor the fruit of arhatship; the pratyekabuddha, nor the state of a pratyekabuddha. He does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor even omniscience. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of wisdom.”

"This is declared to be the Heart of the Goddess on earth, shining with the word *kamala* (lotus) whose middle and final vowels are elided, joined with the Lord (*īśa*), along with the Bindu and Nāda; preceded by the Veda (*nigama*) and ending with 'namas'. When the letter *ma*, the middle syllable of the word *kamala*, has the vowel *a* at its end elided, what remains is *kla*. "The Lord" (*īśa*) is the letter *u*; its beginning is the vowel *ī*. That [letter *k*] is joined with the Bindu and Nāda—that is, endowed with the Bindu and Nāda. The seed-syllable known as *Siddhikāmā* consists of the letters *ka*, *la*, *ī*, Bindu, and Nāda. "Preceded by the Veda" refers to the *Praṇava* (Oṃ). "Namah" is used to denote the actual form [of the mantra]. When the Kāma-bīja is placed between the *Praṇava* and "namas," the four-syllabled Vidyā named the Heart of the Goddess is formed. The passage from "the Vidyā that milks all desires" up to "this is an extreme secret" is easy to understand. Now, regarding "the flower of the water-releasers" (*vārimucām*) and so forth: "water-releasers" are clouds. Their "flower" is water; its seed-syllable is the letter *va*. Of the two letters *da* and *va*, the first is *da*. Those same two letters, *va* and *da*, followed by the "long" vowel—that is, the vowel *ā*—form *vāda*. The meaning is "speech" (*vāk*). "End of the sky" (*khānta*) is the letter *ga*. "Water" (*ambu*) is the letter *va*. "In the same way" (*tathā*) refers back to what was previously stated. Thus, *gvā* is established. Just as *da* and *na* are joined with the "world-vowel" (*lokasvara*)—the "world-vowel" being the vowel *ī*—and having said "like the sun and the moon" (*dinivadavadet*), one should utter "Vāgvādinī. This is the eight-syllabled [mantra]. The meaning is that this eight-syllabled Vidyā serves to illuminate the seed-syllable of Speech (*vāgbhava*). "Brahmā joined with Indra's eye" and so forth: Brahmā is the letter *ka*; Indra is the letter *la*.

*Dṛg* is the letter *i*. "Endowed with *ka*" means joined with the letters *la* and *i*. *Bhaga* is the letter *e*. *Meṣa* is the letter *na*. *Dṛg* is the letter *i*. This means the letters *da* and *na* are joined with the letter *i*. *Kāla* is the letter *ma*. *Ananta* is the letter *ā*. *Viyat* is the letter *ha*; [thus] the letter *ha* joined with the letter *ā*. *Daśana* is the letter *o*. *Saṃvarta* is the letter *kṣa*; [thus] the letter *kṣa* joined with the letter *o*. *Bhīṣaṇa* is the letter *ha*. *Akrūra* is the *bindu* (dot); [thus] the letter *ha* joined with the *bindu*. *Kamalāsana* is the letter *ka*. *Śiva* is the letter *u*. [Thus] the letter *ra* (of *vaiśvānara*) joined with the letter *u*. Such [is the mantra], joined with the letter *u*. Having uttered "klinne," at the end of the word "kledini," it produces great agitation (*mahākṣobha*). This eleven-syllable *vidyā* is that which illuminates the seed-syllable of Manmatha; such is the meaning. "It agitates"—this is easily understood. "Sāvitrī joined with *radana*, beginning with *Mahā-Kālī*, ending with *vyoman*, its limbs adorned with the crescent of the moon; likewise joined with *Mohinī*, *Sarasijabhū*, and *Nirvidya*—this shall be the illuminator of the supreme seed-syllable on earth. *Sāvitrī* is the *praṇava* (Oṃ). *Radana* is the letter *o*. *Mahā-Kālī*: *Mahākāla* is the letter *ma*; [thus] the letter *ma* joined with the *oṃ*-syllable. *Vyoman* is the letter *ha*. Its end is the letter *kṣa*. The "crescent of the moon" is the *bindu*; [thus] the letter *kṣa* joined with the *bindu*. *Mohinī* is the letter *u*. *Sarasijabhū* is the letter *ka*. [Thus] the letter *ra* (of fire) joined with the letter *u*. "Likewise" (*tathā*) implies that the letter *u* follows the letter *ra* as well. Having spoken the word for liberation (*mokṣapada*) ending with the *praṇava*, one should utter the word "kuru. This five-syllable *vidyā* is the illuminator of the supreme seed-syllable. Others say: (Note: The provided text contains a mix of phonetic analysis and mantra construction. The translation above renders the technical descriptions of the syllables and their combinations.)

They interpret "the illuminator of the other seed of the teacher" (*deśikāmaparabījadīpanīkarī*) differently: "Sāvitrī joined with the *praṇava* [is] Mahādikālī. Having uttered the word "Mahā" at the end of the *praṇava*, one should say at the end, "grant liberation" (*mokṣaṃ kuru*). They extract a seven-syllable mantra, wherein one should first utter that which is the illuminator of whichever seed-mantra it may be, and subsequently utter the seed-mantra itself. This is the method of recitation for all three seed-mantras. Regarding the phrase "the Vidyā in the faces of the six limbs": this means that during the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs, one should place the seed-mantras of the respective mantras in the prescribed order, preceded by the utterance of their own specific illuminating Vidyā. The phrase "the Vidyā alone through placement" is explicit. Regarding "the form of the mantra": thus has been declared the nature of the mantra according to the tradition of all Āgamas—the essence of the Smṛtis, the sun to the darkness of all sins, the wind that shatters the bonds of impurity and *māyā*, the moon that awakens the night-lotus of the inner mind, the liberator from all the fetters of worldly existence, and the great guru’s contracted oral tradition. Therefore, having abandoned deceit of mind, wealth, and body, and having received the mantra according to the rules—preceded by service and the grace of the teacher's favor—one should perform the various placements (*nyāsa*) of the aforementioned mantra-locations, and then carry out recitation (*japa*), worship (*pūjā*), and so forth. Not otherwise.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Saṃpradāyadīpikā.

Having thus described the nature of the mantra, which serves as the means for practitioners to achieve all human goals (*puruṣārtha*), [the author now] explains the method of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) as a limb of yoga, in order to eliminate obstacles to those other human goals.

He begins to describe its specific details with the words "Now, this body," and so forth. [The body] is twelve finger-breadths [in height], and fourteen fingers [in width]. Within this physical frame (*apaghana*), there are the principal channels (*nāḍīs*) through which the vital breaths (*prāṇa*, etc. may move freely and be regulated; they are radiant with five colors and their bodies shine forth with the letters *va*, *la*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha*. Because it is of the nature of the *praṇava* (the syllable *Oṃ*), it consists of the letters *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*; or alternatively, it consists of the five deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—or the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*, etc.), represented by the colors red, white, and so on. The lotus-fiber is that which shines within the interior of the marrow. Starting from the phrase "fourteen fingers" up to "by the lords of sages," the meaning is as follows: Here, in this entire body, after the four kinds of food have been consumed, their essence permeates from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head. While there are many channels (*nāḍīs*) serving as gateways for this pervasive essence, there exist fourteen principal channels through which the free movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*, etc. can be regulated. Among those, three are primary: Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā. Even among these, the Suṣumṇā alone is the most primary. It rests upon the spinal column from the *ādhāra* (the perineum) to the *dvādaśānta* (the point twelve finger-breadths above the head), and because it is the support of everything, it stands with its face downward, consisting of the sounds *ṛ*, *ṝ*, and *ḷ*. At its base, resting upon the left and right sides, are situated Iḍā and Piṅgalā. Of these two, the channel named Iḍā takes the shape of a bow; it rests upon the Suṣumṇā at the root of the *liṅga* (the perineum) and extends toward the right side. Having that same shape, it again rests upon that very [Suṣumṇā] at the navel and goes to the left side. Having that same shape, it again rests upon that very [Suṣumṇā] at the heart and goes to the right side. Having that same shape, it again reaches the root of the palate, embraces the palate itself, and goes between the left shoulder and the collarbone (*jatru*).

Or it goes through the hollow by means of the mind. The *piṅgalā* channel, originating from the right side, situated here and there, relies upon the *suṣumnā* and goes to the hollow of the right [nostril]. Wherever there is a connection between *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*, there are five joints (*parvan*) known as Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddhi, and Ājñā. Within the interior of the *suṣumnā*, there exists a certain variegated channel (*nāḍī*), shaped like its interior, shining with five colors, consisting of the five deities, and composed of light. Within that, the light which is the source of all radiance—resembling a lotus fiber, consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*)—shines. The Moon moves in the *iḍā*; the Sun moves in the *piṅgalā*. Therefore, the nectar (*amṛta*) resides on the left side, and the poison (*viṣa*) on the right side; so say the *Yogabindu*. "A wise person should know the rising (*udaya*)," [the text continues]: the rising of the divine vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) occurs for practitioners (*sādhaka*) at the root-center (*kanda*), the *mūlādhāra*, at the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*), and at the junction (*sandhi*). "Rising" (*udaya*) is birth; "setting" (*astamaya*) is dissolution. "Downward movement" refers to night and day; "upward movement" refers to the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*) and the "Lord of Day," the Sun. This is what is meant: in the body of the practitioner, at the location of the *mūlādhāra*, the movement and circulation of the activity of the Kuṇḍalinī power—which consists of consciousness (*saṃvinmaya*) and is the nature of Māyā, the cause of the entire phenomenal world—the collective vital breath (*samaṣṭiprāṇa*) of all things, travels upward through the paths of *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* and exits externally through the two nostrils to a distance of twelve finger-breadths.
