The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a basis for wisdom, nor does he perceive one who possesses wisdom, nor does he perceive the wisdom itself. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye up to the mind; he does not perceive forms up to mental phenomena; he does not perceive the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element; he does not perceive the element of ignorance up to the element of old age and death; he does not perceive the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom; he does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer up to the state of a Tathāgata; he does not perceive all-knowledge, the knowledge of all modes, or the knowledge of all aspects. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the emptiness of form? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form as form, nor does he perceive feeling as feeling, nor perception as perception,

He says that one should draw the Yantrarāja preceded by prostrations at the feet of one’s own guru—[the practitioner] whose pair of eyes is anointed with collyrium, whose mouth-cavity is filled red with a morsel of betel, who possesses a beautiful form like the God of Love (Smara) with a delighted state of mind, and whose heart acts as a bee toward the lotus-feet of Ambikā. With the verse beginning "karpūrakṣodadigdhāṅgaḥ" [his body smeared with camphor powder], he states the materials for writing the yantras. With "kastūrikā... [musk], etc., [he continues]. "Sudhākarakhaṇḍaḥ" means a piece of camphor. "Paṭīraṃ" means red sandalwood. He describes the method of drawing the yantra with "likhed bhūpatrāṇi... [one should draw the earth-leaves], etc. "Bhūpaḥ" means a king. By the word "king," the moon consisting of sixteen digits is meant; thus, the meaning is "sixteen petals. Outside of that are the "month-leaves," which are twelve petals. In the region outside of that again are the "earth-leaves," sixteen petals. Outside those are the "tooth-leaves," thirty-two teeth, meaning thirty-two petals. In its pericarp (karṇikā) is the "great vulva" (mahāyoni); this means a hexagon in the central pericarp. [One should place] the "Leader of the World" (Jagannāyikā) upon the "Swan-God" (Haṃsadeva); this means the Mātṛkā alphabet mounted upon the Haṃsa-mantra. Having briefly stated the drawing of the yantra, he explains it in detail with "ṣoḍaśāra... [sixteen-spoked], etc. "Divided by the vowels of the Lord of Day"—by the vowels of the Lord of Day, excluding the four seed-syllables (piṇḍas), i.e., by the twelve vowels. This means the Kāmarāja-mantra is intermingled [with them]. "The letters beginning with 'ka' shining forth, joined to the head-regions by the digits (kalā), the point (bindu), and the resonance (nāda)"—the digit (kalā) is the Vāgbhava syllable (aiṃ); the point (bindu) is the letter 'sa'; the resonance (nāda) is the letter 'ha'. Thus, it ends with the statement: "intermingled with the letters from 'ka' to 'sa', together with the letter 'e' and the letter 'ha'."

And so it is said in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*: "Outside of that, one should cause all the *Mātṛkās* (mother-letters), joined with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*, and mounted upon the syllables *Haṃsa*, to be placed by the Supreme Goddess. Regarding the phrase "situated within the temple" (*mandirasyodarastham*): "temple" (*mandira*) refers to the letter *Kṣa*; the meaning is "situated inside that. Thus it is stated in the *Asthānabhairava*: "The letter *Kṣa* is Mandara; the letter *Ra* is said to be Meru, O Lord. "Hollow" (*suṣira*) refers to the letter *Ha*; the meaning is that one should surround [the diagram] with the letter *Ha*. This is what is meant: first, having drawn a triangle surrounded by a hexagon, one should draw a circle outside it. Outside of that, a sixteen-petaled lotus; outside of that, a circle. Then a twelve-petaled lotus; again a circle. Outside of that, a sixteen-petaled lotus. On the outer twelve-spoked [figure], excluding the seed-syllables (*piṇḍavarṇa*), one should write the *Kāmarāja* mantra—such as *hlāṃ klīṃ*—intermingled with the twelve vowels. Again, on the first sixteen-spoked [figure], one should write the sixteen vowels beginning with *a, ā, am*, etc. Outside of that, on the thirty-two-petaled [lotus], one should write the twelve letters from *Ka* to *Sa* together with the letters *Ha, E, Sa, Ka*, such as *haisakaṃ haisakhaṃ* up to *haisasaṃ*. One should encircle all of this with the letter *Kṣa*, and encircle that outside with the letter *Ha*. This "majestic king of diagrams," and so forth, ending with "is situated on the ground," is easy to understand. "With scent-elephants" (*gandhasindhurendraiḥ*): with rutting elephants. "With temples smeared by the mud of rut" (*madacitkhkhallaviliptagaṇḍapiṇḍaiḥ*): with the surfaces of their temples reddened by rut. "In the game of dice" (*darodaredyūte*). "Lulāya": a wild buffalo. "Citrakāya": a tiger.

*Bhallūka* is a specific kind of deer; *lolakīla* means flickering or moving flame. Having meditated upon the one situated in the center of the "King of Yantras" within the lotus-heart (*hṛtpaṅkeruha*), specifically in the middle of its pericarp (*karṇikā*), while reciting the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should raise the power consisting of consciousness (*cinmayī śakti*) from the *kuṇḍalinī* at the *mūlādhāra*. Having ascended through the path of Brahman (*brahmamārga*) upward to the limit of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*), one should meditate on Him being bathed by a thick stream of nectar flowing from the orb of the moon situated therein. Then, one should meditate on that nectar-filled [power] descending again to the *mūlādhāra*, then back up to the *dvādaśānta*, then back down to the *mūlādhāra*. By such repeated practice of ascending and descending, the excellent person—who is like the Creator of the world, or like Bhāratī and Mukunda—will be attended by Śrī (Lakṣmī), who, having abandoned her co-wife-hood, will worship his speech (*vāṇī*). The meaning of the passage beginning with "First, in the chamber of Manmatha" and ending with "one should cast this into the belly" is as follows: First, one should write the syllable *klīṃ* (known as Manmatha) in the interior, together with the name of the target (*sādhya*) and the action (*karman*), and the syllable *hrīṃ* (known as Kāmādhirāja). This should be surrounded by a hexagon known as the "pair of Kandarpas. One should write the syllable *bḷṃ* (known as Makaradhvaja) in the six corners. All of this should be encircled by the syllable *strīṃ* (known as Manobhava). The portion of the text beginning with "the Yantra by the previously mentioned Lord of Yantras" and ending with "having well-pierced" is easy to understand. Having meditated thus upon this Kāmarāja Yantra in the center of the pericarp of one's own *mūlādhāra* lotus, and having meditated upon the target within it as resembling the rising sun, blissful, gentle, and consisting of pure consciousness (*cetanamātrarūpa*), one should perform the churning of one's own power according to the sequence of the Guru’s instruction. This is stated in the passage beginning with "Having meditated thus... and so forth.

(183) "O Blessed One, it is certainly so"—this is clear. Regarding the passage beginning with "endowed with the petals of the *kalās*" and ending with "the nectar-mass" (*piṇḍāmṛta*), the meaning is as follows: having drawn the sixteen-petaled lotus of the *kalās*.
Thus ends the seventh chapter.

Having thus explained the manner of constructing the *yantra*, he begins to describe the procedure for external worship with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth. Having performed purification through the initial bathing and other rites, one should prepare a sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) either in a temple or in one's own home, and purify it with water and cow dung; this is what he states with the verse beginning "Purified" (*śuddha*). Regarding the mantra of the Supreme Lord mentioned previously as "the sky, that, fire, the left eye, and likewise": "Bhaga" is the letter *e*; "that supreme" is the letter *ai*; "mouth" is the visarga; and "preceded by that" is the nasal dot (*bindu*), making *aim*. "Sky" is the letter *ha*; "fire" is the letter *ra*; "left eye" is the letter *ī*; and "likewise" refers to the previously mentioned form, the nasal dot. Thus, it is *hrīm*.

He says that one should sprinkle the place of worship with water from *kuśa* grass using a mantra consisting of two seed-syllables (*bīja*), beginning with the words "with *kuśa*-water" and so forth. This refers to the ground and the place of worship. "Akula," "sakula," and so on, refers to the *tarka-bīja* (the seed of logic) joined with the letter preceding *śiva*, together with the crescent moon (*indu-khaṇḍa*). "Akula" is the letter *ha*; "Kula" is the letter *sa*. Its beginning is the *tarka-bīja*. That, in reverse order, is the sixth syllable, *ra*. *Śiva* is the letter *u*; what precedes it is *ī*; the crescent moon is the *bindu*. Thus, by the mantra *hrīm*, one should perform the purification of substances; or rather, by this mantra, [one uses] the *vāgbhava* as the letter *ai*. Together with the staff (*daṇḍa*) and the *bindu*, it is *aim*. "Vasu" is fire; that is to say, the letter *ra*. "Left eye" is the letter *ī*. The crescent moon is the *bindu*. That, in reverse order, is the "fire-gone" (*analaga*). The third syllable is *śa*. "Sky" (*ambara*) is the letter *ha*. The meaning is that the letters *śa* and *ha* are joined with *ra*, *ī*, and the *bindu*. Thus, by the mantra consisting of the three seed-syllables—*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīm*—one should worship the deities beginning with the *bhaga*. The section from "Brahmāṇī, whose vehicle is the swan" up to "the root of the leaf" is easy to understand. "Abdhivaktrā" means four-faced. He states the mantras of the deities beginning with Brahmā with the words "these are their seeds" and so forth. "Ananta" is long; that is, the letter *ā*. "End of sky" (*nabhontam*) means the sky is *ha*; its end is *kṣa*. Long: *ākṣā*. This is the mantra of Brahmanī. "End of eye" (*nayanāntam*) is Indra. "Prāṅgu" means: "end of eye" is the letter *ka*; Indra is the letter *la*. "Tall" (*prāṃśu*) means long. *Ītvā* is the mantra of Māheśvarī. "Beyond the end of the eye" (*dṛgāntaparaḥ*) is the end of *kula*, joined with the inner *rudra*. "Eye" is the letter *ī*; its end is *ū*.

The letter *u* is at the end of that; the letter *ū* follows it. *Kula* is the letter *sa*; its end is the letter *ha*. "Endless Rudra" means the letter *ā* joined with [the previous], i.e., accompanied by the letter *ā*. *Ūhā* is the mantra of Kaumārī. Regarding "Tithīśa with Ananta and Bhṛgu": Tithīśa is the letter *ṛ*; Bhṛgu is the letter *sa*; "with Ananta" means accompanied by the letter *ā*. Thus, *sāṛsā* is the mantra of Vaiṣṇavī. "Hara with Ananta and ending in Baka": Hara is the letter *ḷ*; Baka is the letter *śa*; its end is *ṣa*, which is accompanied by Ananta (the letter *ā*). Thus, *ṣā ḷ ṣā* is the mantra of Vārāhī. "Bhṛtīśa, followed by Baka, with Ananta": Bhṛtīśa is the letter *ai*; Baka is the letter *śa*; "with Ananta" means joined with the letter *ā*. Thus, *śā aiśā* is the mantra of Indrāṇī. "Preceded by Ka, ending in Sūkṣma, and joined with Vana": *Ka* is the crescent moon (*bindu*); before that is the letter *au*. *Sūkṣma* is the letter *i*; that whose end is the letter *i* is the letter *ā*. *Vana* is water, the letter *va*. It has reached the letter *va*. Thus, *āvā* or *auvā* is the mantra of Cāmuṇḍā. "Anuvadana, joined with Śacīnātha": *Vadana* is the visarga (*ḥ*); *anu* again refers to the letter *ā* (vadana). *Śacīnātha* is the letter *la*. "Joined" (*upeta*) means the letter *ā* is merged with the letter *la*. Thus, *aḥ lā* is the mantra of Mahālakṣmī. "Vadana, joined with Vikrānta": *Vadana* is the letter *ā* as mentioned in the eight mantras above. It is also "joined with Vikrānta. *Am* is the letter *a*; its end is the letter *ā*. Following that is the letter *i*. From that, the letter *ū* is obtained immediately after it.

By the word "also" (*api*), the meaning is that the vowel *ī* is obtained as the mode [of pronunciation]. When this is done, the result is: *ā*, *kṣā*, *ī*, *lā*, *ī*, *ūhā*, *ī*, *ṛ*, *sā*, *ī*, *ḷ*, *ṣā*, *ī*, *aiśā*, *ī*, *auvā*, *ī*, *aḥ*, *lā*, *ū*—this is the intended meaning. Now, from "Asitāṅga" up to "by the channel of youth" (*yauvanāḍyā*) is easy to understand. He states the mantra for the Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga: "The third of Hara, joined with Bhaga and Bhūta, also ending with Kula, joined with the eye and Ananda, marked by the half-moon, and 'Asta'. "Hara" is the syllable *ḷ*. "Tantrī" is the syllable *ai*. "Bhaga" is the syllable *ai*. That is the syllable "Bhūta," which is the fifth syllable. "Joined with Bindu" means conjoined with the dot (*bindu*). "Ending with Kula": "Kula" is the letter *sa*; its end is the letter *bha*. "Without Pitta" (bile) refers to the fire, the letter *ra*. Up to "the eye" is the letter *ī*. The "half-moon" is the *bindu*. "Marked at the top" means accompanied by the *bindu*. Thus, the eight Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga are to be worshipped with the mantra *aiṃ hrīm*. From "Yo Hetuka" up to "Bhīmā" is easy to understand. He states the mantras for Hetuka and the others: "By the Lord of the Elements" (*bhautīśa*); "Lord of the Elements" is the syllable *ai*. The "half-moon" is the *bindu*. With that together, i.e., with the mantra *aim*, the Bhairavas beginning with Hetuka are to be worshipped. From "Priyaṅgu" up to "Sādhaka" is easy to understand. "Chagalagati" means having a goat as a vehicle. "Serihāṅgagata" means mounted on a buffalo. "Varaśambaragata" means mounted on a black deer. "Ūrṇāyu" is a specific type of woolly ram. He states the mantras for the world-protectors beginning with Indra.

"Head and so forth, situated in the water-group, with *ka*, head and petal, mountain, joined by *va* and the end; joined with the subtle and the preceding face"—this refers to the Head (*mastaka*). The Drop (*bindu*) is at the beginning, situated in the water-group (the fourth element); that, in reverse order, is the fourth syllable, *ai*. "With *ka*" means with the drop (*sabinduka*), thus *aiṃ*. "Head and from fire" (*mastakādanalagam*): the Head is the Drop; from that, the "petal" is the third letter, *ka*. "Baka" is the letter *śa*; its end is *ṣa*. "Joined" (*yuk*) means the letter *ka* joined with *ṣa*. "Subtle" (*sūkṣma*) is the letter *i*. That which precedes it is *ā*. "Face" (*mukha*) is the Visarga; that which precedes it is the Drop, [thus] joined with the Drop (*binduyuktam*). The meaning is that the world-protectors, Indra and the others, are to be worshipped with the mantra *kṣāṃ aiṃ*. The portion beginning with *vaṭuka* and ending with *amata* is easy to understand. Now, regarding the section beginning with "worshipped by the three worlds, for the sake of the command" and ending with "just as the Lord of the Mountain attained," this is what is meant: Then, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, placing the lotus-feet of one's venerable Guru upon one's head, and performing the recollection of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), one should go to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) as before. Having performed purification, sipping water (*ācamana*), cleaning the teeth, and washing the face, one should perform the ritual bath according to rule. Having sipped water again, one should sprinkle oneself one hundred and eight times with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) using the *kalaśa-mudrā*. Having sipped water once more and reached the bank, one should put on two silken garments (*kṣauma-vāsasī*). Having performed the prescribed twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*), one should meditate upon the Goddess within the solar orb. Having satiated Her, along with Her retinue, one hundred and eight times with nectar-like waters using the root-vidyā, one should offer the *arghya* with the Tripura-Gāyatrī: "We know the Great Mother (*mahāmātṛkā*), we meditate upon Kālasaṅkarṣaṇī; may She, the Goddess, impel us. Thus it is said.

Having given [the offerings] and recited [mantras] according to one's capacity, one should rise and, having prepared a sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) that is beautiful, well-guarded, and firmly enclosed—either in a temple frequented by common folk or elsewhere—wash one’s feet at the entrance, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and enter within. With the mantra *aiṃ hrīṃ*, one should consecrate the pavilion by sprinkling it with water and *kuśa* grass; then, with the mantra *huṃ*, wash the sacrificial vessels. Having arranged an unlimited number of pure materials for worship, one should sit facing either the east or the north upon a *svastika* seat. Having worshipped Gaṇapati in one’s own portion and in the south-eastern portion dedicated to the Guru, one should recognize the individual soul (*jīvātman*) within one’s own *mūlādhāra* as being of the nature of the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*), consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*), and identical with Kuṇḍalinī. By means of the *haṃsa* mantra, one should lead [the soul] through the path of Brahman (*brahmādhvan*) to the *dvādaśānta*. Joining it there with the Supreme Flame-Self (*paraśikhātman*), which is lunar in nature and situated in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus, one should then, by means of the seed-syllable *ram*, draw up the *kalās* from the *mūlādhāra* to Rudra. With that, one should burn the body—which consists of the entire universe—reducing it to ashes. Then, by means of the seed-syllable *yam* located at the navel, one should raise the fierce wind (*pracaṇḍavāyu*) and, with that, scatter the heap of ashes throughout the whole world. Alternatively, by means of the seed-syllable *vam* situated in the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus at the *dvādaśānta*, one should meditate on it as an ocean of nectar. Then, having realized oneself as that undifferentiated (*niṣkala*) form of light being filled by a thick stream of nectar trickling down from above, and having contemplated oneself as firmly established by means of the seed-syllable *lam*, one should perform the *sakalīkaraṇa* (integration of limbs), become composed of mantra, and perform the series of ritual placements (*nyāsa*). For example: *drāṃ drāvaṇabāṇāya namaḥ*; *drīṃ kṣobhaṇabāṇāya namaḥ*.

*KLĪM* salutation to the arrow of subjugation (*vaśīkarabāṇa*). *BLŪM* salutation to the arrow of attraction (*ākarṣaṇabāṇa*). *SAṂ* salutation to the arrow of enchantment (*sammohanabāṇa*). Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five arrows upon the fingers of both hands, starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger, one should thereafter perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) according to the previously mentioned method and the rules for the placement of stability (*sthitinyāsa*), placing them upon the fingers and palms of both hands as follows: *VADAVADA VĀGVĀDINI AIṂ* salutation to the heart. *KLINNE KLEDINI MAHĀKṢOBHAṂ KURUKURU KLĪṂ* svāhā to the head. *OṂ MOKṢAṂ KURU KURU SAUMA* vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock (*śikhā*). *VADAVADA VĀGVĀDINI AIṂ* huṃ to the armor (*kavaca*). *KLINNE KLEDINI MAHĀKṢOBHAṂ KURU KURU KLĪṂ* vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. *OṂ MOKṢAṂ KURU KURU SAUḤ* phaṭ to the weapon (*astra*). Afterwards, one should place the Mātṛkā letters in their respective locations as follows: *AIṂ HRĪṂ KṢAM* on the head. *KṢĀṂ* on the perimeter of the face. *IM* and *Ī* on the two eyes. *UM* and *ŪṂ* on the two ears. *SṚṂ* and *SṜṂ* on the two cheeks. *ṢṆUṂ* and *ṢṆŪṂ* on the two jaws. *ŚEṂ* and *ŚAIṂ* on the two rows of teeth. *VOṂ* and *VAUM* on the two lips. *VAṂ* on the navel. *YAḤ* on the head. Then: *AṂ* salutation to Śrīkaṇṭheśa and Pūrṇodarī Śakti, to both Śiva and Śivā. Having performed the Mātṛkā-nyāsa in this manner, one should then divide the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) and, preceded by their respective illuminators (*dīpanī*), perform the placement according to the sequence to be described: one placement on the head, the secret place (*guhya*), and the heart; one placement on the pair of left [eyes] etc., and the forehead; one on the pair of ears and the mouth; one on the pair of shoulders and the back; and one on the pair of knees and the navel, [extending] upwards and downwards.

One [syllable] is on the right face; another is on the left, the rear, and the middle faces. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the sevenfold *vidyā*, one should thereafter place the previously mentioned six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon the heart and other locations. Then, having placed the five arrows (*bāṇa*) as before upon the secret parts, the navel, the heart, the mouth, and the head, one should next place the five [mantras] in sequence upon the forehead, the mouth, the heart, the navel, and the secret parts: *hrīṃ kāmarājāya namaḥ*, *klīṃ manmathāya namaḥ*, *aiṃ kandarpāya namaḥ*, *blūṃ makaraketanāya namaḥ*, *strīṃ manobhavāya namaḥ*. Having thus performed the placement, one should place the root *vidyā* as a sphere (*golaka*) from the feet to the hair and from the hair to the feet. Having performed this entire series of placements (*nyāsa*), one should worship oneself with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and meditating on oneself as consisting of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), one should recite [the mantra] according to one's capacity. Then, having placed a clean, washed pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) upon the altar, one should smear it with the flow of fragrances—sandalwood, saffron, camphor, musk, and yellow pigment (*gorocanā*)—mixed with lac-juice and combined with self-arisen flowers (*svayambhu*). Then, having prepared the *arghya* mandala according to the rules, one should mentally establish the base of the *arghya* vessel as the fire-mandala (*agni-maṇḍala*) using the *vāgbhava* syllable [AIM], and worship the base with: "Obeisance to the base of the *arghya* vessel, which consists of the ten-fold fire-mandala. Then, having mentally established the solar mandala (*sūrya-maṇḍala*) within any one of the vessels made of gold, silver, or copper using the *kāmarāja* syllable [KLĪM], one should worship the vessel with: "Obeisance to the *arghya* vessel, which consists of the twelve-fold solar mandala. Then, having mentally established the lunar mandala (*soma-maṇḍala*) as the *arghya* water according to the instruction using the third seed-syllable [HRĪM], one should worship it with: "Obeisance to the *arghya* nectar, which consists of the sixteen-fold lunar mandala."

Having thus worshipped the *arghya* nectar and having placed therein—according to availability—fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), *kuśa* grass, barley, sesame, and mustard seeds into the *arghya* water; having worshipped it with the Heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*); having removed the defects within the *arghya* water by means of the Head-mantra (*śiras*); having dispelled them with the Topknot-mantra (*śikhā*); having enclosed it with the Armor-mantra (*kavaca*); having rendered it nectarine with the Eye-mantra and the *surabhi-mudrā*; having protected it with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*); and having worshipped it with the Root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) while meditating upon Amṛteśvarī therein—one should touch the *arghya* water and recite the Root-vidyā ending with "I render the *arghya* nectarine" seven times. Then, with the *arghya* water and the mantra "Hrīṃ," one should sprinkle the articles of worship, the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and oneself. Thereafter, having drawn upon the pedestal a lotus consisting of a triangle, a five-petaled lotus, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square, one should worship the Support-Energy (*ādhāraśakti*) in its center with the Root-mantra. Upon that, one should worship with their respective names followed by "Namaḥ": "Salutation to Ananta," "Salutation to Kūrma," and "Salutation to Pṛthivī. Then, on the legs of the pedestal in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast, one should worship the four qualities beginning with Dharma; and on the sides of the pedestal in the cardinal directions starting from the east, the four qualities beginning with Adharma. Next, upon the pedestal, one should assign: "Salutation to Sattva," "Raṃ, Salutation to Rajas," "Taṃ, Salutation to Tamas," "Salutation to the Bulb (*kanda*)," "Salutation to the Stem (*nāla*)," "Salutation to the Lotus (*padma*)," "Salutation to the Family-Lotus (*kulapadma*)," "Salutation to the Yoni-seat (*yonyāsana*"), "Vaṃ, Salutation to the Fire-circle (*vahni-maṇḍala*)," "Aṃ, Salutation to the Sun-circle (*arka-maṇḍala*)," and "Saṃ, Salutation to the Moon-circle (*soma-maṇḍala*). Having thus assigned them layer by layer, one should worship there with: "Hasauḥ, Salutation to the Great Corpse-Lotus-seat of Sadāśiva. Therein, one should meditate upon her as described, possessing the colors, ornaments, and garments [of the deity], surrounded by a multitude of devoted attendants.

One should invoke the Goddess, whose nature is the consciousness of the Maṇḍala, using the *āvāhana-mudrā* from the pericarp of the heart-lotus through the right nostril into one's cupped hands (*karāñjali*). Having invoked her, one should establish her with the *saṃsthāpana-mudrā*, bring her into proximity with the *sannidhikāriṇī*, bind her with the *sannirodhinī*, and veil her with the *avakuṇṭhana-mudrā*. Having formed the *mūrti* (the body-form) with the *Haṃsa-mantra* and displayed the *yonimudrā*, one should perform the *karanyāsa* and *nyāsa-jāta* upon that form as if it were one's own body. Then, having worshipped with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) and the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) beginning with the *arghya*, having performed the *nīrājana* and prostrated, one should worship the retinue following their permission. As follows: One should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in sequence using the previously mentioned mantras—starting from the Goddess’s surroundings, from the Heart up to the Armor (*kavaca*) in the directions of Fire, Īśāna, and Vāyu; the Eye in front; and the Weapon (*astra*) in the cardinal directions. Then, in the middle of the triangle, one should worship Rati with the *Vāgbhava* syllable (*aiṃ*), who is situated at the tip of the left corner, resembling molten gold, possessing an exceedingly beautiful form, and holding a noose and a goad in her hands. At the tip of the right corner, one should worship Prīti with the third seed-syllable (*klīṃ*), who resembles the moon, has most beautiful limbs, a lovely face, and holds a lotus and a goad in her hands. At the tip of the front corner, one should worship Kāma with the *Kāma-bīja* (*blūṃ*), who resembles the Bandhūka flower, holds a sugarcane bow and flower-arrows, and is adorned with ornaments made of jewels. Then, on the five petals starting from the east, one worships the deities of the five arrows: *Drāṃ Drāviṇyai namaḥ*; *Hrīṃ Kṣobhiṇyai namaḥ*; *Klīṃ Vaśīkariṇyai namaḥ*; *Blūṃ Ākarṣaṇyai namaḥ*; *Saḥ Sammohinyai namaḥ*. These deities resemble camphor, gold, twilight, the color of a ruby, and the Māñjiṣṭha flower respectively; they hold arrows in their right hands, while their remaining hands are joined in salutation, and their bodies are adorned with every ornament.
Having worshipped the Samādās in sequence: *aiṃ hrīṃ bhagāyai namaḥ* | 3 | *bhagajihvāyai namaḥ* | 3 | *bhagapiṇyai namaḥ* | 3 |

Salutation to Bhagākṣī. 3. Salutation to Bhagāhlādinī. Thus, having worshipped the deities beginning with Bhaga in sequence, one should worship Brahmā and the others, bearing their respective colors, garments, weapons, and ornaments, in pairs, as instructed. For example: Ā Kṣā Ī to Brahmāṇī, salutation. Aiṃ Hrīm. Aiṃ Kṣaṃ to Asitāṅga Bhairava, salutation. Ī Lā Ī to Māheśvarī, salutation. Aiṃ Hrīm Iṃ Laṃ to Ruru Bhairava, salutation. Ū Hā Ī to Kaumārī, salutation. Aiṃ Hrīṃ Uṃ Haṃ to Caṇḍabhairava, salutation. Ṛ Sā Ī to Vaiṣṇavī, salutation. Aiṃ Hrīṃ Ṛṃ Saṃ to Krodhīśabhairava, salutation. Ḷ Ṣā Ī to Vārāhī, salutation. U Ḷṃ Ṣaṃ to Unmattabhairava, salutation. Ai Śā Ī to Indrāṇī, salutation. Aiṃ Hrīṃ Eṃ Śaṃ to Kapālabhairava, salutation. Au Vā Ī to Cāmuṇḍā, salutation. Aiṃ Hrīṃ Oṃ Vaṃ to Bhīṣaṇabhairava, salutation. Aḥ Lā Ī to Mahālakṣmī, salutation. Aiṃ Hrīm Aṃ Laṃ to Saṃhārabhairava, salutation. Aiṃ to Hetuka, salutation. Aiṃ to Tripurāntaka, salutation. Aim to Agnivetāla, salutation. Aim to Agnijihva, salutation. Aiṃ to Kāla, salutation. Aiṃ to Karāla, salutation. Aim to Ekapāda, salutation. Aiṃ to Bhīma, salutation. Having thus worshipped, one should worship the lineage of Gurus on the northern side of the pedestal (pīṭha), starting from the northwest (Vāyavya) up to the northeast (Īśāna). Between the two enclosures of Hetuka and Īśa, the row of Guru-pādukās accompanied by mantras should be worshipped: Oṃ Moṃ to the Guru-pādukās, salutation.

Oṃ miṃ, salutation to the sandals of the worshipful Guru. Oṃ miṃ, salutation to the sandals of the Great Guru (*mahāguru*). Then one should worship the lineage of one's own Gurus. Thus it has been declared in secret. Then, outside the eight petals, in the eight directions starting from the east: Aiṃ kṣām, salutation to Indra, the lord of the gods, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand, together with his vehicle and retinue. Aiṃ kṣām, salutation to Agni, the lord of radiance, who holds a spear in his hand, together with his vehicle and retinue. (2) Salutation to Yama, the lord of the departed spirits, who holds a staff in his hand, together with his vehicle and retinue. (2) Salutation to Nṛ-ṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas, who holds a sword in his hand, together with his vehicle and retinue. (2) Salutation to Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, who holds a noose in his hand, together with his vehicle and retinue. (2) Salutation to Vāyu, the lord of the vital breaths, who holds a goad in his hand, together with his vehicle and retinue. (2) Salutation to Kubera, the lord of the Yakṣas, who holds a mace in his hand, together with his vehicle and retinue. (2) Salutation to Īśāna, the lord of knowledge, who holds a trident in his hand, together with his vehicle and retinue. Having thus worshipped, again in the directions of Agni, Nṛ-ṛti, Vāyu, and Īśa: Vāṃ vīṃ vūṃ vaṃ, salutation to Vaṭuka. Gāṃ gīṃ graṃ gaṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati. Dāṃ dīṃ dūṃ duṃ, salutation to Durgā. Kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaṃ, salutation to Kṣetrapāla. Having thus worshipped, outside in the directions of Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Soma: Salutation to the Eight Vasus. Salutation to the Eleven Rudras. (p. 195) The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive one who acts, nor does he perceive one who causes action to be performed. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive forms, nor does he perceive eye-consciousness. He does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive sounds, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness. He does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive odors, nor does he perceive nose-consciousness. He does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive tastes, nor does he perceive tongue-consciousness. He does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive body-consciousness. He does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive mental phenomena, nor does he perceive mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the element of earth, nor does he perceive the element of water, nor does he perceive the element of fire, nor does he perceive the element of wind, nor does he perceive the element of space, nor does he perceive the element of consciousness. He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor does he perceive the realm of form, nor does he perceive the formless realm. He does not perceive the conditioned, nor does he perceive the unconditioned. He does not perceive the past, nor does he perceive the future, nor does he perceive the present. He does not perceive samsara, nor does he perceive nirvana. Subhūti, because he does not perceive anything at all, he is called a ‘bodhisattva. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if there is no perceiving of a self, no perceiving of one who acts, no perceiving of one who causes action to be performed, and no perceiving of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; if there is no perceiving of the eye, forms, or eye-consciousness; if there is no perceiving of the ear, sounds, or ear-consciousness; if there is no perceiving of the nose, odors, or nose-consciousness; if there is no perceiving of the tongue, tastes, or tongue-consciousness; if there is no perceiving of the body, tangibles, or body-consciousness; if there is no perceiving of the mind, mental phenomena, or mind-consciousness; if there is no perceiving of the element of earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness; if there is no perceiving of the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm; if there is no perceiving of the conditioned or the unconditioned; if there is no perceiving of the past, the future, or the present; if there is no perceiving of samsara or nirvana—then, Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, give rise to the thought of awakening? How does he train in the six perfections? How does he enter the stages? How does he fulfill the factors of enlightenment? How does he purify the buddha-fields? How does he mature sentient beings? How does he turn the wheel of the Dharma? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, gives rise to the thought of awakening by means of non-perception. He trains in the six perfections by means of non-perception. He enters the stages by means of non-perception. He fulfills the factors of enlightenment by means of non-perception. He purifies the buddha-fields by means of non-perception. He matures sentient beings by means of non-perception. He turns the wheel of the Dharma by means of non-perception. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are non-perception, then what is the distinction between a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, and a bodhisattva mahāsattva? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are non-perception, yet through the power of their vows and the power of their skillful means, they manifest distinctions. Subhūti, a śrāvaka realizes the fruit of stream-entry through non-perception, yet he does not perceive that fruit. A śrāvaka realizes the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship through non-perception, yet he does not perceive those fruits. Subhūti, a pratyekabuddha realizes the state of a pratyekabuddha through non-perception, yet he does not perceive that state. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the thought of awakening through non-perception, trains in the six perfections through non-perception, enters the stages through non-perception, fulfills the factors of enlightenment through non-perception, purifies the buddha-fields through non-perception, matures sentient beings through non-perception, and turns the wheel of the Dharma through non-perception, yet he does not perceive any of these things. Subhūti, this is the distinction between them.”

"Salutation to all beings. Having thus worshipped in sequence, one should then worship the Supreme Goddess—the creeper-like *pārijāta* tree for those who revere Her, whose body overflows with a mass of the nectar of supreme bliss, and whose nature is indivisible consciousness—with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Having gratified Her along with Her retinue according to the instructions, having performed the *nīrājana* rite, praised Her, and prostrated, one should contemplate oneself as being merged within the form of the Supreme Deity together with the entire host of attendants. Then, having meditated upon Her as the source of the manifestation and dissolution of all worlds, the root of all, consisting of partless light, one should take up a flower from the mandala with the *saṃhāriṇī* mudrā, smell it, and lead it to the station of the heart-lotus. Contemplating oneself as identical with Her, and worshipping with perfumes and other offerings, one should receive Her grace. Having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) and becoming filled with the bliss of nectar oneself, one should wander at ease as one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). May there be auspiciousness! (*Śivam*)
Thus ends the eighth chapter.

Thus, following the description of propitiating the Supreme Deity—which serves as the means for attaining happiness in this world and the next—the author begins to explain the procedure for the fire-sacrifice (*homavidhāna*) with the words "Now, the fire-rite" (*athāgnikāryam*), and so forth. By the passage beginning with "Of the sacrificial hall" (*pūjāgrahasya*), he states the characteristics and rules regarding the construction of a single sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). The meaning is as follows: one should construct a single square pit in the eastern direction, the northeast corner, or the north (the quarter of Kubera) of the altar situated in the center of the initiation pavilion (*dīkṣāmaṇḍapa*) that is about to be described. Next, he describes the characteristics of the initiation pavilion with the words "Measuring nine cubits," and so forth.

This is the meaning: one should construct a radiant pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) measuring nine cubits (*hasta*) on each side—dedicated to Indra, Varuṇa, Yama, and Soma; surrounded by a firm enclosure; adorned with four doors and arches (*toraṇa*); draped with white cloth canopies and garlands of *darbha* grass; and brightly illuminated. Alternatively, it may measure seven cubits, as "mountains" (*śaila*) are counted as seven, or five cubits, as "senses" (*hṛṣīka*) are five. Regarding the measurement for constructing the altar (*vedikā*) for worship, he says: "Then, in its center," and so forth. One should construct the altar in the middle of that pavilion, occupying one-third of its area. Having fixed the pavilion by drawing four lines from east to west and likewise from south to north, when this is done, the pavilion consists of nine squares. Among these, the central square should be made into an altar, two *aratnis* high and twice that in length and breadth, raised gradually like the surface of a mirror, suitable for viewing the reflection of the face of the deity's image, brilliantly radiant, and exceedingly beautiful. In the remaining eight squares of the directions starting from the east, one should construct the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) in sequence as will be described starting with "the four-cornered" (*vedāśra*). "Four-cornered" means square. "Yoni-shaped" means shaped like a horse's vulva or a lotus petal. "Resembling the half-moon" means crescent-shaped. "Fire-shaped" means triangular. "Elephant-shaped" means eight-cornered. "From the horse of Hari" means starting from the eastern direction. Others, however, say: one should make a circle between the directions of Indra and Īśāna (northeast), a pentagon in the northwest, and a heptagon in the northeast.

He describes the method for laying out the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*): "The eastern thread," and so forth. First, having stretched a thread from east to west, one should mark its center with a fish-sign (*matsya*). Using that measurement, one should place two fish-marks in the southern and northern directions. One should stretch a north-south thread between those two northern fish-marks. One should extend the ends of that pair of threads according to the aforementioned rule. Holding the threads, one should place four fish-marks at the four corners. One should stretch four threads through the four ears of those fish-marks in the four directions. When this is done, a square mandala consisting of four parts arises. This square pit faces the east. Relying on this very square, he says that other pits should be constructed, beginning with "here one should produce others," etc. Having cast [the lines] upon the field—that is, upon the original square—one should stretch two threads toward the southeast, northwest, southwest, and northeast. Then, having divided the square into five parts, one should extend the eastern end of the middle thread outward from the south-north thread located in the eastern direction by one part. Then, having divided the corner-thread situated in the western part into four parts, one should discard one part at the edge of each corner-end and, using the measure of the remaining three parts, draw a circle around the corner itself like a crescent moon. One should do the same for the upper corner as well. Then, holding the two ends of the north-south thread at the lower corner, one should stretch two threads reaching to the end of the middle eastward thread, just like the corner-threads. One should erase the other [excess] threads.

This *yonikuṇḍa*, shaped like an *aśvattha* leaf, is situated in the south-eastern direction. Having set aside two parts as previously stated and having made a square according to the prescribed measurement, one should strike nine lines from east to west between the north-south and east-west threads, with equal intervals. When this is done, eleven lines from east to west will have been struck, and the square will be divided ten-fold. Among these, having set aside the southern and northern portions, one should take the remaining nine-line portion and, using the measurement of the eight-part field for the south and north, fix upon the middle of the north and east threads and extend [the line] from the eastern end of that east thread to the western end. Again, by that same measurement, starting from the middle of that thread at its eastern end and ending at its western end, one should draw a curve like a crescent moon. One should erase the other segments of the thread. This is the *kuṇḍa* called "Half-moon," situated in the southern direction. Regarding the phrase "half-portion of the Lord of Day" (*vāsareśārdhabhāga*): having divided the original square field into sixteen parts, one should extend the eastern end of the central east-thread outward from the north-south thread by one part out of the two parts. Then, starting from the center, one should draw a circle around it with that same measurement. One should erase the other segments of the thread. This is the circular (*vṛtta*) *kuṇḍa*, situated in the western direction. Regarding the phrase "eight parts of the earth" (*bhūpāṃśa*), etc.: having divided the original square into eight parts, one should extend the eastern and western ends of the central east-thread by one part out of the two parts. Then, starting from the center, one should generate a set of four "fishes" (*matsya*) on both sides with that measurement. There, by drawing six lines within the bellies of those fishes, a hexagonal (*ṣaṭkoṇa*) *kuṇḍa* shall be formed.

That [circle] is situated in the northwestern direction (*vāyavya*). Regarding the phrase "in a tenth part": the original square field is divided into ten parts; with one of those parts, one should draw a circle outside the previously mentioned circular *kuṇḍa*. Again, with that same measurement, one should draw another circle outside that. The meaning is that one should form the pericarp (*karṇikā*) with the central circle which constitutes the *kuṇḍa* itself, the filaments (*kesarāṇi*) with the second circle, and the four-petaled or eight-petaled lotus with the third. This is the lotus-shaped *kuṇḍa* (*padmakuṇḍa*), and it is situated in the northern direction (*kaubera*). Regarding the phrase "one should project the field": having divided the original square field into twenty-four parts, one should extend the eastern end of the central line outward from the north-south line by one part. Then, with that same measurement, one should construct an outer square enclosure. Furthermore, using half the measurement of the original square, one should mark points on both sides of its two arms, starting from the corners of the outer square. One should mark the other corners in the same manner. Then, one should strike four diagonal lines connecting the pairs of marks at the four corners. One should also rotate the lines between the marks in the cardinal directions as they stand. One should then erase the corners and the fragments of the lines. This becomes the eight-sided *kuṇḍa* (*aṣṭāśra-kuṇḍa*), and it is situated in the northeastern direction (*īśvara*). Regarding the phrase "in a seventh part": having divided the original square field into seven parts, one should extend the eastern end of the central east-west line outward from the north-south line by one of those parts. Then, with that same measurement, one should conceive a surrounding circle. Furthermore, having divided the square into four parts, one [should take] one of those parts...

Having attained parinirvāṇa, he does not again undergo birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, or despair. This is called the fruit of the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Having abandoned [the previous measurements], one should measure the remaining three [sides] according to the internal dimensions. Having measured the third side fivefold and having made five marks thereon, one should strike five long lines from mark to mark. One should erase the other fragments of the lines. This is the five-cornered *kuṇḍa* situated in the northwest corner. Regarding "the width of the field": having divided that square field into ten parts, one should extend the tip of the central eastward line outward from the south-north line by one part; then, with that same measurement, one should rotate a circle around it. Again, having divided the square into sixty-four parts, one should discard thirty-one parts and, with the remaining thirty-three parts, measure the circular line sevenfold. Having made seven marks there, one should strike seven straight lines from mark to mark. The meaning is that this seven-cornered *kuṇḍa* is situated in the northeast direction. To whatever measurement the width of the *kuṇḍa* corresponds, to that same measurement one should also make the excavation (*khāta*). He states that the girdles (*mekhalā*) should be of the same shape as the *kuṇḍa*. Regarding "to whatever measurement," etc., he gives the general characteristics of the girdles and the vulva (*yoni*) for single *kuṇḍas* with the passage beginning "three [girdles] in the *kuṇḍa*" and ending with "here in the direction of the Hotṛ. "The size of a fist" means measured by the fingers of a closed fist. Alternatively, "fist" (*muṣṭi*) is a term for two spans (*tāla*). Regarding the height and width of the girdles in a *kuṇḍa* measured by a fist, he says: "two fingers, one finger, half a finger," and so on, up to eight cubits (*aratni*).

Regarding those sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), he states the characteristics of the height and width of the girdles (*mekhalā*) with the passage beginning "In the case of [pits] measuring one cubit (*aratni*)" and ending with "eight cubits (*vasuhasta*). In the case of [pits] measured by one *aratni*, the dimensions are two fingers (*dvy-aṅgula*), three fingers (*try-aṅgula*), and one finger (*ekāṅgula*). In the case of [pits] measured by one cubit (*hasta*), they are four fingers (*yuga-aṅgula*), three fingers (*arpita-aṅgula*), and two fingers (*netra-aṅgula*). Here, *yuga-aṅgula* means four fingers; *arpita-aṅgula* means three fingers (the meaning of *agni-aṅgula*); and *netra-aṅgula* means two fingers. In the case of [pits] measured by two cubits, they are six fingers (*rasāmbhodhi-aṅgula*). Here, *rasāṅgula* means six fingers. In the case of [pits] measured by six [cubits], they are eight fingers (*aṅkuśa-aṅgā-ila*). Here, *aṅgāṅgula* means ten fingers, three fingers, and eight fingers respectively. In the case of [pits] measured by eight cubits, they are twelve fingers (*bhāskarapaṅkti*), eight fingers (*gajāṅgula*). Here, *bhāskara-aṅgula* means twelve fingers; *paṅkti-aṅgula* means ten fingers; and *gajāṅgula* means eight fingers. He describes the method for constructing the navel (*nābhi*) in the center of the pit with the phrase "the navel is like a lotus. Regarding the length and width of the navel and the vulva (*yoni*) in a pit measured by one fist (*muṣṭi*), he gives the definition starting with "six oceans" (*rasāmbhodhi*). The meaning is that one should construct the vulva—four fingers in length and width, tapering down to two fingers at the end like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, with its tip entering the edge of the pit by one finger—and the navel in the form of an eight-petaled lotus, four fingers in length and width, tapering down to two fingers at the end. This same definition for the navel and vulva applies to all three types of pits measured by one cubit. Thus he indicates the definition of the vulva and so forth, and by the phrase "that indeed is the measure," he refers to the two-cubit [pit] and others.

(p. 202) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent self-nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the perfected self-nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the nature of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-svabhāva*). "Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is the grasping of names and signs (*nāmanimitta*) based on the objects of perception, which are themselves non-existent, and the subsequent attachment to them as having the characteristics of substance and attributes. This is called the imagined self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the dependent self-nature? It is the manifestation of various appearances that arise from the causal conditions of the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of false discrimination; it is like a dream, a mirage, or a reflection. This is called the dependent self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the perfected self-nature? It is the state of the dependent self-nature when it is completely free from the imagined self-nature, being eternally unchanging and devoid of the duality of grasper and grasped. This is called the perfected self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the nature of reality as it is? It is the realization that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, transcending the reach of speech, thought, and conceptualization, and is the very essence of the Tathāgata-garbha. This is called the nature of reality as it is. "Therefore, Mahāmati, you should cultivate yourself by thoroughly understanding these four kinds of self-nature."

One should construct the base (*yoni*) and the navel (*nābhi*) of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), increasing each by one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) respectively. One should increase the base (*yoni*) by two barley-corns (*yava*) for each [pit]. Alternatively, one may make the navel circular, conforming to the shape of the pit. It is stated that in a *yonikuṇḍa* there is no base, and in a *padmakuṇḍa* there is no lotus; this is established by the passage beginning with "by one finger-breadth each" and ending with "one should fashion up to the navel. Others, however, describe the construction of the base for a pit of limited size in a single day, from the passage beginning with "of the pit, one... and ending with "...the form of the seat of enlightenment (*bodhiṣṭhāna*). Here, "elemental" (*bhūta*) refers to two finger-breadths; "elemental and so forth" (*bhūtādi*) refers to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), meaning eight finger-breadths per finger-breadth. "Width" (*vyāsa*) means length (*āyāma*). In that context, the number six refers to six finger-breadths; "one and two" refers to one and two finger-breadths. It conforms to the petals of the seat of enlightenment, having the shape of an *aśvattha* leaf. This is what is meant: for a pit measuring one cubit (*hasta*), one should make the base eight finger-breadths long, six finger-breadths wide, and two finger-breadths deep, with a tip gradually tapering like an *aśvattha* petal. Regarding the previously mentioned division of the navel and the pericarp (*karṇikā*), from the passage beginning with "two and elemental finger-breadths" and ending with "at the end of the pit," the meaning is as follows: having divided that [area] into three parts, each four finger-breadths in length and width, one should make the pericarp with the middle portion and the eight petals with the remaining two portions. Regarding the construction of the fist-sized pits and others, he says "by one finger-breadth each. Regarding the construction of the rims (*nemi*) for the two-hand-sized pits and others, he says they increase by half a finger-breadth each in succession. From the passage beginning with "starting from the two-eyed hand" and ending with "according to the stated order," he asks: "What is a finger-breadth? (implying the measurement).

(p. 203) The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by means of his profound Prajñāpāramitā, perceives that all five aggregates are empty, and thus he delivers all beings from their suffering. Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; form is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than form. What is true of form is also true of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, and no mind; no sight-object, no sound, no smell, no taste, no touchable object, and no object of mind; no realm of sight up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no aging-and-death and no extinction of aging-and-death; no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; no cognition and no attainment. Therefore, Śāriputra, because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on Prajñāpāramitā and dwells in the mind free from hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; transcending all error and delusion, he reaches ultimate Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on this Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the peerless mantra; it removes all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of Prajñāpāramitā is proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. (p. 204) Thus spoke the Blessed One. With one voice, the Venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, humans, asuras, garuḍas, and gandharvas—praised what the Buddha had said.
