[The measurement] is by either the length or the width of one's own finger. That which is not mentioned among other measurements is as follows: the finger (aṅguli) is of five kinds according to the difference in characteristics: the *mānāṅguli* (measurement-finger), the *mānāntarāṅguli* (intermediate-measurement-finger), the *mātrāntarāṅguli* (intermediate-unit-finger), the *muṣṭyaṅguli* (fist-finger), and the *dehalabdhāṅguli* (body-attained-finger). Thus it is stated in the *Śrīpañcarātra Tantra*: "The atoms (*paramāṇu*) are the subtle particles that spread within those rays of light which shine upon reaching the path of the window. Eight of those [atoms] constitute a hair-fiber (*keśāgra*); eight of those make a nit (*likṣā*); eight of those make a louse-egg (*yūka*). Eight of those make a barley-corn (*yava*), and eight of those are declared to be a finger-breadth (*aṅguli*). It is said that the middle finger-breadth consists of seven barley-corns, while the smallest is said to consist of six; this is the *mānāṅguli*. The *mānāntarāṅguli* is formed by eight barley-corns placed crosswise. Or, the intermediate measurement (*mānāntara*) is formed by three grains of rice (*śāli*) placed in water. The *mātrāntara* is declared to be the length of the space between the joints of the middle finger on the right hand of the preceptor (*ācārya*). The *muṣṭyaṅguli* is known as the measurement made by the remaining fingers excluding the thumb, divided into four parts; one of these parts is remembered as the *muṣṭyaṅguli*. Here, the measurement is made by the four fingers of the preceptor’s hand, starting from the little finger, spreading crosswise at the middle joint of the middle finger of the great sage. Whosoever, for the sake of curiosity, divides the height [of the body] into ten parts, and further having made twelve divisions, one of those parts is called the *dehalabdhāṅguli*; this is the *mahāmānāṅguli*. The *mānāṅguli* is the term for the measurement established through the sequence of atoms. In the construction of the height of an image, the *mahāmānāṅguli* measurement is used."

(p. 204) The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, contemplates form as empty of intrinsic nature, feeling as empty of intrinsic nature, perception as empty of intrinsic nature, formations as empty of intrinsic nature, and consciousness as empty of intrinsic nature. He contemplates the eye as empty of intrinsic nature, the ear as empty of intrinsic nature, the nose as empty of intrinsic nature, the tongue as empty of intrinsic nature, the body as empty of intrinsic nature, and the mind as empty of intrinsic nature. He contemplates forms as empty of intrinsic nature, sounds as empty of intrinsic nature, odors as empty of intrinsic nature, tastes as empty of intrinsic nature, tangibles as empty of intrinsic nature, and mental phenomena as empty of intrinsic nature. He contemplates the eye-consciousness as empty of intrinsic nature, the ear-consciousness as empty of intrinsic nature, the nose-consciousness as empty of intrinsic nature, the tongue-consciousness as empty of intrinsic nature, the body-consciousness as empty of intrinsic nature, and the mind-consciousness as empty of intrinsic nature. He contemplates eye-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, ear-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, nose-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, tongue-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, body-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, and mind-contact as empty of intrinsic nature. He contemplates the feeling born of eye-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, the feeling born of ear-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, the feeling born of nose-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, the feeling born of tongue-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, the feeling born of body-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, and the feeling born of mind-contact as empty of intrinsic nature. He contemplates the earth element as empty of intrinsic nature, the water element as empty of intrinsic nature, the fire element as empty of intrinsic nature, the wind element as empty of intrinsic nature, the space element as empty of intrinsic nature, and the consciousness element as empty of intrinsic nature. He contemplates the conditioned co-arising as empty of intrinsic nature, and he contemplates each member of the conditioned co-arising, from aging and death down to birth and existence, as empty of intrinsic nature. He contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness as empty of intrinsic nature, the four right efforts as empty of intrinsic nature, the four bases of psychic power as empty of intrinsic nature, the five faculties as empty of intrinsic nature, the five powers as empty of intrinsic nature, the seven factors of enlightenment as empty of intrinsic nature, and the noble eightfold path as empty of intrinsic nature. He contemplates the four dhyānas as empty of intrinsic nature, the four immeasurables as empty of intrinsic nature, the four formless attainments as empty of intrinsic nature, the eight liberations as empty of intrinsic nature, the nine successive attainments as empty of intrinsic nature, the ten bases of totality as empty of intrinsic nature, the four analytical knowledges as empty of intrinsic nature, the four fearlessnesses as empty of intrinsic nature, the four grounds of self-confidence as empty of intrinsic nature, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as empty of intrinsic nature, and the great compassion as empty of intrinsic nature. He contemplates the emptiness of emptiness as empty of intrinsic nature, the signless of the signless as empty of intrinsic nature, the wishless of the wishless as empty of intrinsic nature, the dharma-sphere as empty of intrinsic nature, the reality-limit as empty of intrinsic nature, the suchness as empty of intrinsic nature, the unaltered suchness as empty of intrinsic nature, the unerring suchness as empty of intrinsic nature, the unchanging suchness as empty of intrinsic nature, and the dharma-nature as empty of intrinsic nature. He contemplates the dharma-position as empty of intrinsic nature, the established order of dharma as empty of intrinsic nature, the fixed sequence of dharma as empty of intrinsic nature, and the specific characteristics of all dharmas as empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature.”

In the construction of palaces, gate-towers (*gopura*), and the like, one must use the *mānāṅgula* (standard measurement finger), and not the *antarāṅgula* (internal measurement finger) nor any other. The ritual implements for yoga, such as the *srava* (ladle) and others, as well as the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), must be done using the *mantrāṅgula* (mantra-measurement finger). The image and the limbs of the deity must be made using the *muṣṭyaṅgula* (fist-measurement finger), and not by any other means. The ritual implements for yoga, such as the *srava*, [should be made with the *mātrāṅgula*]. Thus it is stated in the *Śrī Pañcarātra Tantra*: "The height of the image should be based on the *mahāmānāṅgula*. One should construct palaces and so forth using that very measure or another. Furthermore, the arrangement of altars, pedestals, palanquins, chariots, and the like, should be done using the *mānāntarāṅgula* alone, and not by any other. One should indeed make the ritual implements for yoga using the *mātrāṅgula*. The components for the fire-oblation (*homa*), such as the *srava* and others, should rely on the *muṣṭyaṅgula*. One should fashion the limbs of the image using the *dehalabdhāṅgula* (body-proportioned finger). A surface measuring twelve *aṅgulas* is a *tala*; two *talas* make a *muṣṭi*; twenty-five *aṅgulas* is a *prājāpatya*; twenty-six *aṅgulas* is a *dhanurmuṣṭi*; twenty-seven *aṅgulas* is a *hasta*. Synonymous names for these terms, such as *kuṇḍa* and others, are recited: *niṣku*, *prājāpatya*, *dhanurmuṣṭi*, and *dhanugraha*. Thus it is stated in the *Śrī Pañcarātra Tantra*: "Twenty-four *aṅgulas* is a *niṣku*; twenty-five is *prājāpatya*; twenty-six is *dhanurmuṣṭi*; twenty-seven is *dhanugraha*. For initiations (*dīkṣā*), daily and occasional rites, pacificatory (*śāntika*) and nourishing (*pauṣṭika*) rituals, festivals, and the like—specifically for the festival of the temple (*vimāna*) and the construction of the site (*vāstu*)—the *prājāpatya* is used; for the construction of the site, the *muṣṭi* is used; and for the location of villages and so forth, the *dhanugraha* is used. Alternatively, the *kiṣku* alone is intended for all tasks whatsoever.

(p. 205) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature as the basis for the manifestation of all phenomena."

Likewise, in the *Śrī Pañcarātra Tantra*: "That which is your *kiṣku* for Śani, the *vimānaka* for Prajāpati; for the *vāstu*s it is a fist-measure (*dhanurmuṣṭi*), and for villages and the like a bow-measure (*dhanurgraha*); and for all ritual acts, it is indeed the *kiṣku* on the left. How can it be said that there is a correspondence between the *Saṃvit* and *Pañcarātra* Tantras, which are so extremely distinct? We understand that because there is no difference between the deities propounded by them, there is no difference between the Tantras themselves. The conventional usage of their distinction arises merely from the difference in the names of their respective *saṃhitās*. It is not appropriate to accept a difference between the Tantras based merely on the fact that the *Puruṣa* is predominant in the *Pañcarātra Tantra* and the *Saṃvit* is predominant in the *Saṃvit Tantra*. Thus it is stated in the *Śrī Pañcarātra Upaniṣad*: "Oṃ, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is the supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*), more exalted than even the manifestations (*vibhūti*); He Himself becomes the source of all beings. And likewise in the *Śrī Pauṣkara Saṃhitā*: "She who is the supreme primordial nature, whose characteristic is the name Vāsudeva, whose body is the sixfold qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*), endowed with all powers and the principles of reality, having attained the state of being a sheath, is herself characterized by bliss. And likewise in the *Śrī Sātvata Saṃhitā*: "In the space at the end of sound (*nāda*), the eternal Lord Ananta is peaceful, whose very form is consciousness (*saṃvit*). Out of a desire to grace His devotees, that power which is His own essence is called the Sovereign Lady (*Īśvarī*). And likewise in the *Vairiñca-nṛsiṃha-vyūha-prakaraṇa*: "The Vaiṣṇava power, which is the Māyā consisting of Vāsudeva, is imperishable. Those who are indeed averse to Her remain wandering in the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*)."

Thus, in the *Īśvara-saṃhitā*: "O son, know the Supreme Nature (Parā Prakṛti) to be named Vāsudeva; she is the partless (*niṣkalā*) body of that array of powers (*śakti-vyūha*), serving as its sheath. And likewise in the *Jāyā-saṃhitā*: "When the conscious self (*cid-ātman*) is liberated from the body and exists in its absolute state, the Great Bliss arises—that indeed is the supreme Vaiṣṇavī power. Having made the individual soul (*jīva*), the performer of actions, one with herself, she rises there and remains established therein. O Nārada, that state is free from conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*), inexpressible, and beyond ritual injunction. And so it is stated in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*: "Those who have attained yoga behold the divine power hidden by her own qualities," and "He who presides over the womb," and "These [powers]... Likewise, in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "Because of the distinction between power and the possessor of power, he is called Vāsudeva. The possessor of power resides in power, and even within the powers—from Brahmā down to an ant—he dwells. In the abode of the Mūlādhāra, upon the couch of Śeṣa, the Lord Vāsudeva, consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*), whose nature is the Vaiśvānara fire known as Kāma, lies there. And thus says the *Śruti*: "In its center, for a very long time, subtle... and so on, ending with "...facing in all directions. And likewise in the *Śrī Bhagavad Gītā*: "Becoming the Vaiśvānara fire, residing in the bodies of living beings, joined with the Prāṇa and Apāna breaths, I digest the four kinds of food. Furthermore, the *Prapañcasāra* shows the supreme station of Viṣṇu as the fruit for those who worship Consciousness (*saṃvit*): "Having known which, and having cast off all bonds of karma, this [state] belongs to Viṣṇu..."

One attains the supreme state once again. One should constantly mutter and worship this very *Hṛllekhā*, who is the life-force (*jīvabhūtā*) born in the world. He who would practice this praise with reverence—along with the rules for the muttering of *Hṛllekhā* and the specific modes of worship—having indeed attained supreme glory, reaches that pure state which is the dust of the supreme abode. Thus it is said. In this way, the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Āgamas, each vying with the other, establish the very identity of Prakṛti and Puruṣa. These are not written here for fear of excessive length; this should be understood. The section beginning with "the sacrifice of fifty" (*śatārdrahoma*) and ending with "the source of the womb" (*randhatāyonih*) is easy to understand.
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the Saṃpradāyadīpikā.

Thus, following the procedures for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), he begins to describe the procedure for the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*), starting with the words "Now" (*atha*) and ending with "the practitioner should burn the surrounding grass" (*sa paristarāṃ dahen mantrī*). The meaning of this is as follows: Now, for the sake of accomplishing the aforementioned rite, one should commence the oblation either in one of the previously mentioned pits or on a sacrificial mound. For example, having prepared a square mound on the eastern side of the altar—either twenty-five finger-breadths in length and width and raised by the thickness of a thumb-joint, or twenty-seven finger-breadths in length and width and raised by four finger-breadths—one should remove nails, hair, clods of earth, and other impurities. Then, having smeared the pit with cow-dung water and sprinkled the mound, one should dry it with the seed-syllable of Air (*vāyubīja*) and purify it with the seed-syllable of Fire (*agnibīja*). Therein, [one should place] that which is called the Heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*).

Having drawn three lines—starting from the south and extending northward, and starting from the west and extending eastward—using double-folded *barhis* grass with the *vāgbhava* mantra ending in *namaḥ*; and having meditated upon Brahmā, Yama, and Soma as the presiding deities of the middle, western, and eastern [sections] respectively on those lines running northward from the south, and Īśa, Śrīśa, and Sureśa as the deities of the middle, southern, and northern [sections] respectively on those lines running eastward from the west; and having sprinkled [the area]; then, having placed the sacrificial materials such as sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) on the right side, and having placed *darbha* grass on the left side; and having arranged the vessels mentioned above in pairs, face-down, upon that [grass]; and having prepared the *pavitra* strainers and consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* water; and having touched it and empowered it three times with the root-vidyā while meditating upon it as containing all sacred fords (*tīrtha*); and having sprinkled the collection of materials and the vessels situated on the right side with that *darbha*-grass brush using the previously mentioned Brahmā-mantra; and having mentally conceived a *yogaviṣṭara* (sacrificial seat) made of *kuśa*, sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken rice in the center of either the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) or the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and having worshipped it with sandalwood paste and other offerings; and having visualized therein Vāgīśvarī, whose limbs are dark like the petal of a blue lotus, the mother of the entire world, who has bathed after her menses; and having brought the fire—either produced from a sun-crystal, from a forest fire, or from the house of a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*)—and having placed it in a purified vessel with the fire-seed mantra (*vahni-bīja*); and having discarded a small piece of charcoal as the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyād*), and having purified it with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), veiled it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*), and rendered it nectar-like with the cow-mudrā (*dhenumudrā*) using the nectar-seed mantra (*amṛta-bīja*); and having raised it and circumambulated the mound or the pit three times in a clockwise direction, and having turned it toward oneself, one should place it down with the root-mantra and kindle it.

(p. 209) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are the four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the nature of reality (dharmatā-svabhāva). Among these, Mahāmati, the imagined self-nature consists of the various appearances of objects such as form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena, which are grasped by the ignorant through names and signs; this is called the imagined self-nature. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the dependent self-nature refers to the manifestation of the mind and its mental factors arising from the habit-energies (vāsanā) of false discrimination; this is called the dependent self-nature. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the perfected self-nature refers to the state where the dependent self-nature is realized as being eternally free from the imagined self-nature; this is called the perfected self-nature. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the self-nature of the nature of reality refers to the fact that all dharmas are established according to their own characteristics and do not deviate from them; this is called the self-nature of the nature of reality. (p. 210) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three kinds of nirvana. What are the three? They are: the nirvana of the extinction of the particular and general characteristics of all dharmas, the nirvana of the non-existence of the self-nature of all dharmas, and the nirvana of the realization of the non-arising of all dharmas. Among these, Mahāmati, the nirvana of the extinction of the particular and general characteristics of all dharmas refers to the cessation of the grasping of names and signs regarding the particular and general characteristics of all dharmas; this is called the nirvana of the extinction of the particular and general characteristics of all dharmas. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the nirvana of the non-existence of the self-nature of all dharmas refers to the fact that all dharmas are devoid of a self-nature because they are empty of the imagined self-nature; this is called the nirvana of the non-existence of the self-nature of all dharmas. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the nirvana of the realization of the non-arising of all dharmas refers to the realization that all dharmas are originally unborn and unceasing, being like a dream, a mirage, or a reflection; this is called the nirvana of the realization of the non-arising of all dharmas. (p. 211) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of the Tathāgata-garbha. What are the two? They are: the Tathāgata-garbha that is the storehouse of all seeds, which is the cause of both samsara and nirvana, and the Tathāgata-garbha that is the ultimate reality, which is the realm of the Tathāgatas. Among these, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata-garbha that is the storehouse of all seeds is the basis for the manifestation of the seven consciousnesses, including the ālayavijñāna, and it is the cause of the production of all dharmas; this is called the Tathāgata-garbha that is the storehouse of all seeds. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata-garbha that is the ultimate reality is the dharmakāya of the Tathāgatas, which is the realm of the Tathāgatas, the self-realized wisdom, and the state of liberation; this is called the Tathāgata-garbha that is the ultimate reality. (p. 212) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are five kinds of bodhisattvas who have attained the stage of non-retrogression. What are the five? They are: the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the vow, the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the dharma-nature, the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the practice of the path, the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the transformation of others, and the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the spontaneous activity of the Buddha. Among these, Mahāmati, the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the vow is one who, having made a great vow at the beginning, never abandons the aspiration for enlightenment until the end of samsara; this is called the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the vow. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the dharma-nature is one who, by realizing the true nature of all dharmas, naturally abides in the stage of non-retrogression; this is called the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the dharma-nature. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the practice of the path is one who, by practicing the six perfections and the various stages of the path, attains the stage of non-retrogression; this is called the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the practice of the path. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the transformation of others is one who, by the power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, is transformed and led to abide in the stage of non-retrogression; this is called the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the transformation of others. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the spontaneous activity of the Buddha is one who, by the effortless and spontaneous activity of the Tathāgata, enters the stage of non-retrogression; this is called the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression through the power of the spontaneous activity of the Buddha. (p. 213) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three kinds of the wheel of the Dharma. What are the three? They are: the wheel of the Dharma of the four noble truths, the wheel of the Dharma of the non-self of persons, and the wheel of the Dharma of the non-self of dharmas. Among these, Mahāmati, the wheel of the Dharma of the four noble truths is the teaching given by the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; this is called the wheel of the Dharma of the four noble truths. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the wheel of the Dharma of the non-self of persons is the teaching given by the Bodhisattvas who have entered the stage of non-retrogression; this is called the wheel of the Dharma of the non-self of persons. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the wheel of the Dharma of the non-self of dharmas is the teaching given by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksambuddhas; this is called the wheel of the Dharma of the non-self of dharmas. (p. 214) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of the gate of liberation. What are the four? They are: the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, the gate of liberation of wishlessness, and the gate of liberation of the nature of reality. Among these, Mahāmati, the gate of liberation of emptiness refers to the realization that all dharmas are devoid of a self-nature and are empty like a dream or a mirage; this is called the gate of liberation of emptiness. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the gate of liberation of signlessness refers to the non-grasping of the signs of all dharmas because they are originally unborn; this is called the gate of liberation of signlessness. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the gate of liberation of wishlessness refers to the absence of desire for the arising of all dharmas because they are like a reflection or a magical illusion; this is called the gate of liberation of wishlessness. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the gate of liberation of the nature of reality refers to the direct realization of the dharmadhātu as it is; this is called the gate of liberation of the nature of reality. (p. 215) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three kinds of the body of the Tathāgata. What are the three? They are: the body born of parents,

Having offered seven oblations each for the rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the quickening of the male fetus (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), and the birth ceremony (*jātakarman*) with well-refined clarified butter while reciting the previously mentioned heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), [one should meditate upon] the Great Bull (*vṛṣabha*). This Bull has seven tongues consisting of the meters: Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī; three feet consisting of the Gārhapatya, Āhavanīya, and Dakṣiṇāgni fires; two heads consisting of the sacrificer, his wife, and the Self; four limbs consisting of the Adhvaryu, Hotṛ, Brahman, and Udgātṛ priests; a body bound by the three pressings of the day—morning, midday, and evening; five horns consisting of the Vedas, the worlds, the Ādhika, the Pañcarātra, the Pāśupata, the Buddhist, and the Jain systems; two nostrils consisting of the offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*); and four ears consisting of the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan Vedas. His form is blazing and vast, raining down the desired objects of the practitioner. From his right mouth issues Hiraṇyā (Golden), Kanakā (Gold-like), Raktā (Red), and Kṛṣṇā (Black); from his left mouth issue Suprabhā (Radiant), Atiraktā (Deep Red), and Bahurūpikā (Multiform). With four right arms he holds a spear (*śakti*), fire, a large and small sacrificial ladle (*sruk-sruva*); with three left hands he holds a javelin (*tomara*), a palm-leaf fan (*tālavṛnta*), and a golden vessel filled with clarified butter. With one leg hanging down and the other two in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), he sits upon the pericarp of a reddish lotus. He is many-formed, of a reddish hue, the Lord of Beasts (*Paśupati*), and shines in the directions of Parjanya, Agni, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, and Marut. Between the southern and northern petals, his colors are respectively golden, red, black, radiant, deep red, like refined gold, lapis lazuli, the young sun, the blue lotus, ruby, and the color of gold.

(p. 210) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna-svabhāva). Among these, the imagined self-nature consists of the various names, signs, and conceptualizations that are established by the ignorant based on the forms of objects, such as 'this is a cow,' 'this is a horse,' 'this is a man,' 'this is a tree,' and so forth. The dependent self-nature is that which arises from the causal conditions of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), being devoid of the characteristics of subject and object, and appearing like a dream or a reflection. The perfected self-nature is the state of the dependent nature when it is free from the imagined nature; it is the non-dual reality, the suchness (tathatā), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). The self-nature of the Great Vehicle refers to the fact that all phenomena are without self-nature, that they are unborn and unceasing, and that they are the realm of the Tathāgata. [The text concludes: "Therefore, Mahāmati, you should abandon the views of existence and non-existence and cultivate the insight into the non-arising of all phenomena. (p. 210)

Having meditated upon Jātavedas (Fire), who has seven tongues—namely, those of the colors previously described and the multiformed one (*bahurūpikā*)—and whose faces are turned inward, outward, and upward; having worshipped him with the services beginning with water for the guest (*arghya*) and feet (*pādya*) and ending with incense and lamps; then, having spread *darbha* grass with tips pointing eastward and northward around a single-ringed sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), or below the ring, or between two rings, or on the middle ring of a three-ringed pit; and if on a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*), having placed three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) on the outer south, north, and west sides, and having placed two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) in the southeast and northeast directions as a support, and having sprinkled [water] around; then, having offered seven oblations for each of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with the naming ceremony (*nāma-karaṇa*) and ending with marriage, using the previously mentioned *hunmantra*; then, having mentally constructed the aforementioned seat of worship (*pūjā-pīṭha*) in the center of that [fire], having invoked Ambikā there in her described form along with her retinue and worshipped her; having offered one oblation for each of the remaining attendant deities; and having offered ten oblations with the root-mantra (*mūla-vidyā*); and having thus offered oblations with the prescribed substances and in the prescribed number for the sake of the intended purpose, saying "Svāhā! O Dear One, O Power-filled One, O Perfected One!"; and having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, praised, bowed, and propitiated; immediately thereafter, one should offer the Great Utterances (*mahā-vyāhṛti*). As follows: "Bhūḥ! To Agni and to the Great One, Svāhā! and so forth, making four such offerings. Then: "Ām! Whatever has been thought by me from this point forward, through my vital breath, intellect, body, and the authority of my duties, in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, whether by intention, speech, action, hands, feet, abdomen, or genitals—whatever has been remembered, whatever has been spoken, whatever has been done—may all that become an offering to Brahman, Svāhā!"

Having offered eight oblations with the *brahmārpaṇa* mantra and having performed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should dismiss the Supreme Goddess along with her retinue, lead her to the abode of the heart, and worship oneself with perfumes and other offerings. Considering oneself to have accomplished all that was to be done, one should satisfy the Brahmins according to one’s means and dismiss the Fire-god together with his retinue. In the case of an occasional (*naimittika*) homa, one should burn the enclosing sticks (*paridhis*) and the sacrificial grass mats (*paristaras*); in the daily (*nitya*) homa, one should not burn them. Where there is a desire for specific results, one should offer oblations using the materials assigned for those purposes. The materials are as follows: jasmine, fresh *mallikā*, sprouts of green grass, and *dūrvā* blades; the *āghāra* offering of clarified butter; white mustard seeds; flowers of the enemy of Hari (the *arjuna* tree); red *karavīra* flowers; *kāsamarda*; *pauri*; *bu* [unidentified]; substances such as *viḍa*; *kiṃkarātaka*; *kuraṇḍa*; a small portion of goat meat; a small portion of elephant meat; a small portion of ram meat; the bones of Nagnajit; cotton seeds; blue lotuses, *nīlotpala*, *saugandhika*, *kalhāra*, *kaṅkelī* flowers, and *aśoka* flowers. The rest is clear.
Thus ends the tenth chapter of the Saṃpradāyadīpikā.
I worship the venerable sandals of Śrī Tejānandanātha Saṃvidāmbā.
This [work], a lamp for the tradition, has been written by the scholar Kṛṣṇānanda, the disciple of Tejānanda, by the command of Ambikā.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Puruṣottamānanda. (p. 212) Salutation to Śiva.

In the corners [of the mandala]: one should worship Brahmāṇī with Asitāṅga, Māheśī together with Ruru, Kaumārī with the one known as Caṇḍa, Vaiṣṇavī with Krodha, Vārāhī with Unmatta, Indrāṇī with Kapālin, Cāmuṇḍī with Bhīṣaṇa, and Caṇḍikā with Saṃhāra. [The mantras are: "Am, to Asitāṅga-Bhairava"; "Āṃ, obeisance to Brahmāṇī," and so forth; one should worship on the petals with these names, using the vocative case followed by the fourth case ending (dative). "Āṃ, obeisance to Brahmāṇī," etc.

"Bhairavāya," and so forth; again, [he worships] Indra and the others in the directions, and then the Vajra and the rest on the outside. Having thus worshipped the retinue with scents, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), saffron, and drops of nectar (*amṛtabindu*) upon the form of the Goddess, having performed the forty-four root-mantras, having offered incense and lamps, and having performed the *ārātrika* ceremony, he offers well-cooked rice from the *śāli* variety along with ghee, plantain, coconut, sugar, and honey as the sacrificial food (*naivedya*). Having performed the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), he scatters the offering (*bali*) with the mantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ, to all beings (*sarvabhūtebhyaḥ*) who have come once, huṃ svāhā. Having given water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) as nectar and dismissed the sacrificial food, he gives it to her with the mantra: "Aiṃ, O Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī Mātaṅgī, O you who bring all under control, svāhā. Having given betel-nut (*gaṇḍaka*) and other items, having performed the propitiatory worship (*prasannapūjā*), having performed the offering to Brahman (*brahmārpaṇa*) and the offering of the self (*ātmārpaṇa*), and having accepted the holy water (*tīrtha*), he praises and bows. Having himself become one with that [deity], he performs the limb of dissolution (*layāṅga*).

Having performed the ritual installation (*ātma-nyāsa*) and the dismissal (*udvāsana*), having performed the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) within oneself, and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) once to the Goddess both in one's own self and in the image, one should worship the conch, place it [in its stand], and recite the mantra at the appropriate time according to one's preference, preceded by the *nidhāna* and *āṅgariṣya* rites. Having performed the yogic practices, one should become identical with the Deity; may there be auspiciousness! Regarding the phrase "consisting of the supreme and the non-supreme" (*parāparamayīm*), in response to the inquiry as to what that supreme form is and what the non-supreme form of the gods is, he first states the supreme form: "The mother of sounds" (*śabdānāṃ jananī*). O Vāgādinī—one whose nature is to cause speech or the organ of speech to speak—thus is the address. Likewise, O Sarasvatī, here in this world consisting of sound and meaning, you are called by the wise the "mother of sounds. This is because you have evolved through the sequence of Parā, Paśyantī, and so forth, into the nature of the fifty phonemes, and because all sounds characterized by the Vedas and other scriptures are composed of those [phonemes]. We do not say this merely out of habit; rather, even Keśava, Vāsava, and the rest—the primary deities themselves—manifest from you at the beginning of a Kalpa, let alone others. This is certain (*dhruvam*). Since meaning is a transformation (*vivarta*) of sound, as they say: "Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is contemplated according to its power through the contraction and expansion of hundreds of words. Here, there are two types of meters (*vṛtta*): the meter of measures (*mātṛvṛtta*) and the meter of syllables (*varṇavṛtta*). Among these, where five groups (*gaṇa*) are arranged by four measures each, verses (*śloka*) are composed. *Note: The asterisks indicate a lacuna in the source text.*
